THE young fellow who has expectations finds no difficulty in sailing about on his hetrahip. BULL-DOGS are an accepted type of courage, but we have known the lowly and despised kitten come tip to the scratch. Lizzrz, did the doctor propose to you to-day?" "No, mamma; he only asked if you would live with me after I got married." WHEN a fop was trying to become the lion of a fashionable party, a wit remarked that he could ZeVer be anything but a dandy-lion. Hg-" I wash my hands of you for ever." She— " And let me suggest, George, that you also change your cuffs." "I DO love dress," exclaimed a young society "Then I should think you would wear more •of it,' replied a cynical bachelor. "I UNDERSTAND you are one of the fair graduates, Miss Pease?" "More than fair, Mr. Fleecy. I Stood 96 in all my examinations." "WHO is the author of fiction whose skill you 23205 t admire, Mrs. Marriedayear ?" Mrs. Marrieda- year (promptly)—" My husband." SMART BOY—" Do you keep all the brands of teas?" Grocer—" Yes, sir; what kind do you prefer?" Smart Boy—" Socrates or Hippocrates.' "BLonsoN—" Most women have a strange habit of talking to themselves. Does your wife do it ?" Dumsey—" Not when I'm around." A CLERGYMAN said he never knew a rogue who was not unhappy. Of course not; it is the rogues who are not known that are the happy ones.

"I HAD once a dog that was so clever he could easily distinguish rogues from honest people, but I had to give him away, for one day he bit me." "I HEAR you are going into the law, Mr. Barking. What branch do you take up. patent .or railroad?" "Breach of promise; I'm the defendant." MISS CHARITY—" Is your husband addicted to the use of alcoholic stimulants?" Recipient of alms—" No, indade, mum, not he; his only failin.' ig drinkin'." "So you have broken off with Mr. Smith ?" gab! Maud. Well, I never could make him out." "I found him quite a conundrum myself," replied Clara, "so I gave him up." SIR ROBERT PEEL, on the occasion of a minis. terial fish dinner, after he had ousted the Whigs, gave as a toast, "May we keep their plaices with, out their flounders." _ _ .

MRS. AEGONOT—" Drunk again! Oh, John, you promised me you would never touch a glass to yom lips again." Mr. Argonot—" Right, M'riar. Wasn't glass; wuzer bottle." A GENTLEMAN remarked to Judge Hoar that there was but a single lily in the floral decorations of a newly-dedicated church. "Well," said the judge, "you must remember that there was only one rose at the resurrection." PERKINS—" Well, Smith, after many _failures,

have at length struck a dead sure thing 1" Smith— "l'm glad, indeed! What are you at now 7" .Per- kins—" I'm an undertaker." BEIANDA—" And do you really think that you would be happy with me as your wife, Alphonso '' Alphonso—" Oh, yes, I'm sure. I have always been a lucky fellow in gamqs of chance." PRETTY NEAR THE TRUTH.—" Oh, mamma," exclaimed little Edith, running into the house nearly out of breath, "there's going to be a mar- riage deception over to Mrs. Uppam's this . even- ing. ), AN old lady who had several unmarried daugh- ters fed them largely on a fish diet, because, as she ingeniously observed, fish is rich in phosphorus, and phosphorus is the essential thing in making matches. WIFE—" You missed the baby greatly while we were away, didn't you 2" Husband " Yes. couldn't sleep at all for a while, till I put a saw- horse and wheelbarrow in the bed and hired a max to play an accordion in the room at nights." TEACHER—" Tommy Slimson, how is that your clothes are all torn and dirty ?" (No answer). "Look at Bobby Smitem, how tidy he looks. Stand up, Bobbie, and tell the school why yom clothes are not dirty, like Tommy Slimson's: Bobbie—" 'Cause I licked him."

RBTURNED TOURIST "You wouldn't believe half the wonderful things that I could tell you about India. Why, in some of the temples of the Brahamins they have fires that have been burning for 2,000 years." Chicago Man "Great Scott they ought to have our fire deipartment there for few minutes."—New York Truett.

STRUCK HOME.—At an evening party a lady was called upon for a song, and began, "I'll strike again my tuneful lyre." Her husband was observed tc dodge suddenly and start hurriedly from the room. muttering: "Not if I know it, she won't." "I'LL teach you to play pitch and toss 1" said an enraged father. "I'll flog you for an hour. I will!' "Father," instantly replied the incorrigible, as hE balanced a penny in his thumb and finger, " I'll too you to make it two hours or nothing." SOME people are born to ill luck. An old woman who has pasted nearly five thousand medical recipes in a book during the last forty years has not had an opportunity to use one of them, because she has never been ill a day in her life, and she is growing discouraged. JOHNNY—" Mamma, I slapped sister. Now, ain't I a good boy ?" Mamma—" No, you are a very bad boy. You ought to be ashamed to strike your little sister. Why do you think you are a good boy?' Johnny—" For telling you of it." BOSWELL told Johnson that such a thing as beggar starving to death in the streets of a Scotch city was unheard of. Johnson replied—" This does not arise from the want of beggars, but the impossi- bility of starving a Scotchman. ' "PRISONER, you are charged with beating you! wife. Don't you think you ought to be ashamed•ol yourself ?" "No, I don't. She's six inches talles nor me, an' two stun heavier. If she had the pluck of a mouse, she'd ha' licked me easy." MR. BRUCE, the traveller, was asked what musical Instruments were used in Abyssinia. He replied, with some hesitation—" I think I saw several tree there." Selwyn whispered to a friend—" Yes, and there is one less since he left the country." A YOUNG miss of sixteen asks what is the proper thing for her to do when she is serenaded by a party of gentlemen at a late hour. We should think that the proper thing for her to do would be to steal softly down stairs and untie the dog. A SMALL boy began his regular prayer in his regular way :—" Now—l—lay—me—" and then he stuck fast. "Down," said his mother, prompting. Whereupon Johnny started again with great alacrity and fluency—" Down came a blackbird and nip, off her nose." MRS. SKINNPHLINT (anxiously)—" James, I am alarmed about Johnny. He has been away all the afternoon. lam afraid he is lost." Mr. Skinnphlint —" It's more likely he has run away for good. Aria It's been only three weeks since I had that boy vaccinated. (Gloomily)—Cost me a dollar!" OMAHA lawyer (to wife on witness-stand, who had sued for a divorce)—" Didn't you know before your marriage that the man you loved had con- tracted the liquor habit?" Neglected Wife—" Yes, I knew he had contracted, I should not have com- plained; but after marriage the habit expanded terribly." SUNDAY-SCHOOL TEACHER "Now, Johnny Cams°, it is your turn. Recite your verse, please." Johnny (reciting)—" A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among thorns, and the thorns sprang up and choked him.' "Did you learn that verse out of the Bible, Johnny r "Nome. Pop taught it to me." TEACHER—" I shall have to punish you for being late to school." Tardy boy "It was Johnny Smith's fault, who lives next door. His pa Was goin' to give him a lickin', and I had to stay and bear him howl." "HALLO 1" ejaculated an anxious guardian to his lovely niece, as he entered the sitting-room and saw her in the arms of a swain who had just popped the question and sealed it with a smack, "what's the time of day now ?" "I should think it was now about half-past twelve," was the cool reply. "You see we are almost one." "BROWN and Jones are no end of chums, aint they, Smith? I never see one taking a 'drink with- out the other." "Exactly, old chappiel Booze 'um friends."

div.p: "CAPITAL CHAT."

, A story is told of the late Lord Milltown which speaks volumes for his kindness of heart. One night a very young man lost to his lordship (then " Harry " Lesson) a very large sum of money, far more than he could pay for years. Mr. Lesson for- gave him the debt on his promise never again to gamble.

A "Sir Walter Scott" Club has been formed in Glasgow. Writing in commendation of the scheme, the Duke of Argyll says :—" I have always thought that Scott ought to be quite as much honoured as Burns by his countrymen. His genius was more European, and has been recognised over the whole literary world."

Members of the House of Commons have returned to their Parliamentary duties with increased hos- tility to the Inflammable Liquids Bill. The number of notices for its rejection now amounts to the un- precedented total of fifty-two. A peculiarity of the demonstration against the Bill is that its opponents are drawn from every section of the House.

"An intimation has been conveyed to Mr. Justin McCarthy that Miehael Davitt will not be accept- able to the Government as a member of the Labour Commission. Mr. Davitt's name was submitted by the Irish leader, with the assent of his colleagues, as the Irish representative, but some one else must now be proposed."—This statement is made in the Sunday edition of the Labour World," Mr. Davitt's own paper.

In Spain says a Madrid Correspondent, the pro posed labour demonstrations of May Day are causing serious agitation among the working-classes of Cata- lonia, Biscay, Linares, and the large town generally. The Government and authorities are quietly taking precautions to meet all emergencies. Most of the Trades Unions in Spain have adhered to the proposals of the Socialists and Anafchists in the great towns for a general cessation of work on May 1.

The Sultan Abdul Ilamid at present has in his harem five wives, thirty " favourites,"each of whom is entitled to be called princess, and nearly three hundred female slaves, the whole being guarded by a staff of upwards of five thousand persons. A cer- tain number of slaves are regularly weeded out of the Imperial harem every year, and these discarded favourites are married usually to Turkish officers or civil servants, each one receiving an adequate dowry.

Lord and Lady Carlisle had a large house full for the wedding of Lady Cecilia Howard, their second daughter, to Mr. Roberts, which took place on Mon- day. Mr. Roberts is a fellow of Exeter, and was distinguished in his university career. He is going to settle as a tutor in Oxford, and he and Lady Cecilia have taken a house in the parks. Lady Carlisle has now got two professorial sons-in-law, and, as they are both Radicals, and not possessed of worldly riches, she must be a happy and satisfied mother.

Among those who speak in parables Sir Wilfrid Lawson has few equals. Explaining tha other day the confusion of many electors in the 1886 election, whPn, as he said, even some of our great captains went over to the enemy and carried all the money with them, Sir Wilfrid told the story to a farmer in his county who said—" I was against Home Rule at that election; it came upon us so suddenly. It reminded me of a man I knew. Ile took his boy to school and said to the master, 'Here's my boy; now, then, none of your A B C's or reading-made- easies ; ram the New Testament into him."

Sir Thomas Sowler, the proprietor of the "Man- chester Courier," who died on Saturday at his house in the fashionable district of Victoria-park. was son of the founder of the Conservative organ of Cottono- polls, and became proprietor of the paper on the death of his sire. A brother of his was, we believe, a barrister of reputation. Colonel Sowler derived his military title from the Volunteer movement, in which he had always taken a lively interest, the artillery being the branch to which he was especi- ally devoted. His wine cellar at his Manchester residence was so excellent as to have gained for him the rank of a connoisseur. Colonel Sowler had sent at least one of his sons to school at Harrow.

The so-called "necktie camera" does not, it ap- pears, meet with the approval of the "Societe Francais() de Photographic." M. Londe, one of the members, has reminded the Society of the embar- rasing indiscretions that have been committed by i amateurs going about n a reckless fashion with "detective cameras!: With the " photo-cravate," as Frenchmen call this. new instrument of terror, the case, it is prophesied, be much worse. When this comes into fashion it will be difficult for the most astute to avoid being occasionally caught. As, however, the lens 18 fixed conspicu- ously in the head of an unusually large scarf-pin it will, as "The Photographic News" points out, be- come advisable to avoid all persons with a cravat of that kind.

Who is to succeed Lord Granville as leader of the Liberal party in the House of Lords? The interest of the question is prospective rather than imme- diate. The importance of the matter lies in its bearing on the future. The choice of a Liberal leader must be regulated by reference to a Liberal victory at the polls and the formation of a Liberal Government. It is highly improbable that Mr. Gladstone would consent to incur for more than a very limited period the burdens of a fourth Premier- ship. It is generally admitted that Sir William Harcourt, though admittedly qualified to lead the House of • Commons, cannot form a Government. Lord Rosebery's and Mr. Morley's claims, if nothing else, would prove an insuperable difficulty. Failing the Liberal leader in the Houso of Commons, the Queen would constitutionally turn to the Liberal leader in the Lords, as she turned to Lord Granville in 1880 when Lord Hartington declined the task. Who will that Liberal leader be? Here is the in- terest of the selection which is now to be made.

Brighton, beaining beautiful under the blazing sun of the suddenly-roused spring, is still an object of tender concern to scandal hunters who know that Mrs. O'Shea is still residing there. Brighton has never had a bigger thing for gossip than the Parnell case. At this time both Capt. O'Shea and his late wife are living at Brighton. But they are as far apart as theyean get. The Captain is staying right out at the East End, where the massive family man- sions of the county sets are situated. Mrs. O'Shea is at the West End, near the scene of the most comic escapade in the case. Medina-terrace, in Brighton slang, is known as Fire Escape-terrace. The house where the episode occurred is an end one. Nothing is more gratifying to the feelings of a Brighton cabma. n than to show you how easy it was for the culprit to creep down the fire-escape at the end of the house, and to walk round to the front door as bold as brass. Since the meeting of Parliament Mr. Parnell has half lived at Brighton. To those "in the know," Mrs. O'Shea's hooded buggy has become a familar sight on the occasions of his arrival and departure from and to town. Mrs. O'Shea drives him herself in the vehicle. It is in the form of an American buggy with a hood.

THE KINDERGARTEN.
BY H. iVIIITHAM.

Carlyle wrote, "Our school hours are all the days and nights of our existence, whose lessons stream in upon us with every breath we draw." If we keep this saying in our minds, it will be well for us. We are always learning. I well remember how sur- prised I was, during a short visit I paid to Germany some years ago, to find the workmen I saw around me as skilful and as handy with their tools as those I had left at home. I learned a great deal during those few days. I learned to be less conceited as an Englishman. I found out all at once, that England was not all the world; and I found out, also, that there was a hungering atter a purely secular educa- tion such as England had no idea of. A strong, nay, I should say, the overpowering will of the people was showing itself in the effort to throw off the Church incubus which had so long held the people in its octopus-like grasp. The emigration from Europe to this country has brought about a result which, perhaps, the native American is scarcely aware of. America is to-day

MORE SOCIALISTIC THAN GERMANY, and is taking hold of. German methods for educa- ting her youth in a more determined and systematic fashion than Germany can as yet avail herself of. As Professor Bryce, M.P., writing in the "Contem- porary Review" for January, says :—" In Germany the pride of intellect has disappeared, giving place to a general unrest of socialistic agitation." This unrest is accounted for when one understands the true inwardness of Bismarckism. In America the " unrest " manifests itself by a determination to get hold of the political machine, and it hopes by getting hold of the young to make the world of the future much different from what we see it at present. No part of the European Continent, not even this America, which boasts so much, has anything like the political liberty which has been fought for and won for England by the steady persistence of her reformers. The freedom and secrecy of the polling boottican gain for the English workman whatever in reason he desires. Now is his opportunity; he must use it or he will be left behind in the intellec- tual race of the future. All education must be OR a scientific basis, and, commencing with the child just able to toddle, should have a psychological basis. I know of no more interesting or pleasurable way of spending an hour than going to the Kin- dergarten, or children's school. There are no books around, nor any stiff and formal set of rules for the little tots to be plagued with. At from two to six years of age the children are taken and prepared for entering the free schools. That is, their minds are trained. The teachers, who, of course, are all ladies, make themselves thoroughly acquainted with the various dispositions of the children. Whether they are modelling in clay, or designing patterns for weaving, all is done possible for laying the foundation for

div.head: TECHNICAL AND INDUSTRIAL EDUCATION.
div.p: TECHNICAL AND INDUSTRIAL EDUCATION.

Music is an interesting and prominent feature in these institutions, and the teacher must be able, while the children are dancing and singing their beautiful little songs, to accompany them and keep them going by the sweet tones of the piano. Of course these schools are not confined to the very poor. There are over thirty of them in San Fran- cisco alone, and there are over three thousand child- ren attending them. The schools are all supported by private contributions. Although I am sending to your Free (?) Library the reports of these schools I think it well I should quote the following from the president of the Golden Gate Kindergarten Association. Mrs. Cooper says :—" Take the very little child into the Kindergarten and there begin the work of physical, mental, and moral training. Put the child in possession of his powers ; develop his faculties; unfold his moral nature; cultivate mechanical skill in the use of the hands; give him a sense of symmetry and harmony ; a quick judgment of number, measure, and size : stimulate his inven- tive faculties ; make him familiar with the customs and usages of well-ordered lives ; teach him to be kind, courteous, helpful, and unselfish ; inspire him to love whatsoever things are true and pure, and right, and kind, and noble, and thus equipped physi- cally, mentally, and morally send him forth to a wider range of study, which should include some sort of industrial training—that is, the putting of the boy or girl into the possession of the tools for tech- nical employment or for the cultivation of the art of drawing, and kindred employments, and still further on the boy or girl shoula have a completed trade. Thus will they be prepared to solve the rugged problem of existence by earning their own living through honest, faithful work." Thus it will be seen from tl:e wise words of this good lady that if the citizer of the future is not an improvement on the citizen of the past, he will have only himself to blame. The practical founder of this system. August Froebel, a native of Thuringian Forest, saw during his conferences with teachers that the schools suffered from the state of the raw material brought into them. Till the school age was reached, the children were entirely neglected. Froebel held that each age has a completeness of its own, and that the perfection of the latest age can be attained only through the perfection of the earlier. if the infant is what he should be as an infant, and the child as a child, he will know what he should be as a boy. Every stage, then, must be cared for and tended in such a way that it may attain its own perfec- tion. Froebel describes his object as "to give the children employment in agreement with their whole nature, to strengthen their bodies, to exercise their senses, to engage their awakening mind, and through their senses to bring them acquainted with nature and their fellow-creatures." Of course, no results can, as yet, be seen of this great and good work. Ten years age none of these schools existed. As I have stated, no public money is expended upon these schools, but, as is well known,

div.head: CRIAIE IS THE COSTLIEST PRODUCT
div.p: CRIAIE IS THE COSTLIEST PRODUCT

of our civilization, and we pay more for what we desire least. I see great things in the future pro- ceeding from these efforts. The street arab will, in spite of himself, find more pleasure in the school than in the street. He will be taught to understand that as a question of policy, it nothing else, honesty pays best. The people will see that prevention of crime is possible, while thereclaiming of a hardened criminal is impossible. More than this, it will throw considerable light on the question which is trou- bling hundreds of philanthropic souls to-day, viz., how to prevent the growth of "back slums." I look upon General .Booth's. scheme as simply a for- lorn hope; nay, as impossible of giving satisfaction to any one. " Stop the supplies;" until you do this your back slums will grow and grow. Get hold of the children in schools such as I have faintly described. Don't let the various theological quacks muddle their young minds, but give them an educa- tion which will enable them to judge for them- selves. Through the children it is a certainty you will get hold of the parents, and so the work will be done. . 810, Bay-st., San Francisco.
THE LYNCHING AT NEW ORLEANS.

Owing to the great moderation of the demands of the Italian Cabinet, the controversy with the United States has entered upon a quiet phase, and all dangers of com- plications have been avoided. Even the Opposition papers in Rome are full of praise for the remarkable tact shown by the Marchese di Rudini in the matter. . _ _ _

- A depot and store at Constitution have been blown up with dynamite, and this outrage is also thought to be due to the Italian desire for vengeance. In an interview with a Pressrepresentative, the detec- tive O'Malley, who is charged with bribing the jury in the Hennessy murder trial, denied that he was guilty. He declared that the man who were lynched were inno- cent, and that the people made a great mistake, for which-they should apologise to the widows and orphans of the victims. The committee leaders have held a con- ference at which it was decided that O'Malley should not be molested, and that the law, in his case, should be al- lowed to take its course.

It is stated at St. Joseph, Missouri, that Doctor Leach, an American citizen of that place, is being kept a pri- soner in Italy by order of the Government. The attorney and his assistants who planned and carried out the lynching of the prisoners at New Orleans have given evidence before the Grand Jury. A list of the Committee "who planned the lynching" was pro- duced. There is some talk of a " test " case being laid before a criminal court. The Grand Duke Michael, first cousin to the Czar, having contracted a secret marriage with a German lady, has been struck off the roll of the Russian army, and thereby deprived of several lucrative commands.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 11, 1891. OTES ON THE SHIP CANAL.' PERCIVAL GORDON; THE CHILD OFOR'REE REGIMENT. BY SYLVANUS COBB.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 11, 1891. OTES ON THE SHIP CANAL.' PERCIVAL GORDON; THE CHILD OFOR'REE REGIMENT. BY SYLVANUS COBB.

BY its "The ancient village of Theiwall has seen a full share of the changes which have been wrought by the Ship Canal Works. The " cyty " founded by Bing Edward the Elder in the year 920 and called Thel wall, was originally famous for its river fisheries, which were in fact at one time of so much value as to make it worth the while of no less a personage than the " good " Duke of Lancaster—otherwise known as" Wryneck "—to put in a claim for their possession in the reign of Edward 111 It is a long time since Thelwall, along with other places on the Mersey, lost its fisheries, owing to causes which are too well known to need recapitulation. Now, it has not only lost its fisheries, but through the making of the Ship Canal it has been cut off from tke river , itself. Until about a couple of years ago, the Mersey at Thelwall took one of its most sinuous curves, but now it has been diverted into a straight channel cut across the base of the curve; and between the village and the river the Ship Canal takes its course. Formerly there was a ferry by which a person might pass from Thelwall to the other side of the river, and it is satisfactory to know that this convenience is not to be abolished, only in future the traveller will have to be ferried across the Ship Canal and then pass over the diverted river channel by a bridge. This, however, is with regard to the future; up to the present the changes have all been to the advan- tage of the traveller, who can, by means of bridges, pass on foot from Cheshire into Lancashire. About twelve or eighteen months ago the section near Thelwall was one of the busiest parts of the Ship Canal, but an abrupt termination was put to all work of a progressive character by the unfortunate inundations of the winter. Since then a great deal of energy has been concentrated on the work of pumping out of the canal cutting into the river. On the canal, directly opposite the village of Thel- wall, there has been erected a fine and effective piece of mechanism, in the shape of a steam pump, which, it is saisl, was equal, when working to the height of its power, to pumping water at the rate of 32,000 gallons a minute. The constant stream of water which rushed impetuously down the conduit leading from the canal to the river into which it fell cataract-like, was an ocular demonstration of the power of the pump, as was also the rapid rate at which the water sank in the canal whilst it was at work.
CHAPTER VI. PERCIVAL'S MISSION.

_ It was toe first undisturbed, refreshing sleep that Percival had enjoyed since the night before the battle of Talavera. He had lain himself down with no thought of when he should awake, for he believed himself entirely safe in his comfortable eyrie, and his conscience was clear. The brigands were within his ken, and they could make no movement without his knowledge. So he slept soundly. It was the sound of human voices that finally awoke him, and when he opened his eyes and looked around he concluded that he had slept well. The sun, he thought, was just setting: but when he had arisen and stretched himself, and felt how particularly fresh and balmy the air was, and how bright were the dewdrops upon the stunted foliage, he was moved to look at the sun again. As he faced the mountain peak the grand luminary was upon his right hand—to the eastward. It was rising I At first he could not credit the evidence of his own senses; but, consider as he would, the sun persisted in rising, instead of setting. He had slept more than fifteen hours, and he had received the benefit. A gentle wind from the west had been broken by the boulder close under which he lay, so that scarcely a drop of dew had fallen upon his clothing. And this westerly breeze served to waft the voices that had awakened him quite distinctly to his ear. The brigands, to the number of thirty or more, with their chieftain in their midst, had gathered upon the broad plateau, and were evidently dis- cussing a question of more than passing interest. Hearing sufficient to convince him that they were consulting with regard to their prisoners, he cast his eyes around to see if there was not, within his reach, a more favourable spot for hearing. He discovered it a few rods distant—a point of rock higher than the spot he now occupied, nearer to the station of the brigands, and to be reached without difficulty or danger, the path thither being flanked by a low hedge of bushes. Arrived at the place, he sat down and bent his ear attentively; and he was not a moment too soon.

"Then we are agreed," he heard Don Lopez say, "that his ransom shall be the same as the other 1" Whereto there was a general assent. "And his companions shall be set at one thousand crowns each V said the chief; and another assent followed. _ _ _
"The same as the other," Percival repeated to himself. What did that mean? Who was "the other 7" Ah—hark _ _

"Perhaps," suggested one who appeared to be a subaltern of the troop, "the English lord will pay the ransom for Sir Richard, in case his friends do not help him." "I have thought of that," returned the chief, "and I shall present the case to his lordship. He appears to be a generous-hearted man, and I do not believe he will see a countryman—and a baronet, at that—put to death, when fifty thous- sand crowns will save him."

"Aye," put in another, "and Sir Richard may be considered sure to pay as soon as he gets home. Ho! I can fancy the chagrin of the cold-blooded brother when he finds the owner of the title in his own land."

Our hero understood the Spanish language so well that he did not lose a word of this conversa- tion; and when the conference finally came to an end, and the brigands turned to answer the call of a woman to breakfast, he was thoroughly enlightened. The ransom of Col. Maxwell had been fixed at fifty thousand English crowns, while the ransoms of the sergeants and the driver had been fixed at one thousand. Further—there was in the cavern, also a prisoner, another Englishman, a baronet— Sir Richard—somebody—whose ransom was the same as Maxwell's, and which they hoped the latter would pay, because the friends of the unfortunate man neglected to respond in his behalf. Could it be possible that the significant hint of the last speaker had foundation in fact? Could there be a brother in England so wickedly and treacherously cruel? Hark A knot of the freebooters had remained behind for the purpose of discussing a point that had not been touched upon. The question was, Should a certain companion of the English baronet be suffered to go without a price? A few more words gave him to understand that they spoke of Sir Richard's child—a daughter. "1 don't care for the nurse," said one, "but the little lady ought to pay." "Hush !" interposed another. "Our law is— ' All children over six yea's of age shall be put to ransom.' This girl is not over six. She has not seen her seventh year. If the stout lord will pay full ransom for the father, do not let us make trouble about the little one." And with this the party went in to their breakfast, the fumes of which the listener fancied he could small.

The boy's feelings were wrought up to a pitch of wondrous excitement. Here was a girl of his own age, and he pictured her, of course, as beautiful and seraph-like. 0, if he could set her free ! No knight-errant of the age of chivalry ever felt his heart bound with deeper or firmer resolve to do his knighly devoir in behalf of lady fair than was Percival's to feel in that hour.

But, by and bye, when the opposite plateau had been for some time deserted, the boy began to realize, with a sharp reminder, that he was hungry. He went back to the place where he had slept, and gathered a quantity of wax-berries. They were not wholly ripe, but their taste was far from dis- agreeable, and he knew them to be safe and nutritious. They were white, about the size of a pea, and were more spicy and pleasant to the palate than they would have been dead ripe. He ate as many as his appetite craved, and then zathered a lot and put them into his peel:et. And now, what more should he wait for there g He was well assured that the brigands planned to keep their prisoners in that cavern until their ransoms should arrive. He knew the exact location, and he knew the path, and, after considering the matter in all its bearings, he resolved to retrace his steps, and descend the mountains; and he set forth with strong, firm steps. He found the sentinels—three of them,—posted exactly where they had been on the previous day, and he had no difficulty in avoiding them. Further- more, he took careful surveys, so as to know exactly where to look for them should he have occasion again to travel that same way. That their beats were fixed, with no liability of the sentinels being posted at different points at different times, he was assured, because at each of the three points was erected a sentry-box, or convenient shelter, to ' which the lookout could betake himself for shelter in time of storm and tempest. Upon reaching the highway the boy moved with extreme caution. He discovered, after a little search, that the bandits had pulled the ambulance away out of sight, but they were nowhere to be seen. Very likely they had joined their com- panions in the mountain cavern. Nevertheless, until he had got well away from the place of the attack, he kept himself under cover as much as possible, moving on by the road over which the English army had moved on the morning of the previous day. Having thus picked his way, in the shadow of hedge and wildwood, for the distance of a mile, or more, he thought it safe to take boldly to the highway, which he did. Certainly the little adventurer had reason for gratitude in view of the good fortune that fell to his lot in this season of disaster and trial. He had been on the road not more than an hour when he came to a hut by the wayside, before the door of which were two or three children, playing in the dirt, while to a post in the yard was hitched a stout, good-looking horse, belonging evidently to the English cavalry, with the saddle, bridle, and housing of the —th Hussars. Percival's belief, as soon as he distinguished the trappings, was, that the animal had strayed, and that the people of the hut had found it; and upon that proposition he resolved to act. " .Bendito Dios!" he cried, as he met a clownish- looking fellow—blacked like a charcoal-burner,— coming around the far corner of the miserable "1 have found my horse at length, and shall save myself a severe reckoning. Where did you find him ?" " Ho ! the brute found me, I should say; and a pretty mess he has made of it. One half my tender cabbages he eat clean up, besides the mischief he did in ploughing his iron hoofs into my new-made garden." "Look you, my friend," said Percival, pleasantly and persuasively, "had my colonel known, or even thought, that the horse had done damage to a worthy man, he would have furnished me with the means of remuneration; but he did not dream of such a thing. However, I have a bit of silver, to which you are welcome if it will satisfy you. Ho —ho,—my sergeant will laugh when be sees my horse." And in his chuckling, as he drew forth his purse, he gave thp impression that said sergeant, with several companions, was not far away.

..-.lle made out little more than a dollar, with which the poor man was entirely satisfied; and the more especially so, as the boy brought from another pocket a pistareen, which he offered for a good meal, and a bit of bread and cheese to carry in his haversack. This last piece of silver the host turned over to his wife, who very quickly set before the young guest a big pan of milk, together with a loaf of very good bread; and while he eat, the charcoal-burner told him that he had found the horse in his garden when he arose that morning, and that he had come from the westward; and he went on to declare that, had the animal belonged to the French, he would have shot him through the head before he would have restored him. But he liked the English; and he knew that the horse was English, not only from the ornamentation of the saddle-cloth, but he had seen the whole English army pass his place on the previous day.

It was a little after noon when Percival climbed into the saddle, and he judged that the rear-guard of the army was a good twelve hours' march ahead of him. He thanked the honest cotter and his wife for their kindness—for kind they had certainly been—and then rode away. He found his horse strong and eager, and he was greatly puzzled to understand how so fresh and valuable an animal, where there were hundreds well-nigh worthless, oould have been suffered to wander away. How- ever, the mystery was soon to be solved.

He had been in the saddle perhaps an hour, speeding along at a round pace, when his horse suddenly gave a sharp snort, and shied to the left, coming very near to throwing him from his seat. Upon reining the animal back into the road, he looked to see what had caused the animal's fright, and discovered an English soldier—a hussar—lying beneath some bushes close by the side of the road. He dismounted, keeping the rein in his hand, and found the man dead, a man whom he at once recog- nised as a corporal of Maxwell's regiment, lately attached to the commissariat. He had probably fallen out from the column overcome by sickness, his comrade& never thinking that he would not overtake them. The horse must have remained with him a considerable time, or he would have followed the army instead of turning back to the cotter's garden. There was a plain gold ring upon the dead man's finger, which Percival removed, hoping that, in time to come, he might restore it to a friend or relative who would prize it. There was also silver in one of the pockets to the amount of very nearly two dollars. This might prove a saving power in his possession, and he took it; also the sword, and a small silver-mounted pistol, which was loaded and primed. Then the boy laid his hand reverently upon the brow of the dead, and breathed a fervent prayer—he could do no more—after whioh he remounted, and sped on his way. Towards nightfall he came to a mountain brooklet, the water of which was clear and cold, while the grass that grew around was green and luxuriant. Here he stopped, and allowed his horse to rest and feed, while he made a hearty meal from the bread and cheese he had taken from the cotter's wife.

_ At the end of an hour—he knew it would be an hour well spent in recruiting .the strength of his horse—he pushed on again; and little more than an hour after night had fallen he reached a small village, where there was an inn and a small pretty church. At the inn his English uniform commanded respect, and he allowed the host to believe that be was a courier on special service. There he learned that the rear of the English Army had left the place not more than an hour before noon, intending to halt for the night at Torrameda, a considerable town fourteen miles distant.

Our hero considered the situation critically. I know it will appear strange that one so young should be so mentally strong and effective; but remember, in the first place, the boy was by nature wonderfully precocious; and then, from the day of the dawning of his understanding, his lot had been cast amid scenes that had tended to sharpen his wit and develop his intellect. He was, in fact, a marvel to all who knew him; and very few, who did not know the fact, could be led to believe that he was not beyond his seventh year. He considered the situation in all its bearings, and finally resolved that he would take lodging for the night at the inn. His horse should be well fed, and by setting forth at daybreak he would come up with his hussars before they had broken camp. His horse would be fresh and strong, and he could speed him without fear of his failing. He left word with the host that he should be called, if he did not awake of his own accord, and he paid his reckoning before he retired. He was not called, however, as he was awake a full hour before daybreak. He eat his breakfast, and was in the saddle just as the first flush of dawn appeared in the east, and by half-past five o'clock he rode into the town of Torrameda, where he found Maxwell's troop, sad and sorrowful, at their breakfast.

We will not attempt to describe the me( ting. Percival m (de his way first to the quarters of the geld officers, and when they saw him they were like men possessed. His story was quickly told. Had any other boy in the world told such a story those battle-scarred warriors would have given him credit for wonderful powers of romantic invention for one of his tender years; but to him they listened as they would have listened to a chief ot division, and when he had concluded they knew that they had listened to the simple truth, the only thing lacking being the narrator's failure to give himself due credit. However they could readily supply all that.

The officer in command of the regiment in the absence of Maxwell was Lieut.-Colonel Arthur St. Vincent, a florid, healthful, true-hearted man, and a brave and gallant soldier, of middle sge, slightly inclined to corpulency; but he was lithe and active, for all that, and possessed marvellous powers of endurance. _
"Are you sure," he said to the little hero, after he had asked numerous questions, which had been promptly answered, "that you can lead us to the mouth of that cavern without the sound of an alarm?"

"It ought to be done, sir," the lad replied, unhesitatingly. "I am very sure that I can point out the stations of the sentinels; and, further, that I can guide two or three of our men so that they can be taken by surprise." "Do you feel able to take to the saddle again and ride with me to the quarters of our commander- in-chief ? "

"Certainly, sir. I have only ridden fourteen miles this morning." St. Vincent ordered his groom to make ready two of the best horses as quickly as possible, and when they had been brought to the door he and Percival mounted and sped away. Sir Arthur Wellesley was found two miles dis- tant, just up from his breakfast, and as soon as he had been informed of the presence of Col. St. Vincent and the boy corporal, he ordered that they should be admitted. He listened to the saying of St. Vincent, and then to the briefly told story of the boy. His first movement, when he had heard, was to lay his hand upon Percival's head and bless him for a true hero. Then he arose and took one or two turns across the room. He never gave an important decision upon impulse. Finally he resumed his seat, and addressed the officer,

"Colonel St. Vincent, I will not hamper you in any way. It is your desire to lead the force for the relief of your chief. You may turn over your command to your major, and proceed at once upon the expedition. Take as many men as you wish. I would suggest a full squadron of two hundred. With regard to rejoining the main army, you will consult your own convenience. I shall proceed direct to Montalvao, where I plan to make a lengthened stop for the help of our sick, and thence to Lisbon. So you will know how to find me. Take your pick of horses, and call upon the commissariat for what you want. Heaven send success !"
During the forenoon of the fifth day of his cap- tivity Maxwell was waited upon by the brigand chief, who wished to know if the letter had been written.

"It is all ready, sir," the colonel replied. "And," he added, as he drew the missive forth and opened it, "I trust it will suit you. I will tran- slate it if you wish." But Don Lopez said he could read it with sufficient accuracy, and he took it and ran his eyes over a closely written page. For a little time he seemed entirely satisfied, and even pleased; but at length his brow darkened, and he uttered an oath.

"That will not do! I would not let that go on any account. See: You write, Up the mountain ;1 and here you speak of the grandest cavern I ;,ver saw.' And do you observe, the reader of that letter would know where you were captured, and from that spot, once found, he could not fail te locate our cavArn. No, no, you must do better than this. Look: Write to here—to this point— and then leave out the cavern entirely. Leave out everything, only that you are in a prison from which there is no possible escape. -Will you do it in that manner 2"
Maxwell seem_ed_ both_ suprised and sorry. _fic

could see, now that his attention had bee; calico to it, where the trouble was. Certainly h would try again; and he had no doubt of success in the second essay. The chieftain was anxious. "My lord," he said, with emphasis, "you must write the letter so that I can send it off to-morrow. Let me hope there may be no mistake this time. I plan to go to Talavera on the morrow, and thence I can forward the missive safety and surely. I wish to see what the French are doing. A division of their army marched in yesterday, a courier informed me, who arrived an hour ago. You will not disappoint me ?" "To-morrow morning," said the colonel, "you shall have the letter, and I think I may promise that it shall entirely satisfy yeti." The brigand, though evidently eager to have the letter in hand that evening, did not press the matter further, and. shortly thEreafter he withdrew, remarking as he went that Sir Richard would probably spend a portion of the remainder of the day with him. On that evenivg both the baronet and his daughter took tea in Maxwell's apartment. The three sergeants and Wilson were served at another table at their own request. At ten o'clock Sir Richard proposed to retire. "If you sleep at all," whispered Maxwell, "be sure sleep lightly." "My dear Maxwell, is it possible you hold such unbounded confidence in that bit of a boy--a boy only a few weeks older than this cherub of mine ? "You would do so, Archer, if you knew him. I have considered the matter critically, and I have given him until this very night to reach us; sir, he will come if he is alive and at liberty. Please seek your pillow with that assurance." The baronet smiled, and said he would try to have faith. At all events, he would be prepared, and would see that his nurse was not behind.

Left alone, Maxwell called his comrades to a brief consultation. Both O'Grady and Dunbar had improved wonderfully since they had been in the cavern. One of the Spanish women was a gypsy medicine woman of wide renown, whose special gift was the cure of wounds, and she had brought them up so rapidly that they could walk quite comfortably. Toni Crawford was almost as well as ever.

_ "If I am not mistaken," said the colonel, after he qad expressed his firm belief that their little hero would show his hand before the dawning of another day, "the stars are shining bright and clear to-night, and there is no moon; so a man might pick his way up the mountain without being discovered at a distance." Tom nodded assent. He was as confident as VISE his chief. _ _ _

At midnight the captive hussars sought their beds, but they did not undress. An hour later they were upon their feet. There had been an alarm towards the entrance to the cavern. The voice of Don Lopez was heard calling his men to arms, and anon the sharp clash of swords rang through the mountain chambers miLgled with the report of pistols. (To be continued).

div.head: LATCHFORD LOCKS.
div.p: LATCHFORD LOCKS.

If work, apart from pumping operations, is slack near Thelwall, no imputation of this kind can be made with regard to Latchford locks, which lie a short distance westwards. Looking down the steep sides of the canal here one sees a veritable busy line of industry. There are many kinds of artificers at work, but all their various labours are directed to one end—the completion of the gigantic lock gates which will here be put sn situ. Away at the western end of the locks is another busy scene, but of a different sort, for, in cyder to contemplate it, instead of looking down into the "abysm "—that is rather too tragic a word for the occasion, but it will do-- of the locks, we have to look up to the "giddy heights" of the new bridge which will carry the Warrington and Altrincham railway over the canal. This bridge, we anticipate, will, after it is completed, be one of the local wonders to which Warringtonians will take the friends who come to visit them from a distance. As bridges go in this locality, it will be a giant amongst pigmies, though to the workmen engaged upon it, it may seem only a" wee bit of a thing" for many of them are veter- ans of the Forth bridge, and for a long time past have been accustomed to gaze upon the stupendous spans of that unrivalled structure. Messrs. Tan- cred, Arroil, and Company of Glasgow, who secured the contract of this railway bridge, as they did that for the Forth Bridge, seem to be pushing the work forward in a business-like way, as might be ex- pected from a firm which has at command so much of the highest type of manual skill, and the most modern of mechanical appliances.

div.head: SWING BRIDGE AND HIGH LEVEL BRIDGE.
div.p: SWING BRIDGE AND HIGH LEVEL BRIDGE.

Going towards Latchford Station we find that pre- parations are being made for laying the foundations of the swing bridge that is to continue Knutsford- road over the canal. The foundations of this bridge on the north side of the canal will be of the natural sandstone rock, which is very thick and solid at this point, and it seems to be pretty much the same on the other si(ie of the canal, though it is not yet so deeply cut into. At the west side of Latchford sta- tion,that is,between Grappenhall-rd. and Wash-lane, the excavations have been made for the foundations of the at one time much-debated high level bridge. The foundations go down to a considerable depth and are being laid in concrete. The great argument for this high level bridge was, it will be remembered, that it would be available at all times for crossing the canal, and especially when the swing bridges were open to allow of the passage of vessels. The bridge will be made wide enough for vehicles to pass over, and will also provide a means of access to the new Latchford railway station which will be placed at the top of an embankment. It will have approaches, with rather steep gradients from both, Wash-lane and Grappenh all.

div.head: NEW ROADS.
div.p: NEW ROADS.

No one can go over the Ship Canal in the neigh- bourhood of Warrington without taking note of the new roads that have been made along the south bank. Commencing at Morris Brook farmhouse there is a sttetch which reaches to the railway crossing at Cross-lane; and then from the other side of the crossing there is another stretch to Latchford Station. Here there is a break of only about one hundred or two hundred yards, which, however, is sufficient to necessitate a troublesome detour to get into Common-lane, but, once in the latter roadway, the pedestrian finds a new highway which runs right through, parallel with the canal, to Stockton Heath. The latter and greater part uf this road, that from Wash-lane to Stockton Heath, may be described as an "after-thought," for it was not in the original project, but was the result of one of the comparatively recent variations on the first plan. But, however that may be, the roadway is now almost an "accomplished fact" for much progress has already been made with the making of it.

div.head: ALLEGED WIFE AfURDER AT GLASGOW.
div.p: ALLEGED WIFE AfURDER AT GLASGOW.

Late on Saturday night James Japp, a labourer, went to his lodgings at 79, Elderslie-st., Glasgow, and quarrelled with his wife, Isabella Glen, sr Japp. He afterwards left the house in a great passion, and when he had gone the woman informed her landlady that Japp had kicked her in in the abdomen. She was bleeding profusely, and expired before medical aid could be pro- cured. Japp was afterwards apprehended.

div.head: CATASTROPHE AT AIANIPUR.
div.p: THE CATASTROPHE AT AIANIPUR.
CAPTURE OF A FORT.

The news has reached the Government that Lieutenant Grant advancing from Tarnmu with his 80 men of the 12th Burmah Regiment, captured a fort which is within about ten miles of Manipur (probably Fort Thabal), on March 31, a full week after the capture of the British Residency at Manipur. This fort was held by a garri- son of 800 Manipuris, and was carried by assault by the small British force.

Later accounts received by the Government state that Lieutenant Grant and his 80 men were surrounded at Waitank by the enemy on the 30th ult., and that a mes- senger who was despatched from Tammu, to warn him not to proceed, was unable to reach him in time. On the 31st ult. Lieutenant Grant captured the fort of Thabal, situated eleven miles south of Manipur. Later despatches, however, report this officer to be now con- fronted by a larger force of Manipuris with guns, and it is feared that unless reinforcements speedily reach him, the small detachment under his command may be anni- hilated. _ _ _ _

Captain Presgrave, who left Aukstaung• with 150 men of the 12th Burmah Regiment and some Mounted Infan- try to reinforce Tammu, has moved forward thence to Lieutenant Grant's relief with 100 Rifles and a mounted detachment. _ _ .

Reports have been brought to Tammu by native tra- vellers from Manipur that Mr. Quinton and his party were killed on the day of the outbreak at that place. These rumours' however, are regarded as merely a repe- tition of the alarmist news which was circulated in the first instance.

A Simla telegram of Wednesday says that no doubt now exists as to the massacre by the Senaputty at Mani- pur of Mr. Quinton and the other British civilians who were recently captured after the defeat of the Ghoorkas. A "Times" second edition telegram from Calcutta on Thursday confirms the reported massacre of Mr. Quinton and his party. DEFEAT OF THE ENEMY WITH HEAVY LOSS. THREE CHIEFS KILLED. _ -

A Reuters telegram received on Thursday afternoon states that the Manipuris have attacked Lieutenant Grant's force at Thobal, and after three hours' fighting were driven back with heavy loss, Sennaputty and two chiefs, whose names are not known, being among the killed. Captain Presgrave has relieved Lieutenant Grant. The Manipur villagers declare that they are ready to recognise British rule the moment the British enter Manipur.

div.head: NOBODY WANTS THAT GOLD RING,
div.p: NOBODY WANTS THAT GOLD RING,

For nearly 100 years a certain family of working people living in Paris have ended their lives by suicide. From father to son, from mother to daughter, has des- cended a plain gold ring, and on the finger of every one• of these suicides, as they lay in death, this ring has been found. Only last year the body of a young man who had killed himself was brought to the Morgue, and on his finger was the fatal golden circlet. He was the last of his race. The ring was buried with the corpse, from which no one acquainted with its history will have the • courage to remove it. The mental taint in this family came from some re- mote ancestor, and was intensified by their recognition of it until it became a controlling force: and the ring was accepted as imposing upon its possessor the obliga- tion to committee suicide, after the example of the per- son who last wore it. This form of mania usually orig- inates in a disorder of the nervous system, which in its turn arises from anzemia, or poverty of the blood, one of the results of imperfect nutrition. A recent letter from a gentlemen living in Norfolk contains the followingi assertion : "I longed for death; I was afraid of the night; I was afraid to be alone, yet I hated society. I was afraid that in some one of those hours of deep gloom. and depression I should lift my hand against my own life, for I knew that many had done so from the the same cause." The dark blurs became a time of terror to him, so he says. He tossed and tumbled on his head, wondering if morning would ever dawn again. In this case it was not an accusing conscience, as he had committed no offence; the cause was purely a physical one—yet all to common in England—indigestion and dyspepsia, with the long chain of consequences dragging after it, nervous collapse among them. He relates that his skin and eyes had been more or less discoloured for years, often of a ghastly and repulsive yellow. This was due t) the presence of bile in the blood and tissues, where it had no business to be. But as the weak and torpid liver could not remove it, no other result was possible than the one our friend experienced. His head frequently ached as though fiends had turned it into a workshop, and pains chased one another through his body as though he had at least i half the maladies catalogued in the popular books on disease.

Yet one thing, and one only, was responsible for all the mischief, namely, the poison introduced into the blood from the decaying food in the stomach and intes- tines. The cold feet, the loss of appetite and ambition, the mental despondency, the sense of weariness and fatigue, the bad taste in the mouth, dry cough, giddiness, palpitation, chills, weakness, &c., are a broad of foul birds hatched in one nest, and the mother is always indi- gestion and dyspepsia. Time passed somehow, as it always does, whether we laugh or cry, and this man grew heartily tired of a life thus burdened and spoiled. He longed to see the end oF it, and no wonder. But the last page of his letter is pitched in a higher key. He says, " When I think of what I was, and what I am now, I can hardly realise the change. For the past six months I have been using a preparation known as Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup, and it has actually revolutionised my whole system. Ono of my tenants recommended it to me, and I tried it just to please him. Now I praise it for myself, and thank the men who make and advertise it. My troubles are over, and I feel (at 57) as light, elastic, and gay as a boy on his summer vacation. I tell my doctors they are beaten at their own trade by an old German nurse, and so far as lam concerned they can't deny it. I have no more hor- rible thoughts of self-destruction, for I find too much en- joyment in living. My thanks are too deep for words." The author of this letter consents to the publication of so much of it as is here printed, but declines to allow the use of his name, at least for the present, for reasons we are bound to respect. But the evident sincerity of his story will carry conviction to every candid mind.

div.head: FUNERAL OF LORD GRANVILLE.
div.p: FUNERAL OF LORD GRANVILLE.

At Stone there was an impressive scene at the funeral of Earl Granville on Saturday. The body was conveyed in the special section attached to the nine o'clock train from Euston, by which relatives, former colleagues, and friends of the late statesman travelled, the mourners including the Earl of Rosebery, Earl Spencer, and Mr. John Morley. At St. Michael's Church, Stone, the ser- vice was conducted by the Bishop of Shrewsbury and the Bishop of Lichfield. In speaking of the manifestations of sorrow everywhere observable, our correspondent says that 4oHe was visibly and literally a town of mourning. A full choral memorial service was held simultaneously at the Chapel Royal, St. James's, at which as many peers, members of Parliament, and foreign representatives as the edifice would hold, attended. Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone came up specially from St. Leonards to be present.

Mr. Wilson, secretary of the Seamen's and Firemen's Union, was sentenced to six weeks' imprisonment with- out hard labour, at Cardiff, on Tuesday, for unlawful assembly and riot during the recent strike. div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.--MoNney.

The House of Commons re-assembled after the Easter 'recess, the Speaker taking the chair shortly after three • o'clock. There was a very small attendance of mem- bers, about twenty being present at prayers. QUESTIONS.—OnIy four questions had been put down •on the paper. The ArronNET-GENERAL, replying to Mr. 0. V. Morgan, said that, except in regard to occasional licences, the licensing magistrates had no power in the regulation of hours, these being fixed by Act of Parlia- ment. Mr. Sum', asked by Mr. Howell whether the Government had refused Mr. Davitt's nomination as a member of the Labour Cemmission, said he hoped to be able to give the whole of the names in the course of the week. Mr. SMITH also stated that the House would go into committee on the Irish Land Bill on Thursday. Sir 'JAMES FREW:M.4ON explained to Sir George Campbell the causes which rendered the Manipur expedition necessary, and added that adequate measures would be taken to restore order. Mr. SMITH informed Mr. Morton that no communication had been received from the French Government, re the purchase of the Newfound- land Treaty rights, in reference to British occupation in 'Amt. SUPPLY.—The House went inte Committee of Supply on the Civil Service Estimates, and reductions moved by Ur. Labouchere on the votes for Royal palaces and Marl- borough House were negatived. HOUSE OF COMMONS—TUESDAY.
The Speaker took the chair at five minutes past two o'clock.

MISCELLANEOUS.—The London and North-Western (Ad- ditional Powers) Bill was read a second time, an amend- ment by Sir J. Swinburn finding no seconder. A new writ was ordered for Woodstock, in room of Mr. F. W. Maclean, who has accepted a Mastership in Lunacy. Mr. S. Smith gave notice of a resolution regarding the cur- rency. Mr. Raikes informed Mr. Watt that a scheme for compensating owners of lost or damaged parcels which had been registered will probably come into operation on June Ist. Mr. Brookfield brought in a bill for the holding of fire inquests. The Savings Bank Bill as amended was read a third time, an amendment by Mr. Howell to increase the annual and total limits of deposits to £6O and £4OO respectively being rejected. The Army Schools bill went through Committee, and the merchan- dise Marks Bill was read a third time. At the evening sitting, Mr. W. H. James not being present to move his amendment on the Rating of Machinery Bill, it was read a second time amid great cheering. UNEXPECTED AuJousionwr.—The other orders of the day were rapidly run through and postponed, and the House; amidst laughter, adjourned at five minutes past nine o'clock.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.-WEDIiESDAY,
The Speaker took the chair at a quarter-past twelve o'clock. At that hour there were only three members present, and even at half-past twelve o'clock only sixteen were actually in the house.

Tits HARES BILL. - Colonel DAWNAY moved the second reading of the Hares Bill, expliiining that its object was to enable a close time to be fixed for hares, which worp in danger of becoming ex- tinct. Mr. BencLey moved and Mr. Coss seconded an amendment that the bill be read a second time that _day six months. Mr. HERIdON HODGE spoke in favour of the bill, which Sir William Harcourt strongly opposed, en the ground that it was an extension of the Game Laws, 'Which he regarded as a great evil. Sir Henry James James defended the bill, which was read a second time by a majority of 61. _

DISSENTERS' MARRIAGES.-MT. CONTBEARE moved the second reading of the Religious Equality Bill, the object of which is to permit the registrar's presence at marriages in Dissenting churches to be dispensed with, and also to .Procure concessions in regard to Nonconformist burials. Air. TALBOT moved that the bill be reid a second time That day six months, remarking that if hon. members Wished to promote religious equality they must go to the root of the matter and begin with disostablishment.—Mr. OssonNE MORGAN urged the need of further amending the Burials Act in favour of Nonconformists, and after further discussion the debate was adjourned. OTHER BiLis.—The Electoral Disabilities Removal and Army Schools Bills were read a third time and passed. Several bills were introduced.

THZ ATTACH BY CHINS ON A BRITISH DETACHMENT.— Sir JAMES FERGIISSON, in reply to Dr. Farquharson, said: --I am able to state that a telegram has been received from the Viceroy of India, dated the 6th inst., to this effect :—" Reported from Chin country that detachment horn 39th Bengal Infantry. under Lieutenant Mocatta, detailed from Hatea, was attacked 4th April, while re- turning towards Hatea, by a large gathering of Chins of the Klanglang tribe. The detachment continued the March fighting till met by .a force from Haka of the same regiment, under Mainwarmg. Lieut. Forbes wounded Severely in arm, five men killed, twelve wounded. This disturbance is believed to be local, unconnected with events on the Manipur side. Steps will be taken to punish offending tribes." The house adjourned at a quarter to six o'clock. ROUSE OF COMMONS.—THURSDAY.

LANCASHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL BILL.—The Lancashire County Council Bill came up as an unopposed Bill, and being unopposed, was read a third time and passed. QIIESTIONS.—Questions were asked about the alleged •• failure to supply Welsh census schedules at Tryddvn, in Flintshire, the Gwlywr Sett Quarry lease, the Indian troubles, and other matters. Mr. W. H. Sairrs was un- able to give the names of the Labour Commissioners, Was doubtful whether he would be in a position to do so to-night, but promised that they should be submitted to the House on Monday at latest. SCCYrrISH PROCEDURE.—Some time was occupied in the nomination of the Scottish Private Bill Procedure Committee, a difference of opinion arising as to whether it would be best to appoint a large or small body. Mr. Gladstone was in favour of the former, and supported an amendment of Mr. Munro-Ferguson that the Com- Mittee should consist of all the Scottish representatives and 30 other members to be nominated by the Com- mittee of Selection.

IRISH LAND QUESTION.—On the report of the Commit- tee of Supply authorising the payment "out of the Con- solidated Fund" of the salaries of the Commissioners un- der the Irish Land Bill, Mr. FOWLER moved an amend- inent substituting the words "out of moneys to be pro- vided by Parliament." Mr. BALFOUR argued that it was necessary that the Commissioners should be protected from the pressure which could be exercised by party majorities. Mr. T. HEALY, Mr. W. Rus- lanm„ and Mr. LEA spoke in favour of the amendment, and Mr. J. Morley appealed to the Conser- vatives to support it on constitutional grounds. On a division Mr. Fowler's amendment was defeated by 180 to 142. An amendment by Mr. Healey restricting the re- solution to the purposes of the Land Purchase Depart- Meat was rejected by 134 to 81. On a division being taken on the main question the Government resolution Was carried by 192 to 121. The House afterwards went into Committee on the Purchase of Land and Congested bistriets (Ireland) Bill. Discussion thereon was adjourned at midnight.
