div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.

A monthly meeting of this Council was held aJ the Town Hall on Tuesday evening. The Mayor (Alderman Francomb) presided, and there were also present Aldermen Burgess, Chandley, Holmes Sutton, Wright; Councillors F. A. Roberts, Black- , hurst, Walker, Voisey, J. Shaw-Green, Dixon. Green- ing, Jenkins, liepherd, H. Roberts, Monks, Flood, R. T. Fairclough, Beaman Hill, Hutchinson, Bolton, Taylor, Heaton ; Messrs. J. L. Whittle (town clerk), Chorley (borough treasurer), Longdin (borough•sur- veyor), and Dr. Gornall (medical officer.)

„ THE LATE MAJOR LITTON. The MAYOR said that since last they met they had lost by death Major Litton. who was for many years a member of that Council, and did during that time the very best he could for the town of Warrington. (Hear, hear.) He moved a vote of condolence with Mrs. Litton and family. Alderman BURGESS, in seconding the proposal, referred to the painstaking way in which Major Litton discharged his duties as a member of the Council. A vote of condolence was then passed. RESIGNATION OF ALDERMAN DAVIES.

The MAYOR Said he had a letter to read which he had received from Alderman Davies, but he had been advised by the Town Clerk that they could not take any action in the matter that night. The letter was as follows "Buxton, April 7th, 1891. Dear Mr. Mayor,—l am so much away from Warrington that I am reluctantly com- pelled to send in my resignation as an Alderman of the Borough of Warrington, and herewith send the necessary shilling. lam grieved to leave so many of my fellow members of the Council, with whom I have worked so many years in the interests of my native town of War- rington. With kind regards to you and every member of the Council, and wishing you all success, I am, dear Mr. Mayor, yours very faithfully, Josspn DAVIES. To Alderman Francomb, Mayor of the Borough of Warring- ton." His Worship added that Alderman Davies had ceased to be a member of the Council by the fact of pay- ing the shilling, but the vacancy could not be declared until the next meeting, , Councillor JENKINS thought it would not be altogether inappropriate for him, as one of the youngest members ot the Council, to suggest that something should be done to mark the feeling of the members with reference to what Alderman Davies had done for the welfare of the borough. (Hear, hear.) Councillor H. ROBERTS said he thought with Councillor Jenkins that they should at least put on record their sense of the loss which the Council and the town gener- ally had sustained by the resignation of Alderman Davies.

The MAYOR: The Town Clerk advises that that should be done when we declare the vacancy. Alderman HOLMES, referred to the great services which had been rendered by Alderman Davies, after which the subject was left over for discussion at the next meeting.

div.head: WATCH COMMITTEE.
div.p: THE WATCH COMMITTEE.

The minutes of this Conimittee contained the follow- ing :—That a license be granted to Mr. Thomas Holland for the performance of stage plays in a certain building called the "Pavilion Theatre, on the Fair Ground, for three months from this date, subject to the usual con- ditions upon which such licenses were formerly granted by the Justices; and that the tender of Mr. Henry Hoult I for the colouring and cleansing of the Bridewell at £lO be accepted. The total of the estimate of expenditure of the Com- mittee for the coming year amounted to £2.772 4s. The Committee also recommended, after a visit by a sub- committee, that, the proprietors of the Empire Theatre, the Public Hall, and thA Theatre Royal, be requested to carry out several minor alterations, presumably as a precaution against fire. The Committee further recom- mended the Council to adopt various new regulations with regard to the police force. They include a pro- vision that one shilling per day shall be deducted from the pay of a constable when absent from duty through sickness, except when absent through injury received in the execution of duty without his own default. If sick- ness continue for more thau four weeks a further sum of ed. per day is to be deducted ; and if it continue for more than 12 weeks such sum per week may be deducted as the Watch Committee may determine. The minutes were adopted on the motion of the Mmron.

STREET IMPROVEMENT AND LIGHTING COMMITTEE. The minutes of this Committee contained the follow- ing :—That the plans of the following buildings, &c., be approved :—Eleven cottages in Garibaldi-st., for Mr. Stephen Dale; laboratory for the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co., Limited; new bank in Bridge-st., for the National Provincial Bank of England, Limited; addi- tions to Drill Shed for the Ist Volunteer Battalion South Lancashire Regiment; extension of fustian cutting shop in Wakefield-st., for Mr. Joseph Wilkinson; cottage in Winwick-road, for Mr. Barlow; new Board room, for Messrs. P. Stubs and Co., Limited; additions to 3, Wilson Patten-st., for Mr. Thomas Hesketh ; extension to the works of Messrs. Rylands Bros., Limited; six shops at Bank Quay, for Mr. Thomas Williams; eight houses in Wellfield-st., for Mr. Jos. Tyldesley ; stable in Catherine- st., for Mr. Peter Woodward; warehouse for the Anglo- American Oil Co.. Limited, in the London and North- Western Railway Co.'s Goods Yard; Welsh Presbyterian Chapel in Crosfield-st.—Resolution, that theplan of a new building line for the works of Messrs. Rylands Bros., Limited, be approved subject to the payment to the Cor- poration of £3O; that the tender of Mr. John Chorley for house-numbers at 4s. 3d. per gross be accepted ; that the sum of £l3O be paid to John Platt, Esq., and that suffi- cient land to enable him to erect thereon a cottage, ac- cording to the plan now produced, be conveyed to him in consideration of his allowing the Corporation to pull down the cottage in Lythgoe's-lane belonging to him, and to set back the property to the new line of the street.
The minutes were adopted on the motion of Alderman SurroN.

SANITARY COMMITTEE.—THE ESTIMATES .—A SINGULAR MISCALCULATION AT LONGFORD. The following estimate of expenditure for the coming year was submitted by the Sanitary Committee :—Night- soil department, £3,589 5g.; scavenging department, £2,988 9s. ; intercepting depots, £790 14s. 5d.; Long- ford depot. £1.948 14s. 98. ; hospital department, £1,264 125.; total £10,381 15s. 2d., as compared with a total Lek year of £9,992 3s. 11d. The minutes also contained the following resolutions :—That the tender of Mr. D. Pickton, for the repair of a van at £22, be accepted; tiler the tender of Messrs. W. Smith and Sons, of Barn- ard Castle, to supply two sanitary tumbler carts at £25 each, be accepted; that the tender of Mr. J. Bonnell for the purchase of the grinding or clay mill at Longford depot at £35 be acccepted. The Town CLERK reported that he had applied to the County Council, and had obtained the repayment of the proportion of the ex- penses due to this borough under the Contagious Dis- eases (Animals) Acts for the years 1884-89, amounting to £205 9s. Bd. , Alderman BURGESS, in moving the confirmation of the 'minutes, said the estimates were a little inure than last year, but only just about as much as marked the growth of the population and civilisation of the borough. There was one item rather high and that was for Longford depot, being due to the raising. of the salary of the manager. Alderman SUTTON seconded. Councillor JENKINS asked the Chairman of the Com- mittee if, in the face of the report that had been received by the Finance Committee during the week, it was the intention of the Committee to pay Mr. Warner the mana- ger the increased salary granted him, Councillor Dixox said he should like to know what it was that had come to the knowledge of the Committee during the week. Alderman Bneoess said, in reply to Councillor Jenkins, that he could only say that the fresh arrangement with the newly-appointed manager did not begin till the 25th March, and he had not been paid anything on the advanced salary. The Council, would, perhaps, be for- bearing with him and not expect that he should say what the Committee would do or could do. The intor- mation upon which the Finance Committee acted only came to his knowledge on Saturday, and he thought it o be his duty to at once inform Mr. Chorley of the discovery that had been made, knowing that the financial arrangements for the year would have to come before the Council. He did that so that the Finance Committee if they had any change to make in the rate might make it before the Council meeting. He might just inform the Council what it was that had come to his knowledge. It was simply this—that the stock of manure that Mr. Owen Warner had given them to understand they had was less by 200 tons than he had furnished. That was a very serious item, and it was very unsatisfactory to the Sanitary Committee. He was very sorry the Finance Committee would be placed in the position of having to make an alteration in the rate of the year in consequence of the mistake, and he still mere regretted that the rate- ravers in Warrington would have to pay 2d. in the £ more than they would otherwise have had to pay. Mr. Warner's delinquency would not and could not affect the working of the system at Longford. What Longford was before Mr. Owen Warner's blunder, Longford was now. The Sanitary Committee would have to take coun- sel together tO determine as to the course that should be taken. He felt in no way 'despondent, but perhaps they should have learned a lessOn that would be of advantage to them all. If it caused members of the Council and a great many other people to ascertain for themselves what Longford is and what it is to Warrington, what teok place then would be of service. Councillor BLACKHURST asked what amount of manure they had stored at Longford. - Alderman BURGESS said he had a return weekly from Mr. Owen Warner, and the previous Wednesday it showed a little over 500 tens. But he had a stock-taking himself last week, and they found there were 200 tons less than that amount. Councillor JENKINS was then proceeding to ask Alder- man Burgess certain questions when the Mayor pointed out that Alderman Burgess had replied, and the minutes closed. Councillor Jenkins was disposed to question this ruling. The MAYOR: You had better take the chair, if you ask questions in that way we shall be here all night. , Councillor JENKINS argued that it did not matter if they were there in the interests of the ratepayers.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 11, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 11, 1891.

r The MAYOR :It is not in the interest of the ratepayers- bothering and asking questions. It has always been understood that when the Chairman replies the debate closes. The Sanitary Committee's minutes were agreed to.
PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE.-THE PAYMENT FOR
STREET MAKING.

At a meeting of the. above Committee, held on the 9th March, it was resolved that the tender of the Warring- ton Slate Company, Limited, to supply 22,000 wood blocks at lie. 2d. per 100 pieces, be accepted, subject to the quality of the wood and the creosoting of the same, being approved by the Borough Surveyor.—At a subse- quent meeting it was resolved that the apportionments of the cost of forming and paving the following streets be approved :—St. Mary's-st., £272 19s. 2d.; Baxter-st., £144 12s. Bd. : £519 Iss. 7d.; Ellis-st., £lBO 18s. 7d. It was further resolved that permission be given to Messrs. Peter Walker and Son, Limited, to con • struct a third crossing over Dallam-lane from the Lon- don and North-Western Railway Company's sidings to their works, subject to the. conditions of an agreement to- be prepared by the Town Clerk, and upon payment of the sum of £s,per annum. The Committee, after fully considering the resolution of the Council of the 2nd December, 1890, relating to private improvement ex- penses, and having obtained information from other towns, are of opinion that it is not desirable that ex- penses incurred in private street improvements should be declared to be private improvement expenses, but they would recommend that the Finance Committee should take into consideration all applications for extension of time for the repayment of expenses incurred in the pay-

ing of private streets. Alderman Wmuoirr, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said the Committee had gone very carefully into the matter in regard to private street improve- ments, and the Town Clerk had given himself consider- able trouble in applying to about 40 towns as to their systems. At least 35 out of the 40 towns allowed no ex- tension of time. Councillor HUTCHINSON seconded. Councillor DIXON moved an amendment to the effect that the minute giving Messrs. P. Walker and Son, Limited, permission to make another crossing in Dallam- lane, be not adopted. He thought that arrangements might be made between the London and North-Western Railway Company and Messrs. Walker, whereby it would not be necessary to make another crossing.— This amendment was not seconded. Councillor H. ROBERTS, speaking in reference to the minute as to private street improvements, said there were one or two facts that might be considered by the Committee before finally abandoning the proposal that he made a few months ago. In the first place, the in- quiries were sent to the whole of the non-county boroughs, a large proportion of which were old, effete, fossilised places that were really not worth five minutes' consideration. kLaughter.) In addition to this, the replies had come exclusively from an official source and his resolution, if it meant anything, did mean additional work for the officials of that Corporation. He could ' well understand that officials did not look with favour upon anything which was calculated to add to their al- ready onerous duties. The most important of the boroughs which had been written to—these which were marked by presperity and progress—had almost univer- sally replied, either directly in favour of the resolution, or in favour of its spirit. Doncaster, Middleton, Wake- field, Blackpool, Darwen, Cardiff, and Crewe were all de- cidedlyin favour. Widnes had years ago adopted the principle, and found it answer exceedingly well. The gist of the matter lay in one of the replies from Hyde, which was:—" We could not obtain payment down without inflicting great hardships on property owners, many of whom are of the working class and build out of money borrowed from building societies." (Hear, hear.) He also strongly objected to property owners having to go before the Finance Committee in forma pauperis, to be for an extension of time for repayment. Mr. HILL supported the arguments of Councillor Roberts, and he remarked that while in some streets the owners had been called upon to make the streets almost I before the houses were occupied, in others the streets had been left unmade for years. Alderman HOLMES said he was glad the Paving and Sewerage Committee had gone no further than they had done. He had a strong objection to Councillor Roberts's resolution. The Corporation had no right to act as a philanthropist, and when a man went in for building property he knew that street-making was part' of the cost, and he should provide for it accordihgly. Councillor Ronewrs said he did not ask the Corporation to be philanthropists. What was wanted was a purely business arrangement on both sides. Councillor VOISEY supported the remarks of Alderman Holmes. He was of opinion that if those who built houses wanted credit they should go for it to their other creditors outside the Corporation. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) Councillor ROBERTS said the Corporation did not stand in the position of creditor, but had the first security on the property of the land. Councillor Mum spoke against the proposal of Council- lor Roberts. He considered they were interested parties who were propagating the idea. (Laughter). Alderman WRIGHT having replied, the minutes of the Committee were adopted.

' were quite as honest and pure-minded as themselves, it was a matter to be regretted and to be put up with, in the best way they could. (Hear, hear.) Councillor Mum : I call Councillor Roberts to order. (Laughter.) He is leaving the subject out altogether. The Meron : Councillor-Roberts is quite in order. Councillor Mum : He is quite wrong. The MAYOR: I do not think anybody should take what was said to themselves. Councillor ROBERTS said if a member chose to put the cap on his head he couldn't help it, but he was quite welcome to wear it as far as he was concerned. (Laughter.) Councillor GREENING seconded the adoption of the minutes, and pointed out that 33,000 of the inhabitants passed through the museum, and that on Bank holiday ' there was an attendance of 731. (Hear, hear.) Councillor Romnrrs said he should like to add that it had been decided that the library should be made free on the 30th September at the latest, and perhaps before that date. (Hear, hear.) The minutes were then agreed to. THE CEMETERY.

From the report of the Registrar to the Cemetery Com- mittee it appeared that the interments for the past four weeks were :—Adults, 42 ; minors, 28 ; stillborn and pre- mature. 12. Corresponding period last year, adults, 54; minors, 55; stillborn and premature. 9. The receipts for the past four weeks were £74 95.; corresponding period last year, £95 10s. 6d. Adopted on the motion of Councillor TAYLOR.

This Committee recommended that the salary of the Superintendent of the fire brigade be increased from £2O to £3O per annum, and that his rate of allowance when attending fires be increased from the first hour from 3s, to ss.
Adopted on the motion of the MAYOR, seconded by Councillor linrcnmsom _
GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE.

The only matter of interest in this Committee's minutes was a resolution that the common seal of the Corporation be affixed to the petitions against the pro_ visional.Order Bills relating to railway rates and charges. The minutes were adopted on the moti3n of the MAYOR, seconded by Alderman Surrow.
FINANCE.-THE NEW RATES.

The Finance Committee's minutes contained resolutions that calls be made on the overseers of the townships of Warrington and Latchford, on borough rate account, for the sum of £10,304 9s. 4d. payable by two half- yearly instalments; that the Finance Committee be authorized to make an improvement rate for the year commencing 26th March, 1891, at 2s. 10d •in the L, which was estimated to produce about £17,578, and that a sewers' rate be made at 2d in the £. The minutes also contained the estimates of expenditure of the various ' Committees for the coming year. Alderman HOLMES na.moving the confirmation of the minutes, said that since the making up of the estimates the Chairman of thetSanitary Committee had informed them that he had ascertained that the quantity of con- centrated manure reported to be in stock at Longford depot was less by 200 tons than stated. This would necessitate an increase of the sum to be raised on the improvement rate to the extent of an additional 2d. in the £. He would, therefore, have to withiraw the reso-

lution on the Committee's Minutes with regard to the improvement rate to be laid. Councillor SnAw GREEN seconded, and regretted the necessity for increasing the improvement rate. Councillor JENKINS said that as he had a motion which would come before the Council at its next meet- ing, he should like the burgesses of the borough to thoroughly understand the position. In the assets con- veyed to the borough treasurer and which he has carried to his account, he had put the value of manure in stock at the depots at £2,265. It was well they should think that matter over, because they had heard from time to time of the perfection with which the sanitary matters of this borough- The MAYOR here interrupted, and said he was advised that Councillor Jenkins was out of order in making these remarks. _ . .

Councillor JENKINS : I bow to your decision. Councillor VOISEY asked the Chairman of the Gas Committee if anything would be given out of the profits of that Committee to help the rates Alderman HOLMES said the question had not been be- fore the Gas Committee, but he did not think it was likely they should be able to give anything in aid of the rates. " They had a large amount of expenditure during the coming year. The minutes were then adopted with the exception of that relating to the Improvement Rate.

div.head: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE.
div.p: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE.

From the report of the Inspector to the School Attend- ance Committee it appeared that 75 cases had been enquired into by the Board of Guardians, and school fees allowed in 71 eases for 174 children,and that 54 cases had been taken before the magistrates, and fines inflicted in 49 cases. Two boys sent to ship " Clio " one case adjourned, one warrant ordered, and one boy ordered to the workhouse. SO cases were brought before the Com- mittee, and dealt with. The average attendance at the public elementary schools during the month of February, was 8,068 ; corresponding period last year, 7,148; increase, 920. The minutes were confirmed on the motion of Coun- cillor SHAW GREEN, seconded by Councillor HEATON. , MUSEUM, LIBRARY, AND ARTS COMMITTEE.—THE LIBRARY

div.head: TO BE MADE FREE,
div.p: TO BE MADE FREE,

At a meeting of the above Committee, held on the 13th March, the following return for February was presented: —Visitors to the museum, 2,313; increase 7 per cent. compared with February. 1890. Books issued in reading- room, 1,709; increase, 7 per cent. Issued in lending department, 2,304, being a slight increase. The gifts to the Museum included the following :—Four parrot skins, from Mr. J. W. Hardy; token of Mary Earle, of Risley, 1668, from Mr. N. Heywood; "Notes and Queries for 1890." in continuation, Mr. R. Pies-point; "Field Club" and "Essex Naturalist." for 1890, from Mr. L. Green- ing; "Proceedings of the Chemical Society" and "Industries," for 1890, from Mr. T. Fletcher; three local pamphlets, from Mr. T. J. Ridgway; ten local pamphlets. from Mr. J. L. Whittle; photographs (19) of objects in the Museum, from Mr. P. Dalton. Councillor HENRY ROBERTS in moving the confirmation of the minutes said the report which had just been issued by the curator—and which was the first report that had been issued—showed that the museum had been visited by 68 per cent., ef the entire population of the borough Another fact was worth noting and that was that only £7 15s. 4d. had been spent in the provision of specimens to increase the attractions of the place. He was almost afraid of sounding the praises of the institution, because one was so apt to have one's motives called into ques- tion by gentlemen who were in the habit of looking somewhat obliquely at things. div.head: TREE PLANTING NOT A SUCCESS.
div.p: TREE PLANTING NOT A SUCCESS.

From the report of the Bathkeeper, to the Town Hall, Park, and Baths Committee, it appears that the income of the baths during the past four weeks was £22 175., and for the corresponding period last year £2 ss. 6d. The Committee recommended that the tender of Mr. W. Fletcher for the painting and decorating of the vestibule and passages, &c., in the Town Hall at £l2l be accepted. Alderman CRANDLEY moved, and Councillor BOLTON seconded, the adoption of the minutes. Councillor FAIRCLOUGH thought several places in the town might be improved if trees were planted. One place he should like to name,and that was down the new cut at Arpley. The MAYOR said that was outside the borough. Councillor FAIRCLOUGU said if it could not be done by the Corporation he should be glad to help with a sub- scription. Alderman BURGESS supported the remarks of Councillor Fairciough, and expressed the opinion that the trees which had been planted in Winwick-st., and Wilson- Patten-st., had been neglected. He thought the south side of Church-st., might be ornamented with trees. Councillor ElzaTos said he had spent £29 in shrubs, &c., in his garden in Winwick-st., but found they would not flourish. Alderman CHANDLEY was of opinion that trees would not grow in the atmosphere of Warrington. Those in the Park were gradually dying. The locality was especi- ally subject to deleterious vapours from St. Helens and Widnes when there were westerly winds which was nine months out of the twelve. The minutes were adopted.

div.head: IItAHERTS.
div.p: THE IItAHERTS.
The minutes of the Markets Committee, which con- tained the resolutions with regard to the stalls in the market which we published last week, were adopted on the motion of Councillor BLACKSURST.
TRH GAS COMMITTER.-GAS FOR PENICRTH.

In the minutes of the Gas Committn it was reported that the average illuminating power of the gas for the past four weeks was equal to 18.31 candles at both works. The following resolutions had been passed: That the necessary mains be laid for supplying the dis- tricts of Penketh and Sankey with gas, and that Mr. Haddock obtain tenders for the pipes required; that the tender of the Warrington Slate Company, Limited, to supply 400 tons of setts at 18s. per ton be accepted; that the tender of Mr. J. J. Lee, of Manchester, to supply 400 I yards of curbs at 3s. per yard be accepted; that the tender of Messrs. Clare and Ridgway to supply 12,000 tiles at 665. 6d. per 1,000 be accepted; that the tender of Messrs. Firmstone and Bros. to supply the following pipes be accepted :-933 yards 6in. at £4 12s. 6d. per ton, 3,333 yards 4m. at £4 15s. per ton, 1,200 yards 3in. at £5 3s. 9d. per ton. Alderman HOLMES, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said that the outlay at the commencement for supplying Penketh and Salikey with gas would be £1,200. Councillor VOISEY asked if the £1,200 would come out of profits. Alderman HOLMES: Yes. Councillor Dom mentioned that complaints had been made about the gas that was supplied to Bold-st. Wes- leyan Church. , The MAYOR: It must be a very dark place. Councillor HENRYRoBERTs, alluding to the proposal to pay for the extension to Penketh, said he hoped the Council would have an opportunity of debating the ques tion. The principle was certainly unsound, and, in its operation, most unfair to the ratepayers of Warrington. (Hear, hear.) Alderman BURGESS was also of this opinion. The prin- ciple involved was a very serious one, and he should be glad if the Chairman of the Comm ittee would be content to have the minutes passed with the exception of one re- lating to the Penketh gas supply. Alderman HoLmes said there could be no objection to the matter being discussed. (Hear, hear.) Councillor MONKS asked where the sepplv for Penketh was to come from, seeing that during the past winter the plant at the Gas Works had been seriously taxed to pro- duce the supply neeessary for Warrington. Alderman HOLMES said that the Committee had con- sidered that part of the question, and were not at all ap- prehensive that they would have any difficulty as a good many retorts at the Gas Works had not been worked. Councillor Dixox again mentioned the gas at Bold-st. Chapel and said he could not see anyone in the building. The MAYOR said that if the chapel was so dark that people could not see in it, the matter should be attended ' to without delay. It was a shame that people should have to pay for gaswhich had not been consumed. Councillor HEATON : Perhaps they were having a dark prayer meeting. (Laughter.) Alderman HOLMES said that the Committee had not re- ceived any complaints from the chapel authorities. If any had come they would have been attelided to. A week or two ago a complaint came from St. Thomas's Church, Stockton Heath. An investigation showed that there were a lot of burners in the church which had been there for the last 40 or 50 years. (Laughter.) And sopit was in most cases. The fault was in the condition of things at the place from which the complaint came and not in the gas. There was abundance of gas and plenty of pressure. The minutes were then passed. THE RIVERS COMMITTEE.—THE NAVIGATION OF THE RIVERS.

The Rivers Committee's minutes contained some cor- respondence that had passed between the Warrington Corporation and the'Corporation of Liverpool as to the conditions upon which the latter were to lay the byewav aqueduct across the Mersey. The Committee had passed a resolution that they could not see their way to recom- mend the Council to waive any of the conditions al- ready submitted to the Board of Trade for the due pro- tection of the interests of Warrington. Councillor FAIRCLOUGH moved and Councillor rivermi seconded the adoption of the minutes. Alderman BURGESS supported the action of the Com- mittee. Financially, he said, the differences between

div.head: COUNCILLOR DIXON AND THE SANITARY COMMITTEE.
div.p: COUNCILLOR DIXON AND THE SANITARY COMMITTEE.

Councillor Dxxori next proceeded to speak on the sub- ject of the minute of the Sanitary Committee of the 3rd March, referring to his visits to the intercepting depots. He wanted all to understand that if it were possible to have the unskilled labour of the town brought into a unioja, steps would at once be taken to draw out the men' who were working at Longford and the intercept- ing depots. He had Visited nearly all the manure works in existence worked by Corporations, and he had never found any working-men doing the same class of work which the men were doing at Warrington. At all the , works better mechanical appliances were provided for the workmen, while at Warrington there were scarcely any. At the intercepting depots he saw, to his astonish- ment,one man washing tubs which excreta had been in, and when he inquired what became of the excreta when it had been washed out, he was told it ran into the main sewer. If he had had a pistol in his hand, he should have used it, (Hear, hear, and laughter.) He was disgusted, when he remembered that some 25 or 30 years ago, when the works in Church-st. were re-laid, the Sanitary Committee would not allow them to pass] anything out that it was possible to retain. Yet the Corporation were- doing the very thing they prevented ethers from doing. At Manchester the contents of all the tubs ran into cis- terns to settle, and there was epreelpitant used, so that the water which ran out was clear water. The men em- ployed in the intercepting depots had no right to do the work they were asked to do, and he for one should always protest that men should not be made slaves of. They could very easily put up some machinery similar to ' what was used at Halifax. He added that he did not for a moment withdraw one word of what he had said at the intercepting depots. They who made the arrange- ment there had made one of the most foolish arrange- ments it was possible to make. He hoped that some one would come into the Council who would make a stand for the position other towns were in. After the Council had approved a petition in favour of the proposed new railway, a copy of which is given in another column, the meeting terminated.

A rumour is current in Dublin that the police hold a warrant for the arrest of an Irish M.P. on a grave and painful charge. The death is announced of M. Edmond de Pressense, the well-known pastor of the Evangelical Free Church in Paris.

It was rumoured in the Law Court on Wednesday that Mr. Big= has accepted the judgeship rendered vacant by the retirement of Mr. Justice Stephen. Intelligence received at Buenos Ayres from Chili con- firms the report that the Government troops are joining the rebels in the north. Doubts are cast on the rumoured mediation of the British admiral.

Alarming riots occurred on Wednesday in connection with the Mayoralty of Chicago, to which Mr. Hempstead Washburn was elected. In one of the encounters a negro ticket pedlar was killed, and in another several participants were seriously injured.

div.head: DEATH OF THE MARLOW MURDERER..
div.p: DEATH OF THE MARLOW MURDERER..

A Maidenhead correspondent telegraphs: The man, Henry Cooper, who on the 28th ult., at his house near the Moor Farm,. Marlow, murdered his wife by cutting her throat, and afterwards attempted to commit suicide in the same way, died on Saturday night. At the inquest on the body of Cooper's wife the jury found a. verdict of "Wilful murder" against Cooper.

div.head: TRE COLLIERY ACCIDENT.
div.p: TRE COLLIERY ACCIDENT.

1 Mr. John Booth, the coroner for North Staffordshire, on Saturday opened the inquest on the bodies of the ten men and boys killed by the explosion in the Apedale Colliery on the Thursday night. Mr. Allen, on behalf of the Midland Coal and Iron Company, asked that the fullest inquiries might be made. After taking evidence of identification, the coroner adjourned the Inquest till the 16th hist:, in order to allow of,time for the examin- ation of the cclliery.
CAPTAIN O'SHEA AD MR. PARNELL.

Captain O'Shea, acknowledging an apology from Father Furlong for a statement made concerning Captain O'Shea's household, says Mr. Parnell insinuated in Com- mittee-room No. 15 that he (Mr. Parnell) paid the house- hold expenses, whereas, the late Mrs. Wood allowed Mrs. O'Shea £3,000.a year for these expenses. Much, he adds, has yet to be revealed, and he (Capt. O'Shea) will certainly gain by the revelation. Capt. O'Shea also en- closes a sample of correspondence for Father Furlong's perusal.

div.head: MR. GOSCHEN AND THE COUNTRY BREWERS.
div.p: MR. GOSCHEN AND THE COUNTRY BREWERS.

The Chancellor of the Exchequer, on Tuesday,received a deputation from the Country Brewers' Society, the Licensed Victuallers' Defence League, and the Retailers and Distillers, who asked for relief from taxation. Mr. Goschen said it would be absolutely impossible to per- suade the House of Commons to take off 3d. from beer with taking a corresponding amount off spirits. A case which might be strong if the consumption of alcohol had declined became a weaker one when the consumption of the article taxed became greater than it was before.

div.head: DEATEt OF MR. BARNUM.
div.p: DEATEt OF MR. BARNUM.

Mr. Phineas T. Barnum died on Tuesday afternoon. Mr. Barnum was born in Connecticut in 1810, and bcgan business when he was 18 years old. He achieved a world- wide reputation in 1844, when he commenced the exhibi- tion of Tom Thumb. Six years later Jenny Lind made a tour throngh the United States under Mr. Barnum's aus- pices. His last adventure as showman was with "The Greatest Show on Earth," exhibited for a hundred days in London in the autumn of 1889. The deceased was four times elected to the Legislature of his native State, and also filled various Municipal offices. He wrote several amusing books, including his own life. Mr. Barnum, the great showman, is reported to have left a fortune of 5,000,000 dollars. His principal heir is a grandson.

div.head: BACCARAT SCANDAL.
div.p: THE BACCARAT SCANDAL.

The action brought by Sir William Gordon Cumming against Mrs. Wilson and others for slander in connection with the baccarat case is about fifty down in the list of London special juries, and is not likely to be reached for two or three weeks. One Court only will sitfor the pre- sent to try these actions, - but it is announced that a second Court will be formed after the list of Bankruptcy matters has been disposed of. Sir Edward Clarke, Q.C., M.P., (the Solicitor-General) and Mr. C. F. Gill will ap- pear as counsel for the plaintiff; while the defendants, five in number, will be represented by Sir Charles Rus- sell, QC., M.P., Mr. Asquith, Q.C., M.P., and Mr. A. Russell.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
THURSDAY.—Before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes. CAUSE LlST.—This list comprised 3 adjourned plaints, 2 default summonses, 109 original plaints, 37 original judgment summonses.

I- CLAIM FOR DAMAGES FOR A DOG BlTE.—Harry Arthur Turner Pickersgill, of 351. Vnutsford-road, Latchford, Icarter in the employ of the Steam Laundry Co., claimed from Arthur Jenks, landlord of the Ship Inn, Liverpool- road, Warrington, £lO for damages sustained through being bitten by the defendant's dog, on the night of the 31st of January. Mr. Browne appeared for the plaintiff and Mr. Forshawfor the defendant. The plaintiff stated that on the night in question he delivered some clothes at Mr. Jenk's house. He had been accustomed to go to the front door, but Mrs. Jenks had requested him to go to the back, and be did so on this occasion; As he was coming away the deg came behind him and bit him on the calf of his right leg. He had to have the wound cauterised by Dr. Joseph. Witness earned £1 a week, and had lost a day's wages, 3s. 4d. through the bite. He saw Mr. Jenks on the following Monday, about the matter, and he said the bite would not hurt him; the dog had bitten many a one.—By Mr. Forshaw : Dr. Joseph was witness's club doctor,and the club would pay his account. The dog had no muzzle on.—Dr. Joseph deposed to cauterising the wound, and said it was an insignificant one, but the size of a wound was no criterion as to its dangerousness. He had very little apprehension about it. The most dangerous time was past. The wound was well, but the plaintiff was not absolutely free from danger of hydrophobia. That de- pended on whether the dog was mad or not.—Police- Sergeant Taylor deposed to warning the defendant about his dog after the plaintiff was hitten,and to Jenks saying that the dog had bitten the man because he went into the kitchen, where he had no right, and he would bite anyone under the circumstances. He had bitten many a one. Witness asked who they were,and the defendant replied, "Ohs I don't know ; but he bit a man one night when he was wrestling with me, but nothing ever came of it."—Mr. Forsha,w submitted that the plaintiff had no case, as he had no business to enter the kitchen.—His Honour said he was there on a lawful errand, and was allowed to enter and not ordered out.—Mr. Forshaw : But he ought to have taken necessary precautions, by knocking at the door.—The Judge: As long as they ad- mitted him, he was there lawfully.—Mr. Forshaw : They did not admit him: he admitted himself.—The Judge: They did not object.—Mr. Forshaw : They were not in the kitchen to object.—His Honour: I should think you had better come to terms.—A verdict by con- sent for the plaintiff for £5, including costs, was subse- quently taken. ANOTHER WATCH TRANSACTION. John Birchall, a shoemaker, residing in Catherine-St.. claimed £2 10s. for breach of contract from Daniel CIO!, furniture dealer, Sankey-st., on account of a watch which was sold to plaintiff, and for which he received a guarantee for 15 years to keep it in good working order. Mr. Jenkins was for the plaintiff, and Mr. Browne for the defendant. —Plaintiff said the watch had dot been kept in proper order, and he alleged that the defendant had refused to repair it. The watch, which plaintiff understood at the time of purchase was an English lever, was, he said, , not worth the amount paid for it.—Abrahara Cohen said he sold the watch to the defendant for £2 17s. and an old watch which he subsequently sold for £1 Ss. He admitted giving the guarantee, but did not sell the watch as an English lever .—His Honour, in giving a verdict for the defendant, said that if he refused to clean the watch in accordance with the guarantee, the plaintiff was en- titled to get it repaired elsewhere and charge the defen- dant for it. A WARNING TO PORCHASERS.—MESSrS. Bradbury and company, sewing machine manufacturers, claimed from Peter John Jackson, of the Rookery,Lymm, the return of a family sewing machine and cover, or its value.—Mr. Arthur Browne, who was for the plaintiff, explained that the machine was hired from the company by Mrs. Theresa Clark, of Orchard-st., Warrington who agreed to pay , is. ed. a week until the full sum °en was paid, when the machine was to become her property. She had paid '£2 3s. on account, leaving £3 17s. still owing. It ap- peared that Mrs. Clark had sold the machine to the de- fendant for 30s. Jackson refused to give the machine up, being of the opinion that he was entitled to retain it. —Defendant paid that when he bought the machine from Mrs. Clark she told him that it was hers.—Mr. Browne offered that if the defendant would make good the hirer's arrears on the machine—£3 17s.—hy instalments to be agreed upon, he would withdraw the ease on payme.it of costs.—The defendant said he could not afford to do that.—His Mawr gave a verdict for the plaintiff for the return of the machine or its value, £3 17s. (to be reduced if returned in seven days), arid costs.

Miners' THE tendency to solidarity on the International part of the workers of the world Congress. is one of the most hopeful signs of the times. It was not without significance that the artizans of Australia sent substantial aid to the dock strikers of London; and there is further evidence of a disposition for toilers to make com- mon cause in the proceedings -4 the Miners' Inter- national Congress which has been held in Paris. It seemed, on Friday evening, that the assembly would be hopelessly and Passionately divided OH tie question of enforcing an eight hours day by means of an international strike, and that no con- clusion would be arrived at. But after the storm there was a calm; and it is due to the Wigan dele- gates (Messrs. Aspinall and Woods) that on Satur- day a way out of the difficulty was found. They suggested that the Congress should affirm not that a strike "is "necessary, but "may become" neces- sary; and their amendment, which was ultimately adopted, was as follows :

"The International Congress of Miners, now sit- ting at the Bourse du Travail, deems that a general and international strike may become necessary to obtain an eight hours day. The Congress, however, before resorting to such an extreme measure, invites the Governments and Parliaments of the nationali- ties represented at this Congress to agree to an in- ternational convention dealing with an eight hours day in mines, whether belonging to the State or' to private enterprise, this international convention to be similar to these which the various Governments have applied for the regulation of the postal, tele- graphic, railway, and navjgation services." It will be seen that the proposal pledges the Con- gress to act on what may be called constitutional lines ; and it is not the first time that the advice of British delegates—ther e were thirty-four present —has had the effect of steadying and strengthening the action of their brethren on the continent. We see no good reason why European Governments should not act in concert in matters of this kind. England, at any rate, has nothing to lose by international procedure, seeing that she is, in the matter of shortening the hours of labour, in advance of every other Power. Startling state- ments were made at the Congress as to the oppressed condition of Belgian miners; and, as it was felt that the first thing to do was to free them from the bondage they are .in, the delegates solemnly pledged themselves to assist them in every possible way, if it should become necessary, lill their particular case, to seek a remedy for their grievances by resorting to a strike on the first of May next. Assuming that the miners of Belgium are much behind their fellows in other countries in regard to rates of pay and hours of work, it is certainly advisable to bring them in line before attempting to take another step for- ward. English manufacturers and workers have suffered in the past through Belgian ironmasterg paying miserably low wages and offering goods at exceedingly low prices. There will be an end of this, or competition will at any rate be placed on a fair basis, if such help can be given Belgian miners as will ensure their obtaining a reasonable rate of wages. The main object of the delegates is, of course, to improvc the condition of the workers; but in accomplishing that they will improve the conditions of competition in trade by making them more uniform. But, be that as it may, the labourer is worthy of his hire, and he is entitled to struggle for something more than what is barely sufficient to keep body and soul together.

The THERE has been a great deal Oxford written during the past twenty Movement years upon what is generally spoken of as" The Oxford Movement "—that stir amongst the dry bones, of theology which had its culmination in the Rev. JOHN lIENRY NEWMAN') the chief actor in it, going over to the Church of Rome. But, apart from the interesting revela- tions in the late Cardinal NEWMAN'S "Apologia, there has been no contribution, to the history of this epoch so informing and so exhaustive as the volume from the pen of ilia late Dean °mynas which has just been published by Messrs. MACMII, LAN and Co. The work acquires a pathetic interest in being given to the world immediately after the death of its lamented author, and from the fact that he was engaged in the task of its revision during the last months of his life. We are told that some of the chapters would have been still further revised had his life been longer spared; but it is not likely that any substantial alteration would have been made, and the work is as it stands , a monument to the good sense, kindly feeling, and delicate discrimination of the late Dean of St. Paul's. He speaks from a personal knowledge of the university men who started and kept alive the movement; and the reader is made to realise that the portraits which are drawn are from the hand of one who nothing extenuates, nor sets down aught in malice. It is something to get a true insight into the characters not only of NEWMAN and P,11031: but of such supporters as JOHN KEBLE,R. 11171°41j' FROUDE, ISAAC WILLIAMS, and OHARLESMARRTOrIi* The fact that the moveiaent, as an inquiry int#o the claims and duties.of the English Church, led to many seeking rest .for ,their sonls in the 11,003 is Church has excited strong prejudice vaingt,-,• it in some quarters; but the impartial historian - not deny that the effort was a true and, earl:tell!

One,. and that the men who were the centre of it had high aspirations, and were single-hearted and affectionate in the pursuit of an unworldly object. Persecution followed as a matter of course, for no Church seems able to tolerate the discussion of new ideas and new principles which cannot be made to fit in with received views. But persecu- tion failed, as it usually fails in such cases, bringing discredit in the end upon the mis- guided authorities at Oxford. Dean CHURCH does not fail to point out the errors that were made, and the consequences which flowed from them; but his catholicity of spirit enables him to! deal gently with the extremists of both sides. As might be supposed, he has no sympathy with those who have contended, and still contend, that NEWMAN remained in the English Church when he had already determined to join the Church of Rome. He believes that that distinguished eccle- siastic was honest and Sincere in all that he did, and that the explanation given in the " Apologia " was throughout written in good faith. The move- ment was undoubtedly a failure as a direct means of Church reform; but it made its mark in the his tory of the time ; and there can be no question that it had an appreciable effect—an effect which is still felt—in awakening the spiritual element which lay dormant in the bosom of the English Church.

THERE were various matters. of Warrington more than ordinary interest under Council Meeting. consideration:at the monthly meet- ing of the Warrington Town Council, on Tuesday; and, as they :cannot be said to be finally deposed of, it will be well if the ratepayers will have an eye to what their representatives are doing on their behalf. To begin with the Library and Museum, it is satisfactory to see that, concurrently with the levy of an extra half-penny in the pound, it is formally announced that, "at the latest, the Library will be made free on the 30th September." This is good news to those who, like ourselves, have for several years been advocating a change which is due to the ratepayers on the grounds of justice,and required in the interest of the community:as a whole. With regard to the proposal for extending time to property owners in paying for street improvements, it would seem that the Paving and Sewerage Com- mittee cannot go further than "recommend the finance Committee to take into consideration all applications for extension of time for the repay- ment of expenses incurred in the paving of private streets." This can scarcely be called a satis- factory conclusion, since it opens the door to What may prove to be a system of favouritism. It would be better, as it seems to us, to go the whole length of the change as proposed by Councillor H. ROBERTS, or else keep to the present plan. Already there is complaint that in the matter of giving notice for the paving Of streets there is a tendency to make fish of one and flesh of another. Whatever system is carried out should be carried out strictly and fairly. The interests of the Corporation should in the first Place be safe-guarded, and after that steps should be taken to ensure the paving of the streets of the town at the earliest possible date. Considering the importance of the subject, it cannot be said that it was as fully discussed as it should have been. It is not sufficient for the Committee to tell the Council that various Corporations" take a certain course; what the ratepayers want to know is why the course is taken. But the chief interest contered,as it has frequently done before,on the state of matters at the Longford Manure Manufactory. Like the poor, it is always With Ili, and it is always requiring attention. We Ventured to predict some weeks ago, that, conse- quent upon the fall in the price of the manufactured article, there would be such a loss at the end of the year as would probably necessitate a rate of twopence in the pound. It appeared, however, when the accounts were made up, that the prospect had improved. But then, as the poet ; tells us," things are not what they seem." There seemed, on paper, to • be a stock in hand of over :500 tons of manure; it was taken at that, , and the estimates were based on that, but When the stock is really taken it transpires that : the return relied upon is wrong to the tune of 200 tons. Taking the price at -,C4 10s. per ton, it will be 110 en that the difference between what is in stock and 'what was supposed to be in stock is the nice little Bura of £9OO. This means an addition to the estimated rates as given last week of twopence in the pound; and the extra twopence is to be de- cided upon, to meet the requirements of the law, at the next meeting of the Council. Councillor JEN- Ir-liNg not unnaturally desired to put a few questions to the Chairman of the Sanitary Committee, but he was only allowed to put one. The MAYOR ruled that he was out of order in speaking again after the Chairman of the Committee had replied but it was his Worship surely who was out of order. Ile does not appear to note the difierence between , replying to a question and replying at the close of a debate. However, the facts must be I disclosed soon or late. Someone has blundered, and the ratepayers who have to dip their hands in their pockets to find the £9OO have a right to kbow who it is that has blundered; how ho has blundered; whether the blunder is confined to the Stuck of this year, or whether it goes further back; and 'finally, whether the blunder has been made ilnder such circumstances as warrant dismissal from the service of the Corporation. We are sorry for the sanitary Committee in finding themselves in this Unexpected difficulty; but their course is clear; it is their duty to get to the bottom of this matter; to take the Council and the ratepayers into their eonfidence ; and let it be seen in everything they do, that they are making the best of a bad job.

Mr. Whitham's letter this week (which will be found on page 2) is on the Kindergarten system of teaching. It will well repay perusal, especially by those who see in it the earliest possible form of technical instruction.

The resignation of Mr. Justice Stephen, on find- ing that he was the subject of discussion as being scarcely equal to the duties required of him, is in every way creditable to him. and there was quite an affecting leave-taking, on Tuesday, at the Royal Courts of Justice. He has set an example that may be followed in other departments with advan- tage to the public service.

The ratepayers of Salford have decided to be responsible for providing oile of the three millions required for the completion and equipment of the Ship Canal. Who can doubt now that, whether the new bill pass this, year or next, the undertak- ing will be accomplished? The shareholders will yet be able to sing—" all together " "We've got the ships, We've got the men, And we've got the money, too."

The life of Prince Ferdinand of Bulgaria is again threatened. Why don't the European Powers put an end to Russian intrigues by recognising him as lawful Ruler ? It is hard on the people of Bul- garia, who have shown such capacity for self- government, that they should so long be left out in the cold. There is room here for a little of that "spirited foreign policy" on the part of the Tories of which we once heard so much, but now see so little.

The Liberal .bazaar at St. Helens has realised £7OO, which is more than was expected—especially by the unsymathetic big-wigs who predicted its failure. The Liberals of Warrington having taken time by the forelock must make up their minds— and their materials—to do as well, or better. There is every evidence that the ladies are working hard and heartily; and the concerts-in-aid which have been given at the Liberal Club hate been in every way successful.

And so it is melanchohly admitted by the Town Council, after sundry experiments, that it is useless to try to grow trees in Warrington. When we are a trifle nearer the millennium—say, a thousand years hence—the people will say—` We will not dwell within an area which is fatal to oak and elm." Meantime we may slightly alter 'Cowper and say Trees cannot grow in Warrington ; if they but Receive our air, that moment they are doomed They breathe our black smoke and their green leaves fall.

There is another cloud in the bright prospect of a reduction of rates for Warrington. Instead of the poor rate being 10d. in the pound less, as it would have been upon last year's basis, it will be 6d. less. The extra demand of the Corporation has caused this, and has necessitated a special town- ship meeting to get over the difficulty. Then the loss at Longford takes another twopence, which is to be added to the previous twopenny increase in the Improvement Rate. What promised to be a reduction:of 10d., or at any rate Bd., has dwindled this week to one of 2d. only!

At St. Helens, there was a meeting of working- men, on Saturday, to consider the question of technical education and how it could be made to benefit them. The report of the proceedings shows that there is some fear of the middle-classes rather than the working-classes benefiting by the money to be granted for this purpose. The workers are right in looking to themselves in this matter; but, apart from this, no scheme of technical in- struction will be really successful which does not reach the mass of the people.

The Duke of Cambridge has been speaking at a Mansion House banquet, and criticising the critics of the army. He is not a reformer, and recognises himself a's belonging to a genaration which is past, for he says of the present generation that it is "not invariably of the same opinion as the authori- Ces." How very profound! But what authori- ties? Those who side with his Royal Highness, or those who agree with Lord Wolsely as an out- and-out reformer? The Duke has had his day, and he would do well to retire, like Mr. Justice Stephen.

It seems at variance with the nature of things that Alderman Davies should cease to be a mem- bJr of the Warrington Town Council. And, yet, having gone to live at Buxton, he has tendered his resignation, paid his shilling, and so far, as mem- bership is concerned, he has ceased to be. Who now will take his place in pouring oil on troubled waters? And who as ready as he in Council or Committee with pleasant jest and lively story? Does not everybody say :

Wives can of course leave their husbands, a la Mrs. Jackson, according to the new reading of the law ; but there are two sides to that as to the other questions. A woman of tho name of Schofield, who had left an indifferent husband, sought the aid of the magistrates of Hyde, on Monday, with a view to getting an order for her support. But the order was not forthcoming. A woman may leave her husband under these circumstances; but—note this of wives—she cannot compel him to keep her. To acomplish that she must be in a position to make out a case for a separation order in the ordinary way.

As will be seen from our advertising columns, agents are wanted for districts in Lancashire and Cheshire in connection with the Company formed for the automatic sale of postage stamps and cards. As things go we shall soon be able to have almost anything, if we will only "Put a penny in the slot." There used to be a conjuror who professed to convert copper coins into golden ones. What is wanted now is a genius who, acting on this idea, will produce a machine which, when we "Put a penny in the slot," will furnish us with a genuine sovereign. It would be a big success; a run on a bank would be nothing to it.

We would direct attention to the well-con- sidered proposal for a new Assembly Hall for War- rington, which is advocated in our correspondence columns by Mr. George Woods. The feasibility of erecting such a hall above the proposed public baths ought certainly to be taken into account. The site for the baths must be central, and the same may be said of the site for a Public Hall. It would be a great saving, to begin with, if one plot of land could be made to serve two useful pur- poses, like the famous piece of furniture of which Goldsmith says:— The chest contrived a double debt to pay— A bed by night, a chest of drawers by day.

The ratepayers of Earlestown and Newton have succeeded in their application to the Local Govern- ment Board for a re-arrangement of polling dis- tricts and an extension of the hours of polling. A draft order has been prepared, and will in due course become law. It is not for the Local Government Board to set up wards; that is with- in the province of the County Council; but the new order recognises this change as possible, in the future by a clause stating that the regulation shall be in force "until the district be altered by the County Council, and made into wards."

It is stated that the personal estate of the late Sir Richard Francis Burton, K.C.M.G., F.R.G.S., the celebrated explorer, who died at H.B.M. Con-, sulate, Trieste, on October 20 last, aged 70 years, has been sworn of the value of £lBB his. 11d, by ;the sole executrix, his wife, Dania Isabel Burton. We should say this is a case, if ever there was one, for the Queen's pension fund. The wife of a man Who neglected his own interests to serve those of his country and of mankind generally ought cer- tainly to he aided—if aid be required. Sir Richard was a great scholar as Well as a great traveller, and, by his translations, enriched the 'literature of the east.

He madna powerful appeal in favour of the jus- tices exercising their powers, and exercising them in various districts with something like uniformity. He aptly described the tied-house system as a monopoly which grasped at the retail profits in addition to the wholesale profits. Mr. W. Long and other magistrates supported Mr. Brunner, and ultimately the following resolution was adopted: —" That a Committee be appointed to examine into the present state and effect of the law relating to the licerising of houses in the county, for the sale of intoxicating liquors, and to report to the next Quarter Sessions.' This is the beginning of a change for the better—the dawn of a better day for publicans as well as the public.

THE JAPANESE FANCY FAIR. Business, to use the ordinary trade phraseology, was brisk at the Streatlam Towers on Thursday and yesterday, and there was no perceptible diminution in the number of visitors. But with the new arrangements wisely made by the committee, so as to stem the inrush of people and give facilities for the thorough inspection of the contents of each stall , by intending purchasers, a great improvement was effected. The stalls are still laden with merchandise of almost every description, and it is possible for the poorest, as. Well as the wealthiest, visitor to acquire some memento of .the novel event now, causing so much intereet.,in the city. The stallr holders were most assiduous in their attention to visitors, and succeeded in disposing of a large num- ber of the articles. The entertainments, musical and otherwise, were of a high standard and judi- ciously diversified. The amount taken was £1,003 6s. id. As will be seen from advertising columns, the fair will be open to-day for the last time. SPRING FASHIONS now Showing at J. & W. InrrTo'N's, Sankey-at.. Warrington.—Adet.

If they were going to force all the paupers into the Rouse they must enlarge their buildings and have more Officials.—Mr. Aaron thought the rules were passed wrongfully, as each member had not an opportunity of studyinc, them. It was wrong to bring old people from TO to eyears of age into the House, or only give theist half-a-crown a week. They might as well place them in the garden, get some soldiers, and make targets of them. He did not know a Board that sifted matters so thoroughly as that Board-omoney was not thrown away, —Mr. Dansey said he did not advocate cutting away all the old cases, but let the rules apply to new cases.— After further discussion the rules were referred to a small committee to consider and report upon them.

The first business was the appointment of clerk, and Colonel Ashton and Mr. H. G. 'Linaker retired. The Chairman said the Committee appointed to consider the applications met on Thursday, and as directed also ascer- tained the emoluments of the late clerk. The statement was as fellows :—Clerk to the Union £9O; Assessment Committee, £B5; School Attendance, £35 : Rural Sani- tary, £B5; Removals, £25 ; Election of Guardians, £l9. Some of these amounts varied, but taking the average of five years, the aggregate amount was £337 2s. Od. There was also the Superintendent's registrarship 'which was worth about £35, and the amount received for contested elections varied; but, taking the average, the annual amount was £24 4s. 9d. ; making a • total of £395 es. 9d. The late clerk had other extras, such as valuations, through his great knowledge of value, which did not come under the head of salary. Last year that extra amounted to £5O. There was also an allowance of £lO a year towards office rent,, but he had. to find coal and gas. , The emolu- Ments of the Clerk were practically 'g395 6s. 9d.; and out of that he had to pay his clerk. _ With reference to the remarks male at the last meet- ing by Mr. Mclntyre, as tp the manner at Little Leigh of conducting the funerals of the inmates of Dutton Work- house, the Rev. J. Lyon Bennett, the Vicar, wrote stat- ing that the coffins wero always taken into the church, except in a case of infectious fever. It happened, how- ever, at the funeral of Rustage, on Jan. 6th last, that the coffin was not taken into the church because a new heating apparatus was being put up. The coffins were always covered, immediately after the funeral, with about a foot of soil; three feet below the surface are planks, which were covered with quite two feet of soil. and the top of the grave was covered with planks. He was able to prove that the relatives who attended Rust- age's funeral stood by the grave side while the sexton covered the coffin. As regarded the other statement chat Rustage's coffin was jumped upon (" danced upon" he saw from the newspaper was the.vice-chairman's ex- prgssion) to get it into the grave, please be good enough to understand that no such thing was done. He could not help saying that it had caused him no little surprise and annoyance that such a serious charge should have been allowed to go forth to the public without proper inquiry having been made; and more especially so since the statements made were damaging to him, not only as Vicar of Little Leigh, but also as Chaplain of the Runcorn Union Workhouse. —The Chairman said he made no complaint, but he brought the matter forward in the interests of the Vicar as well as in the interests of the public. He was glad .to hear that he could deny it, but he must say that he had seen one cf the relatives since, a relative that was at the funeral, and he still maintained that such was the case. He had nothing further to say in the matter.— Mr. Weir thought it a great shame that the grave should be left open.

The Vicar presented the reports of the Charities, no said there were only two charities in which they .wera immediately concerned,the Rigby Charity and the Alcock charity. The Rigby charity consisted of a sum'of '2500 Mt by the late Mr.- Rips- in care of an executor; and the interest bad been for n number of years 5 per cent.,paid by the executor. Interest at the rate of 5 per cent. was not eaSily got, and last year the executor thought it was his duty to transfer the capital to three freehold houses on mortgage which realised Viper Cent. The amount re- ceivable last year *as £l3 10s. fie was afrard that most of the charities were losing a little money, owing to the less amount paid on consols and the difficulty of getting good interest and security. The Alcock Charity was a sum -of money in the hands of the Chitritv Trustees, and hells vicar recoived the interest four dines last year. The total amount for the year was £5 E3s. 4d.

He was a trained. clerk, perfectly acquainted with the Work and having the whole business at his fingers' ends.—Mr. J. The financial statement of the Parish Church showed an income of £405, the chief items being eight special Sun- day offertories £54 14s. lojd. ; five special week day offertories, £l9 9s. 3d. ; mission service offertories, £2l Bs. lid. ; tWenty Saints' days and festival offetings, £7 3s. 10. ; and 47 Wednesday evening and baptisms,week days, £ll 16.3.. 7d. ; 47 Sunday offertories, £258 17s". 3d.; treasurer organ fund,£7 Bs. 4d. ; and vicar's fees towards apparitor's salary, £lO. bn the 'expenditure side the chief amounts were organist's salary,£4o apparitor and extra cleaninz, £37 19s. ; bell ringer's salary, £ll ; gas, £23 ; coals, £9 13s. 7d.; •washing surplices, £7 IEN.; wine for communion, £3 4s. 11d. ; new surplices, £1 175.: new cassocks £2 10s. ; special offertories £79 1.1.5. 9id. After meeting all charges there was a balance 0f,£138 19s. 5d., paid to the Vicar for Runcorn curates' fund.—At St. Michitl's church the receipts amounted to £135 6s. 44d., consisting of collections in church. The expenditure reached a like amount, the principal items being : Mission fund, £l3 145.; curates' fund £53 3s. 3d; organist £10; apparatus £10; choir treat, £5 125. 31.—The receipts at Weston church amounted to £46 15s. 5d., and the ex- penditure to a similar amount.—The various accounts were passed.—The Vicar remarked that the financial condition of things seemed to be flourishing, and it was gratifying to see that the offertories had increased at each church so that they were able to hand over £2OO tO the assistant clergy fund. It showed the good will that existed amongst the members of the church, and that the Work of the clergy was appreciated: Votes of thanks were then accorded to tke various officials and the following lay representatives were appointed: Parish church: Messrs. William. Whittaker and .1. E. Meredith; St. Michael's: Messrs. T. W. Speakman and W. Mellor, Weston; Messrs. E. Aaron and W. Auistrong.—A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the meeting.

The playing nembers were entertained to tea at Anderson's Railway and Commercial Hotel on Tuesday evening,and afterwards a "free and easy" was held. Mr. J. Smith, the Captain, presided, and songs and recitations were given by those present. A very enjoyable time Was spent.
A WARNING TO WIDNES GAS STOKERS.

At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, John Callag- han, a gas stoker, was summoned by the Widnes Local Board for breach of contract.—Mr. Knowles prosecuted. —On the Ist March, the defendant and a man named Cook left their work at Widnes Gas Works without cause and without leave, and the consequence was that the retorts could not be properly attended to, and 15,000 feet of gas less than usual was made, representing a loss of 30s. to the Board. The defendant abscondei, but Cook was dealt with by the magistrates on the 13th ult. .--Defendant now pleaded guilty, and was fined 40s. and costs, or a month's imprisonment in default. SPRING FASHIONS DOW Showing at J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankev-st., Warrington.—Advt. THE CENSUS AT RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

Last week end the census of these two towns was taken by a very large staff of enumerators appointed by the local registrars, and the worx, so far as can be gathered, has been well carried out. So far as Widnes is concerned, the population can be fixed at a little over 30,000 the Local Board having a short time ago held a cen- sus on their own account. At Runcorn, it is confidently anticipated the population has increased to upwards of 20,000, being an increase of about 5,000 during the last decade. It will be July before the Government de- partment will issue any return of the results of the census. . .

RUNCORN BOARD SCHOOL EVENING CLASSES. The examination of the students attending these classes was held on Monday and Tuesday evenings by Mr. W. Ballance, Her Majesty's assistant inspector of schools. Sixty students presented themselves for examination in the various subjects, and a most satisfactory report is expected. On the second evening Mr. Pritchard. the chairman of the Board, Rev. Canon Maitland Wood, Dr. McDougall, Messrs. S. Taylor, and J. J. Howitt were present. The winter session was brought to a conclusion on Wednesday evening by an entertainment consistinc, of a lime-light exhibition of views of London, Scotland', and Ireland. Mr. Moulton described the various places and Mr. Bowyer manipulated the lantern. Sermwo FASHIONS now Showing at J. .BE, W. NuTToN's Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. SANGER'S CIRCUS AT RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

Lord George Sanger's circus paid a visit to Runcorn on Thursday, and was attended by marked success. At noon the usual procession took place, and was witnessed by thousands of people who lined the pavement through- out the town. The afternoon performance was well at- tended ,but in the evening the spacious tent was crowded, fully four thousand persons being present. A capital programme of equestrian feats,gymnastic performances, and balancing tricks was gone through, and several specimens of highly-trained thoroughbreds were shown, and astonishing tricks performed. Elephants, lions, and tigers were also put through various tricks. Yesterday the circus was at Widnes, and met with equal suc- cess.

DESERTION OF A WIFE AT WIDNES. ' Before Mr. G. l'ilkington and Mr. J. Bircball, at Widnes Police Court, on Thursday, Alfred Martley, was summoned by his wife Adelaide for deserting her, and she also desired a maintenance order against him.—Mr. Knowles, who appeared for Mrs. Martley, said the parties had been married about 16 years. On the 26th Decem- ber. 1889, defendant told his wife to get out of the house or he would murder her, and as she had cause to think that the defendant would carry out his threat she went away to her sister's house. The defendant left the town a few days later and did not return until Tuesday. There were five children, one of whom was 15 years of age and earned 7s. per week. The defendant admitted the offence and offered to pay ss. per week. The complain- ant agreed to this, and an or ier was made accordingly. Defendant was ordered to pay Costs. PREMIER SAFETIES, Cash or Hire.—GARLAND, Warrington. —Advt.

div.p: A REMARKABLE CHESHIRE FAMILY.

There has just been interred in Eastham Church- yard, Cheshire, the body of Elizabeth Lee, aged 75. Deceased, whose husband was for 44 years a porter at Ledsham Station, on the Chester and Birkenhead Railway, was mother of 21 children, the grand- mother to 82 children, and great grandmother to 25 making a total of 128.

div.head: DEATH OF A. MEMBER OF WIDNES
div.p: DEATH OF A. MEMBER OF WIDNES
LOCAL BOARD.

Mr. W. J. Hargreaves, landlord of the Prince of Wales Hotel, Widnes, died after a short illness, on Tuesday. A week previous he had attended Mr. Allen's funeral at Halewood,and there he contracted a chill, which ended in bronchitis, a complaint to which he -vi as subject. On Saturday night, inflam- mation of the bowels supervened, and on Thursday night he died. Mr. Hargreaves came to Widnes as a young man, and started the business of a jeweller and watchmaker in Ann-street, about twelve years itgo becoming a licensed victuAller. As a nominee of the Ratepayers' Association, he on live occasions attempted to obtain a seat on the Local Board, but was not successful until 1890. He gave promise of becoming a most useful public servant, and his de- mise, at the age of 52, is much regretted. His re- mains were interred yesterday at Farnworth Parish arch.
ALLEGED ILLEGAL PERFORMANCE OF STAGE PLAYS AT RUNCORN.

Before Mr. James Reynolds and Mr. Henry Rey- nolds, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Mr. J. W. Snape, the proprietor of a travelling theatre, was summoned for unlawfully acting, or cousing to be acted, on the 30th March, a certain part of a stage play, to wit, "Dick Whittington," in a booth on the Fair-ground, such place not being a patent theatre, or licensed under the statute; and that he did continue the offence on two other days viz., March 31st and April lst.—Mr. El W. Humphreys prosecuted on behalf of Mr. Caddick, lessee of the Theatre Royal ; and Mr. J. W. Knowles (Widnes) de- fended.—Mr. Humphroys said he did not wish to make any reflection upon the character of the entertainment given in the booth; but his client was a man who had obtained from their Worships a licence for theatrical performances, and he had to conduct his establishment undez very stringent regulations. Mr. Caddick, there- fore, felt that if Mr. Snape and others were allowed to conic into the town and give performances which were not subject to any such regulations, it would have, very likely, a serious and injurious effect upon the licence of the Theatre Royal.—Mr. Knowles admitted that his client had performed a certain part in the panto- mime of " Dick Whittington and his Cat." The people paid 3d., 6d., and is., to enter the building. —Samuel Whitlow Bretherton. gave evidence as to the performance.—Mr. Knowles contended that the Bench could not convict on the proceediegs as brought before them ; the offence should be described clearly and de- finitely, without duplicity or uncertainty ; but in that case any schoolboy would see that there was duplicity, because they were charged with presenting or causing to be presented.—The Chairman: Has he got a license from the justices ?—Mr. Knowles: No. He had got per- mission of the Local Authority, who had fixed him outa piece of land and had charged him rent for it. Under the 23rd section of the Act, a license was not required from the justices to perform in a booth at a lawful fair or feast.—Mr. Charles Dutton market inspector, said he gave the defendant authority to set up his theatre on the fair ground, and charged him hire, which was paid during the past fifty years. Travelling theatres had been allowed on the ground, and he thought stage plays had been performed. Witness was instructed to get as much money as he could by let- ting the land, and he had had no objection raised.—The Chairman said if Mr. Humphreys could not give any, further argument in favour of the prosecution,the magis- trates had come to the conclusion that the performance was permissible. The case would be dismissed. If any- thing wanted altering, it was the law.

The monthly meeting of this Board was held on Tuesday when there were present Messrs. J. Pritchard, chairman Rev. Canon Wood, Dr. Mc- Dougall, Mr. S. Taylor, Mr. A. Salkeld, Mr. J. The minutes of the School Attendance Committee were read from which it appeared that 'Ti parents had.been summoned before the Committee and 6 parents summoned before the magistrates. The Clerk read the- visitors' reports for the month ending March 20th from which it appeared that the total number of children on the rolls was 3,451, being 160 more than in March last year, and the average attendance was 2,884, being 164 more than in.the same period of last year. This growth in the num- bers is about 50 per cent, greater than the usual annual increase. The percentage of attendance was 83.6 as against 83 last March. The School Management Com- mittee recommended that the wages of W. The following latter was read from Messrs. Linaker and Linalier, solicitors, Runcorn, dated April 6th :—" We beg to inform you that acting upon instructions re- ceived from the Authority we insisted upon the Com- pany undertaking to pay the whole of the Authority's legal and engineering costs and expenses before we con- sented to proceed with the agreement already drawn and abandon the action against the Company and we are pleased that we are in a position to say that we have this morning received from the Company, a cheque for the whole of the lee•al costs up to the sealing of the agree- ment which will come before the Authority at their next meeting to have the seal fixed. We further redeived a cheque for the whole of the engineer's charges from the time the Authority employed him up to and including the superintendence of the various substitution works to be constructed. We have further arranged with the Com- pany that the extra services rendered by the late Clerk to the Authority, in connection with the sewer outfalls shall be paid for by the Companv,and further that if any legal charges are necessarily. incurred bythe Author- ity in connection with the matter the Company shall, pay them without any danger of the amount being disputed. If any extraordinary engineering charges are necessary to be spent the Company will pay this also. This will confirm to the Authority a statement made by the writer at a meeting a few weeks ago that there would be no charges whatever for the authority to pay. We have to- day paid to the credit of the treasurer of the Authority £169 2s. ld., the full amount of costs paid on account to us by the Authority, and in respect to any charges up to the completion of the agreement, we have no claim upon the Authority. We have also by this morning's post sent the Engineer's charges to. him with a request to send back to us a cheque for the amount yid to him by the Authority in respect of his charges, up to June last, namely, £67 10s: and we trust to receive the amount to- morrow, when we shall at once pay it in to the credit of the Authority. We enclose the letter received this morning with the two cheques, as perhaps some members of the kuthority would like to see the matter is amicably settled."—A letter from Messrs.
