THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &C. BY "AN OCCASIONAL CORUBSPONDICNT."

It was by the casting vote of the Chairman that the Runcorn Board of Commissioners adopted the Technical Instruction Act of 1890. Those who voted against the proposal disclaimed any views of antagonism to technical education, and argued that at the present time the course proposed was inop- portune and inexpedient, but as Mr. HuMphreys remarked "by your fruits ye shall know them." In. order to rob the arguments of the opponents of any shadow of foundation, 'Mr. Pritchard added a rider strongly qualifying the terms of his resolution, but nevertheless the opposition was carried to a vote, and the ratepayers are enabled to see who are the true friends ot education.

In the present system of splitting up our public meetings into classes, it is instructive to observe that all those who voted 'against the resolution are Tories and Churchmen. Mr. Imison, whose views on any subject are always worth listening to, as usual took an independent course and deserted his political friends on this important question of education. The testimony of Mr. Wiswall as to the positive value of a technical training is worth more than all the argumentsi of a few advocates of ex- pediency. It s to be hoped that the practical scheme will be forthcoming early. Are there not in Runcorn a few gentlemen who will not allow Mr. Brunner's offer to remain a dead letter?. Are those who are possessed of a large share of the world's goods so devoid of interest in th material prosperity of the town as to remain in- different on such a subject? Even if the amount raised was only £2OO, it would brim:: forth an equal contribution from Mr. Brunner, and would form a capital nucleus for a start. This is a question of great moment to the working classes, and the con- tribution of their mites would swell any fund very considerably... We hope Mr. I Pritchard and those who have acted with him.will attempt some scheme for raising public subscriptions for a technical school. Its early establishment would be an incalculable boon to the youth of the town.

As to the prospects of the success of a technical school in Runcorn, the evening classes at the Board Schools may be sonic guide. The classes were started at the beginning of the season, not without some opposition, but the results achieved by Mr. Moulton, the head master, and his assistants are a full justification of the existence of the classes. Throughout the winter a very good average attend- ance had been maintained, aim the subjects taught I were reading, writing, grammar, arithmetic, mensuration, algebra, euclid, and shorthand. Mr. W. Ballance, MM., Assistant Inspector of Schools, examined the students on Monday and Tuesday evenings,when no fewer than 60 were pre- sented. Mr. Ballance remarked that it was one of the best schools of its kind he had examined and exceedingly good for the first year. He commented upon the good order maintained and the general excellency of the work done. The whole of the students examined in reading, algebra, and short- hand were successful in accomplishing the require- ments of the Code,and were passed by Mr. Ballance, and Very good, if not equally good, results are anti- cipated in the other subjects, when the Inspector makes his report. Many of the students were young men employed in a variety of occupations during the day, and they have no doubt received much de- sired and much needed instruction.

The appointment of a successor to the late Mr. Henry Linaker, as clerk to the Runcorn Union, has created widespread interest during the past fort- night, and the question was settled at a meeting of Guardians on Tuesday. There were only four appli- cations for the post, probably because it was well known that it would be given either to Col. Ashton the Chairman, or Mr. 11. G. Linaker the deputy clerk. Both gentlemen possessed everyqualification for the post, and the choice of the 37 guardians' who assembled. an unusually large attendance, fell upon Colonel Ashton, who received the appointment by 24 votes to 13, an unmistakable evidence of the opinion entertained of his ability and of the respect in which his character is held. Some indignation- has been caused in the Run- corn Union by the adoption of a set of regulations for the distribution of out-door relief as suggested by a conference ,recently held at Northwich, by which the amounts given to the poor people are in some cases to be considerably reduced and in others not granted at all. Mr. Heywood, of Frodsham, made a futile attempt to get them rescinded on Tuesday, but as a result of his action they are to be re-considered by a specially selected Committee, and for th e present the rules are inoperative. There will be considerable' agreement with the views of the relief supervision committee of one township, who were willing to accept the regulations if the salaries of the officials of the Local Government Board were reduced in the same proportion as the pay to the poor people. As Mr. Dansey, the Local Government Board Inspector, was present, the pro- posal was very pointed, and caused much merriment amongst the members. Apparently Mr. Dansey failed to see the joke, for no smile lighted up his features.

The election of Guardians of the poor takes place this week end. The voting papers will be distri- buted to-day (Saturday), collected on Monday, and counted at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Con- tests take plaze at Runcorn and Frodsham. In the former place the candidates are the Rev. Dr. Gas- taldi' Messrs. S. Taylor, H. I. Grice, P. Speakman, J. W. Lightburn, D. H. Jones, Thomas Lea, T. S. Carr, and T. Crosby. The first four named are the retir- ing members. Messrs. Lightburn and Jones have previously served the ratepayers on the Board. Mr. Lea is the nominee of the Sons of Temperance and the Rechabites, and Messrs. Crosby and Carr are in- dependents. The ratepayers pay the piper and they can take their choice.

By the death of Mr. J. T. Allen Widnes lost on Of its most valued public servants, and his place at the public offices will not easily be filled. A "martyr to duty" is the verdict of those who had the pleasure of his intimate acquaintance, and the regret at his sudden demise is universal.

There is no prospect of a diminution of the poor rate at Widnes. The amounts required for poor-law purposes and the County Council and for the School Board keep at the old high figure, and nothinz short of a s. rate for the present year will meet the requirements. Last year such a rate realised £13,0G9, and there was paid to the Union -.C9,134 3s. 11d, and to the School Board £3,900. The Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority have ob- tained a complete victory over the Ship Canal Com- pany. The Authority could make no satisfactory arrangement as to the disposal of their sewage in the extensive district through which the Ship Canal will cut, and at length took the extreme step of securing an injunction from the High Courts of Justice. This extreme step was taken on the advo- cacy of Mr. E. Aaron, whose attitude has been fully justified. The Company have granted all the rights clainted,and paid over all the costs incurred,amount- ing to nearly £530. A weed of praise is due to Messrs Linaker and Linaker, who have been the solicitors in the matter, and who have placed their 1 clients' views in such a manner as to lead to such a satisfactory conclusion.

div.head: NARROW ESCAPE OF THE CZAR.
div.p: NARROW ESCAPE OF THE CZAR.

The Czar is reported to have narrowly escaped becom- ing a mark for an assassin's.weapon. When his Imperial Majesty was about to review the Guards, a suspicious. looking man entered, and presented an admissi6n ticket, the genuineness of which.was doubted. On his being examined a Smith and Wissen revolver was found in his pocket and a globule containing what is supposed to be some strong poison. The man has been lodged in, prison.

ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT WARRINGTON. At the Borough Police Court, on Monday, Isaac Fitetue, a man of mild and respectable appearance, and apparently about 60 years of age, residing at 38, Green-st., was brought up to answer a charge or attempting bo commit suicide by cutting his throat with a table knife, that morning. Chief Constable Hunt said the prisoner used, five years ago, to work at Atherton Quay ironworks, as a labourer. Ho had been for some years subject to epileptic fits, and latterly they had become more frequent. Pre- vious to that morning he had given warning that he had something of the kind coming on. The Chief Constable suggested that he should be handed over to the relieving officer and the doctors for them to determine what course to pursue with him, for he did not think he was resnonsible.—The prisoner's wife, a very respectable-looking, elderly woman, stated that he was the father of eleven children.— Dr. Joseph, who was not sworn, stated that the prisoner had inflicted twa incised wounds, about half an inch iong, in his throat. They were not serious,, though they might have been, as there was considerable 'hemmorhage from them. He had over and over again expressed a decided disposition to commit suicide, in fact homicide, having threatened his wife; and a few rare' ago he had recommended that he should be put under control, but he had then no distinct delusions, and he supposed the medical men would not certify him insane. Now he seemed to have one or two delusions, and these, although not of a fixed character, would certainly render him temporarily insane. Efe would not take hia- medicine , sometimes, fancying that he(Dr. Joseph) pcisoned it ; and he imagined also that his wife wanted to paison him, , and had such delusions as that the birds were always , singing.—Mrs. Fitchue made an unsworn statement, and said she had coped with him for six years, and had not been afraid of him till lately, but had concealed'her fear ii-om him. He had fits once or twice every month. They lasted a week, and then he went quite out of his mind, so that altogether he would be bad for a fortnight. She had had a bard struggle with him.—The Bench ordered that the poor man be handed over to the reliev- inr:offleers to see what they could do with him.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

Nov REPORTING ANIMAL DISEASE. Elizabeth Monks,of Arpley,was charged at the Borough Police Court on Tuesday with failing to report the fact that a pony belonging to her was suffering from " farcy." Mr. J. L. -Whittle, Town Clerk, appeared for the prose- cution, and stated that according to the Act of Parlia- ment such a case of animal disease must be reported to a constable of the borough police force. His instructions were not to press the case, but he must point out that if persons having animals affectbd in this way would only give proper notice the Corporation would be enabled to cope with diseases. Recently the eutbreak of pleuro- pneumonia had cost them £4oo.—Mr. Norman, sanitary inspector, deposed to the defendant having the animal in a stable by itself, apart from her other stables, and to the pony being certified by Mr. Ferguson as suffering from the disease. Other evidence having been given, the defendant pleaded that she did not know the pony was suffering from a dangerous disease.—The Bench considered that she must have known this, she having kept the animal isolated, but contented themselves with record- ing a Conviction, and calling- upon her to pay costs. •

THEFT FROM A 'AmenNo-Housn. At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, Robert Burgess, a coal-yard labourer, who had been a lodger at the common lodging-house, of Francis Robin- son, 93 Tanners-lane, was charged with stealing Bs., from the trousers pocket of John Smith, otherwise known as John Kelly, a fellow lodger. It appeared from the evidence that the following were the circumstances. The prosecutor and the prisoner, who came to the town on Tuesday from Widnes, slept together, and on Satur- day night the prosecutor when he went to bed left his trousers on the bed. The prisoner came to bed drunk, and in the morning the prosecutor found that the money had disappeared. The prisoner was in bed, and he helped prosecutor to look for the money, but it could not be found. Information was given to the police, and the prisoner was apprehended. He denied the theft, and stated that he had not more than 3s. and odd upon him, but there were seven shilling pieces discovered upon him—the stolen money being in that coinage—and 5Ad. in copper. This money he said he had worked for at Richardson's coal yard, La fchford ; but he had earned no mare than is. Bd. there. He had been drinking all the week. He was committed for trial at the Liverpool Quarter Sessions.

div.head: THEFTS BY A BOY.
div.p: THEFTS BY A BOY.

At the Borough Police Court, on Tuesday, Thomas Dawkin, aged 16, lately an errand boy, in the employ of Madame Lilley, milliner and mantle maker, 123, Bridge- street, was charged with stealing Bs. in cash and five penny postage stamps, the property of Annie French, employed by Madame Lilley, also with stealing on Mon- day is. the property of the same lady. Chief Constable Hunt said the prisoner was an illegitimate son whose mother had forsaken him at Penketh some years ago, he being subsequently taken to the workhouse,and after that employed by a farmer at Penketh till three weeks since, and then entering the service of Madame Lilley. He had spent the Bs. in the fair ground in the Market-place. Miss Annie French deposed that on the previous Wed- nesday morning she placed her purse containing the money and stamps in the middle of a box, and on Satur- day she found the purse in the corner of the box quite empty. On Monday morning she placed a marked shilling under the scissors in the shop, and an hour later. during which time the lad had been left there by him- self, missed the coin. He was then given into the cus- tody of Inspector Bowen.—The Inspector deposed to the lad producing the shilling from somewhere in the shop, denying that he had stolen it. and to his admitting the theft of the Bs. and stamps. The prisoner now pleaded ,pilty to the theft of the latter, but asserted that he merely removed the shilling. He was sent to prison for seven days' hard labour for the first-named offence, and in the other case a conviction was recorded. A WOMEN'S QUARREL IN SCOTLAND-ROAD.—Two TRADES- MEN'S WIVES IN COLLISION. At the Borough Police Court yesterday,Susan Murphy, ; wife of Gregory Murphy, hairdresser, Scotland-road,! was charged with using threatening language to Elizabeth Gleave, a married woman, keeper of a herb beer shop, next door.—Mr. A. Browne appeared for the complain- ant and Mr. P. Davies for the defendant. Mr. Browne stated that the complainant was sweeping the entry when the defendant came out, and with an oath remarked that she was sweeping the entry again. Mrs. Gleave replied that it would take one body to be always at it to keep the entry clean, and this led to the defendant call- ing her an English bastard, and charging her with keeping a house of accommodation, which charge had caused unpleasantness between the complainant and her husband. She also threatened the complainant. Evidence having been given on the complainant's side supporting this statement, Mr. Davies characterised the dispute as a storm in a teapot, and said it would be a great deal better if these women would wash their dirty linen on their own premises instead of bringing it before the court. Mrs. Murphy strenuously denied having threatened the defendant or used the language ascribed to her, but said the complainant had called her a drunkea bitch, and she had replied that she was a tallow-faced yellow-faced looking," the sentence being concluded with an unreportable epithet. She denied having charged the complainant with keeping a brothel or having men in her house all night. The case was dismissed.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. gONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman R. W. Fran- comb) and Alderman Harrison. DRUNKENNES3.—Wm. Bennett, drunk and disorderly in Mersey-St., on Saturday night,was fined is. and costs; John Thornley, drunk and disorderly in Corporation-st., on Saturday night, was fined 10s. and costs; Martin Quinn, drunk and disorderly in Bridge-st., on Saturday night, was' fined 25., the lock-up fees; Alice Thomas, I aged 19, 13th appearance, drunk and disorderly in St. Mary's-st., the previous night, also in Scotland-road, on the 26th March, was sent to prison for a month's hard labour ; James Bate, drunk and disorderly in Pinner's- brow, on the 27th ult., was fined ss. and costs; Mary Ellen Fairbrother, aged 19, drunk and disorderly in Bridge-st., on the 25th ult.—The Mayor, addressing.the prisoner, said he was only just asking Mr. Harrison whether it was possible that girls of 19 in any other town in England were brouOt up for being drunk and disorderly. After a severe admonition she was dis- missed; Louisa Hargreaves was charged with being drunk and disorderly m Fennel-st., on the 30th ult. The constable who proved the case said she was sp drunk that he advised her friends to give her salt and water to bring her to her senses. She was dismissed on the pay- ment of 3s. 9d. costs; Daniel Higham, drunk and disor- derly in Quay Fold, on the 28th ult., was fined ss. ; Henry Woods, drunk on the 26th ult., in Buttermarket- s'., was fined ss. ARMY DESSIIRTION.—Frederick William Little, charged with being a deserter since 1883, from the Royal Irish Lancers, stationed at Dublin, was ordered to be con- veyed to Strangeways Jail, to await an escort. BAD LANGIJAGE.—TMX W RON@ MAN SUMUONED.—JaineS Garity WAS charged with Using 'indecent language in Scotland-road, on Saturday night. He strongly denied his guilt, stating he had not been in Scotland-road for seven years, but afterwards altered this period to 12 months. While the case was proceeding P.C. Cooper caused an unusual diversion by stating that the man in the dock was not the man wanted. It appeared that it

was another James Garity who was wanted. The pri- soner was dismissed, and he was ordered to be paid 4s. for the loss of his day's work. PITCH AND Toss.—Edward Smith, Michael Kelly, Cornelius Ward, and Albert Ward, for playing at pitch and toss, for money on Sunday week, in Howley Fields, were fined is. and costs, or Bs., each.—Joseph Wilcock, Alfred Barker. William Johnson, Henry Johnson, and John Dunbobbin, all little boys, were charged with the , like offence in the same place, on the same date, but it appeared that they had only a penny among them and that therefore they had not the means for gambling, and they were all discharged.—William and Edward Walms- ley, James and John Titchett, Joseph Denman, Thomas and William Edmonds, and Alfred Barker, most of them young boys,were charged with playing at pitch and toss for money, at Town End, on the 28th ult. All pleaded guilty except William Edmonds, who could not be iden- tified, and the charge against him was withdrawn. The Walmsleys, Denman, and Barker, were fined is. and costs each, and the iitchetts and Thomas Edmonds the costs each.

HAVING CHIMNEYS ON FlRE.—James Gleason and Henry Turner for having their chimneys on fire on the 31st and 28th ult. respectively, were fined is. each. TITESDAY.—Before Messrs. W. Owen (chairman), and E.
M. Ciosfield.

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—James Flowers,licensed cab d!rver, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bank Quay-se., and refusing to quit the Patten Arms,the previous night. Mrs. Kiernan, the landlady, had dis- charged him for being drunk, but he came back and demanded 2s. 3d. more than she had paid him, and re- fused to leave the house, acting as though he was still employed. The defendant denied being drunk and said Mrs. Kiernan had stopped es. out of his last two week's wages. He was fined ss. and costs. NON-ATTENDANCD AT SCHOOL. .—The following cases were dealt with at the instance of Mr. G. Riley, school attendance officer :—Mary Bennett, 120, Pierpoint-st., fined 2s. 6d. including costs; Peter Gleave, forgeman, 21, Howard-st., 2s. 6d., including costs ; Wm. Dagnall, forgeman, 16, Warburton-st., whose mother pleaded that the child " enjoyed " bad health, was fined ss. in- cluding costs, and had another attendance order made against him; Harry Forster, forgeman, 80, Lythgoe's- lane, fined ss. including costs ; James Holbrook, 9, An- trobus-st., labourer at the manure works, 2s. 6d., includ- ing costs ; John Horan, tanner, 28, Vere-st., had an order for attendance made against him ; Enoch Lockett, forge- man, Gladstone-st.,2s. 6d. including costs; John Rutter, 30, Kerfoot-st., 2s. 6d. including costs. The case of Ellen Wells, shopkeeper, 2, Owen-st., was dismissed. John Wright, hawker, 17, Turner-st., 2.5. 6d. including costs.
THURSDAY.—Before Major Pickmere (chairman) and

Captain Ridgway. MON-MAINTENANCE.—Joseph Rigby, formerly a coal- dealer in Dallam-lane, was charged by Mr. B. Shearer, on behalf of the Guardians, with non-maintenance of his children. He had contributed nothing to their support for four years.—Mr. Pemberton,uncle to the children,said the defendant's father-in-law had set him up in business in the coal trade, but through his drinking habits the business had collapsed.—The defendant said the children were taken from him and he was not allowed to see them. He was in debt and had been unable to pay. He had earned £1 per week from the Canal Company since January,and he would allow ss. a week.—Mr. Pemberton said he could not trust the defendant to pay anything, and he was sent to prison for a month's hard labour. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—John Dillon, drunk and dis- orderly in Buttermarket-st., the previous night was fined ss. and costs, or? days. ARMY DESERTION.—Robert Chambers was charged with being a diserter from H.M. Royal Fusiliers in September last, and sent to Strangeways jail to await an escort. FRIDAY.—Bef..re Mr. John White (chairman), Alderman Harrison, and Dr. J. H. Gornall. ON PREMISES FOR AN UNLAWFUL PURPOSE.—Thomas Leatherbarrow, 12th appearance, was charged with being found at minutes to one that morning on the premises of Mrs. Green, St. James's-st., Latchford, with intent to commit a felony. P.C.'s Priestley and Turner deposed to finding the prisoner in Mrs. Green's hay loft at the time mentioned, with a box of matches on him, and not asleep. He was known to be a convicted thief, and was therefore taken into custody. He was sent for 14 days' bard labour. VAGRANCY.—Joseph Wilson was charged with being found sleeping at 20 minutes past 2 that morning in a straw shed belonging to Elizabeth Monks, of Arpley, and having no visible means of subsistence. He had a pipe and matches on him. He was dismissed with a caution.

NON-MAINTENANCE OF A SON.—Christopher Green- house was charged with not contributing to the main- tenance of his son Edward on board the " He offered to pay is. a week, and an order waS made for payment of this amount. ASSAULTS.—Luke Lowe was charged with assaulting Emma Hayes on the 30th ult. The complainant said she was having her tea and heard the defendant abusing her to a woman living next door. She came out and he took a running kick at her. Mrs. Morris gave corrobor- ative evidence, but a Mrs. Oaks said Hay es was the ag- gressor, attacking her with a jar,and her son coming out to her with the poker. The case was dismissed.—Eliza Ann Morris was charged with assaulting Mary Jane Hayes on the 28th ult. and bound over in her husband's recognisances to keep the peace for six months, and ordered to pay costs.

. RUN CORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. James Reynolds and Mr. Henry Reynolds. TEMPORARY TRANSFER.—The license of the Navigation Inn, Canal-st., was temporarily transferred from Thomas Jones to John Linton. DOG AT LARGN.—Arthur Gough, was fined is. and Asts Bs. 6d. for allowing his dog to be at large unmuzzled. A SCHOOL CASE.—John Tomlinson, of Halton, was fined ss. for neglecting to send his children regularly to school. • DRUNK AND *DISONDERLY.—For this offence John Jack- son, Wm. Rigby, and Wm. Cooke, were each fined ss. and costs; Thomas Millington was ined 10s. and costs and Mary Ellen Wilkinson 2s. 6d. and costs.

div.head: WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS
div.p: WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS

TRURSDAY.—Before.Mr. Pilkington and Mr. BirchalL DRUNKENNESS.—Mary Allen, James Campbell, Bridget Carthy. Catherine Moorcroft, and James Haverty were each fined ss. and costs for drunkenness.—Catherine Owen was fined 10s. and costs. A HALEBANK WOMEN'S Row.—Catherine Jennings of Halebank, was bound over to keep the peace for three months for using threats to Mary Moss.—She was also charged with assaulting Margaret Mercer. Witnesses were called to prove that it was a fight, and she was dis— missed.

- - SCHOOL BOARD CASES.—Twelve parents were summoned by the School Board ,for not sending their children regu- larly to school, and the usual fine of ss. was imposed in each case.—The bench reftmed to grant a commitment against Alice Brown, of IVlVarrington-road,.because she had a husband. The husbuad was, however, away from. home at the time the offence took place.
WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY .—Before Mr. F. H. Gossage and Lieut.-Col. Gaskell.

DRlMlC.—Thomas Leeson, William Bennett, and James- ' Maken were each fined ss. and costs for being drunk and disorderly. VAGRANCY.—James Mulraney, a tramp, was charged with begging, and was dismissed on promising to leave the town. ROBBERIES.—AmeIia Roberts, of Dittont aged ten years, pleaded guilty to stealing a gosling valued at is. 6d. the property of Sarah Conroy, shopkeeper, of Ditton. She was discharged with a caution..—John Red- mond, Pool-st.. was charged with stealing a couple of rabbits on Saturday, the property of Mr. Tames Mc- Cririe, Victoria-road, Widnes. A boy named Richard Wycherley, of Leeton-st., deposed to seeing the prisoner steal ti-e rabbits, but that when the policeman arrived at the prisoner's house the rabbits were dressed and could not be identified.—The prisoner was fined 20s. or 14 days' hard labour. TTIE ALLEGED STABBING AFFRAY.—IhnIa Hyland, of 20, Waring-st., was charged on remand with causing grievous bodily harm to Timothy Burnstby stabbing him on the left thigh on the 28th ult. Dr. Hutchinson said the injur,ed man was still unable to attend the court,and the prisoner was again remanded for a week.

A KNOWING Doct.—The "Liverpool Courier" relates the following true story of a dog.—" On a certain street in Liverpool, one of the drinking troughs supplied by the proprietor of Hudson's Soap, for thirsty dogs, was placed and regularly filled with water, To this trough. at a certain hour every day, a knowing dog came (hav- inig once acquired the habit),sometimes bringing a friend with him. When winter came the trough was taken away, but the dog continued his daily visits to the spot where the trough had been, and would stand waiting, whining, and wagging his tail until the kindly people in the shop brought him his accustomed beverage in a basin. After this touching" appeal perhaps Mr. Hudson will, no doubt, provide this particular suppliant with a water trough both winter and summer.

div.p: 171 E EXAMINER, SATURTAY, APRIL 11, 1891.

minor then fell to the homestera from a kick by Bate. Evans intercepted a pass intended for Carter, and an- other run by Evans ended in his passing to; high to Barnes. The Warringtonians had now evidently realized i their position, for we now found them playing n some- thing like their true form, and after another passing dis- play, Jolley ran in from a line out, Barnes giving his side the lead with a nicely placed goal. A grand run by Fair Turner from the restart ended in his passing forward, and Evans and Bandies each looked like scorers from rushes. Jolley was next prominent, being pulled down on the line, whilst Randles had a similar experience a moment later. Warrington should certainly have scored from a kick by Evans, and two minors fell in rapid suc- cession. However, the Warringtonians still kept on the aggressive, and Mather scored a final unimproved try of a somewhat tame game, which terminated as Warring- , 1-3-4 ; Leeds Parish Church 1-1-1.

Warrington: Sampson, back; Evans, Barn's, and Daniels, threequarters ; J. T. Bate and Mather, half- backs; Ashton, Fair Turner, Frank Turner, Berry, Ban- dies, Jolley, Nevins, Donohue, Povey, forwards. Leeds: firumfitt, back ; Newton, Carter, and Wright, threequar- ters ; Tidswell and Tebbs, half-backs; Broadbent, Eng- lish, L?ach, Hedley, Sharp, Richardson, Sutcliffs; Wor- rell and Phillips, forwards. Referee, Mr. T. Hunter, Manchester.
ASSOCIATION.

ST. ELPHIN'S ASSOCIATION V. WARRINGTON ASK.CIA- TION.—This return fixture was played on the ground of the former, off Manchester-road, before a fair number of spectators. The home team kicked off against a slight breeze, and the visitors, getting possession, made tracks for the Saints' goal, where Powell notched the first point three minutes from start. From the re-start, the sphere was kept in mid-field for a few minutes, when, Clayton and all getting away, the latter player notched the second with a splendid shot. The visitors made strenuous efforts to increase their score, but the home backs played a stubborn defence, repeatedly clearing their charge. The Association were, however, rewarded with another goal, after several futile attempts, this being from the. foot of Onions,thus bringing half-time, with Warrrington. 3 goals, St. Elphin's 0. After the restart, the Saints' , managed to keep the visitors' backs busy for a time, while at the other end fruitless attempts were made to add to the score, but the home backs were too many for them. After about 15 minutes' play, the home scored their first goal,. and, again re-starting, the visitors' for- wards, through a neat bit of passing, enabled J. Mather to score a splendid goal two minutes later. Through a scrimmage in front of goal the home team scored another goal, while the Warrington forwards made several at- tempts to lower the Saints' citadel. Thus ai good and pleasant game ended in favour of Warrington by 4 goals to 2. Warrington team : Jones goal ; Philips and Davies backs; Warburton,. J. Mather, and Parry (captain), half backs ; Clayton, .Ball, Onion, Powell, and T. Mather, for- wards. Referee,. Mr. A. Avlihg.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

"„* Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street, Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.

RUGBY. RUNCORN v. LEEDS.-.--The return match between these teams was played on Saturday, at Headingley, the at- tendance not being large. Hughes put the ball into operation on behalf of Runcorn. The home team soon displayed good form, and, after five minutes' play, Sum- mersgill scored a try. A little later on Naylor added a mond, and this surprising play stimulated the Runcorn men, who at once saw the necessity for strenuous work. An attempt to score proved unsuccessful, and Leeds again spurted, and the game was transferred to the Runcorn quarters. Summersgill essayed a pass; but Crompton received, and the sphere was taken to mid- field. Potter ran in, and before half-time was called the home team had scored a goal, two tries, and two minors, Runcorn not having scored a point. In the second half an additional try and a minor were registered, and, not- withstanding all the efforts made by the visitors, they were unable to avert a decisive defeat, having only ob- . tallied five minors as compated with their opponents one goal, three tries, and three minors. WIDNES V. ROCHDALE Sr. CLEMENTS.—The return fix- ture between these two clubs was played on the ground of the latter, at Rochdale, on Saturday. Widnes were short of Brennan and Lyons, but St. Clement's had a very strong team. The ground was in a very bad state, and consequently the game was very slew and uninterest- ing. St. Clement's kicked off against the wind,and play settled in the centre. Thompson got possession and put in his kick, but the ball being wet and heavy, and the ground at this point several inches deep in mire, Hartles failed to pick up, and Thompson following up his kick carried the ball over the line, and scored a try. Barton, however, failed at goal. Widnes now had a look in, and for a few minutes pressed the homester. Taylor finding he was linable to get through, attempted at goal, and narrowly failed. Half time score—St. Clement's, One try ; Widnes, two minors. On changing ends Rig.., the home full back, got away, and was only brought 'down by Drummond and Taylor just in time to prevent him scoring. From this point to the close of the game Wid- nes had slightly the advantage, although they had the wind against them. At the sound of the whistle, the score was St. Clement's one try and three minors to Wid- nes three minors. TUEBROOK V. RUNCORN.—The Runcorn team engaged with Tuebrook on Wednesday evening, and as the weather was of a gloomy character only a fair number of spec- tators turned out to witness the contest. The visitors were not powerfully represented, and played 14 men throughout the game. A steady pressure was sus- tained in the visitors' 25, but the home lot being pen- alised, were driven to the other end, where Hughes initiated a passing movement among the backs, but the lost ground was recovered by a good forwaid play, and again the Runcornians were forced to defend. Exchanges took place between the respective backs, and Eccles was unfortunate in kicking into Crompton's hands, for that player had a fairly clear course, and ran in near the posts, but failed at goal. Half-time was called, with the score—Runcorn, 1 try; Tuebrook, nil. The home lot restarted, and the Runcornians got away with a rush. For a time the Brook line was jeopardised, until the home centre ran the ball out and parted the Ellams, who made further headway. A long spell of even play followed, when Crompton received from Hughes, and after dodging a trio of his opponents, kicked nicely into touch near the home line. Morris put in a magnificent run but was pulled up near the line—an effort which was fully deserving of scoring. Following a couple of packs at halfway, Abrams made off, and being closeblattended by Riley, the latter player obtained a grand try, but again the place kick failed. The home lot pulled themselves together, and all but crossed the line; but Houghton was in splendid form, and tackled and kicked in a masterly style. No other points were scored, and Runcorn won a capital game by 2 tries and 1 minor to nil.

div.head: WARRINGTON v. ST. HELENS RRCREAT lON.
div.p: WARRINGTON v. ST. HELENS RRCREAT lON.

The above clubs were engaged in a charity match on Boundary-rnad ground, St. Helens, on Thursday even- ing on behalf of the St. Helens Hospitals. Fine weather favoured the match, and the response to the appeal was in every way praiseworthy, considerably over 5,000 witnessing the tngtch. The clubs have met twice before this season, and each team claimed a win on their own ground. Warrington had a good team up, although the absence of James Bate and Jolley- had to be regretted. The Recs., however, were determined to avenge their recent defeat, and had the assistance of "'Buff "Berry (International), and Foulkes (half back for the St. Helens town club.) Seddon kicked off, and in the first few' minutes Hodgson scored from a pass by Berry, Ellison failing at the place. Nettled by this reverse, the Warringtonians attacked, and fruitless, endeavour to score were made by Barnes; Bate, and Evans. The homesters once more attacked,. but the' fine footwork of the Warring,tonians near the call of half-time was instrumental in Berry scoring for them near the corner flag.. Frank Turner took the pface, the oval striking the posts. With the scores level, the game was re-started, and a series of scrimmages monopolised the opening stages. Seddon had a shot at goat from a free kick, but luck was with the Saints a few minutes later, for an opening was presented FlOdgson from a pass by Turfon, and the Recreation were again given the lead. Ellison failed to augment. The staying powers of War- fington became especially manifest in the latter portion of the game, but the defence was stubborn,.and the final result found the score as—St. Helens Recreation, 0-2-1; Wallington, 0-1-1. The following represented Warring- ton :—Boscow, back;: Eirans, T. Barnes, and Daniels, three-quarters; J. T 1 Bate. and Mather,. half backs; Ashton, Fair Turner,. Frank Turner, Bandies, Povey, Berry, Donohue, Davies, and A. Barnes forwards. WARRINGTON v. LEEDS PARISH CHURCH.

Warrington had as their opponents ;Leeds Parish Church on Saturday, and, in the expectation of witness- ing a capital game, considerably over 5,000 turned Lout to witness the contest. In this they were disappointed, for our local team, treating their opponents in too light a fashion, had a tendency to become loose in their play, and until the last fifteen minutes there was an entire absence of that combination.which has been conspicuous of late in the Warrington ranks. The homesters were without Boscow, who had strained himself on Monday against Hartlepool Rovers, and James Bate. NV. Nevins made his re-appearance after an absence extending over four months, and met with a hearty reception. The Leeds men having arrived late, it was 3.45 before Frank Turner kicked off against the strong wind, the ball going in touch at the quarter flag. From the first throw out, Nevins lalasconspicuous in a rush to the line, and although Newtoretemporarily staved off the attack, another rush, headed by Jolley, resulted in his scoring near the corner flag. The game had only been in pro- gress a minute, and the onlookers prepared themselves for a record score. The Tykes, however, upset these calculations, for some smart play by Broadbent soon had the oval at the home quarters, and Sampson being smart- ly tackled, play hovered dangerously near the Warring- ton posts. Evans and Barnes shone with respective efforts, and Jolley was again to the fore, with a run and pass, the latter being mulled. Fair Turner with a huge kick drove the visitors back to their quarters. Frank Turner, Povey, anctAshton dribbled finely, but again the loose character of Warrington's play neutralized the efforts, and Wright and Sutcliffe, with individual dis- plays in the dribbling lin*, had their efforts seconded by Newton, the latter with a long kick placing the game at the home quarters. Wright tackled Sampson with the oval in his possession, but Berry and Donohue in a combined dribble took the oval to neutral territory. Jolley put in another fine run, and Evans failed to gather a bad pass, or a disaster most assuredly have befallen the visitors' citadel. A penalty kick against Warrington was charged by Nevins, and a passing movement by Mather, Bate. and Barnes was finished by the latter punting to Newton, who had the better of the exchange. Repeated calls from the home supporters for a glimpse of the Warringtonians' proper form were but poorly responded to, and although play was generally confined to the Tykes's 25, the play of the homesters fell off considerably in the final stages. Jolley almost scored from a line-out, but some smart play between Wright and Tebbs gave relief to the visitors, and another tall kick by Newton took play chaser to the home line. Tebbs was alnaost in from a short rush, but a moment later the oval was driven over, and Wright, taking advantage of some hesitation on the part of a home forward, promptly fell on the ball, a loud cheer greeting Newton when he placed the goal. Exchanges were frequent on the re- start, and a minor subsequently fell to the visitors. Near the call of half-time, the homesters made an effort, but Brumfitt saved, and the score at the interval read as Warrington 0-1-0; Leeds 1-0-1. With the wind in their favour, the home supporters flocked to the pavilion end, evidently under the impression that play would be confined to this quarter. Contrary to expectations, the Leeds men attacked, and altheegh Fair Turner headed a rush be3-opd the half-way flag, Wright by the aid of a heavy kick found Frank Turner placing the oval in touch at the Tykes's quarter flag. Worrall was foremost in a dribble which harrassed the home defence, but Sampson kicking well. the Churchmen now defended. The War- ringtonians still adopted their loose tactics, and Fair Tumor making his mark, his brother took the place, the oval being charged. Newton and Broadbent soon had the oval out of danger, and then the Churchmen had a look in, for a fine rush by Worrall and Leach resulted in the former scoring, Newton striking the posts with the place. The Warringtonians now realized their positloa, for they were still three points to the bad, and had only twenty minutes to play. On the drop out, a speedy ex- cursion was paid to the Leeds quarters, and Daniels being prominent with some short kicks, Carter was promptly ackled by Ashton. From the scrimmage which ensued, Mather, Bate, and Evans passed well, and the latter run- ning strongly deceived Brunifitt at the fioi3li, and scored a grand try, the same player failing to augment. div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. FOOTBALL.-RUGBY.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. FOOTBALL.-RUGBY.

Bradford 5s said to hold the best record of club per- formances, not only in Yorkshire but in England, even though the nominal Tbrkshire championship, as evidenced in the holding of the Yorkshire Cup, has not fallen to the club's lot. They have closed their official season, and have only two other benefit games to play, neither of which will count in the club's records. The season's re- turn stands at 25 wins,.three losses, and three draws, and the score made is 52 goals and 36 tries against 13 goals and seven tries.
This is rather flattering ! Mr. Murray, the Swinton secretary, received a letter on Saturday, addressed as follows :—" The Secretary of the famous Swinton Rugby football 15, Swinton, Lancashire."

The good luck which has followed Huddersfield in the Yorkshire Rugby Cup competition deserted them on Saturday, when they were knocked out by Wakefield Trinity, who have shown most consistent play in the ties. The game was fiercely contested in Bradford, rain falling heavily and drenching_players and spectators alike. J. Dawson, one of the Wakefield forwards, scored the only try of the afternoon late on in the proceedings, besides which they were credited with six minors, to the cup- holders' nothing at all. The other semi-final resulted in the success of Pontefrace,.who beat Cast Word decisively enough at Dewsbury. The final tie is fixed for the Headingley ground at Leeds to-day (Saturday.)

Just before the match between the Trinity and Huddersfield concluded Dyson made a remarkable run amid very great excitement, and looked like getting through. In fact, he had passed all but the full back,and was doubling on him when he was caught by the jersey. It was the " feattsre " of the match, the only good run during the afternoon, and he was deservedly cheered by friends and opponents alike. It looked like being another Dewsbury finish, and had'the ground been dry, I have little doubt that he would have pulled the match out of the fire. The ground was fearfully heavy and much against him.

Mr. J. W. Maclean, of Manchester, was referee in thp match Leigh v. Walkden; at Leigh, last Saturday, and at the finish he was mobbed 17 the spectators, who took exception to one of his decisions in disallowing a claim for a try. He was rather roughly handled, and but for Graham (a Leigh forward) a spectator and the police, would have fared very badly. This sort of referee mobb- ing is getting beyond a jOlte,,and the matter is likely to be brought under the notice of the Lancashire Rugby Union Committee this week.

div.head: ASMit'rAT/ON.
div.p: ASMit'rAT/ON.

The takings at the final tie between Blackburn Rovers and Notts are a record 'fbr English football, and have only once been beaten, and that was in Scotland last sea- son at the International match. The Aston Villa and Preston North End Cup tie a few years ago realised 21,200, but the gate at the final *was £454 65., out of which the Surrey C.C. take £359 Its. 6d., and the Association is credited with £1,954 14g. 6d. £359 is a largesum to pay for the use of the ground'and _expenses for one afternoon, and it is probably the last time the game will be played at the Oval on the same terms. For taking £1,296 155.4 d. in the two Cup ties between Sunderland and Notts, the Bramall-lane,neople receive 297 48., and it is hard to see why the Surrey C.C. should have morethan anyone else.

Whether the 'absence of any of the Rovers from the English team kept many away er not, as was supposed, the attendance at the international at Blackburn on Sat- urday was disappointing. There would not be more than 8,000 or 9,000 spectators present, and a large number of these had travelled by the Scotch trips. Rain held off during the afternoonv_and the splendid ground did not appear to have been much affected by the heavy showers which fell in the early part of the day. A stiff wind which blew from goal ^to goat hampered the play some- what, the Englishmen having the benefit of it during the first half. It was easily seen that the Scotch forwards were neither so good individuallyinor collectively as their antagonists,who were quicker on the ball, and combined beautifully. The efforts of the Scots were of a spasmodic order, but the English front rank frequently worked the ball the length of the ground by admirably executed passing. Goodall was the first to score after grand play by Chadwick, the latter following on with it second point, after smart work by the Derby County man. In the last quarter of an hour Watt secured the only goal for Scot- land, who were beaten by two to one.

There was certainly more than a goal in difference in the play. The cleverest forwards on the ground were the Everton left wing Chadwick and Millward, who n played magificently when facing the wind in the second' half. MillwArd's centres were remarkably well thred,, and more gcals ought to have resulted from them. Geary did fairly well in centre. but Southworth would have- done much,better. Goodall put in a lot of useful work,. but he deserved better assistance than he got from; Bas- sett. Holt-was luite a success at half back, where Ske ton did moderately, but Smith was much bolo* par. Both Howarth and Holmes came off creditably at back, the only weakness being the fondness of the first-named for dribbling the hall away from an opponent. Moon kept goal in a very clever fashion. and was superior to•Witson, his Scotch vig-ci-tti, who was rather unsteady. Walter Arnott is still unrivalled as a full back, and worked desperately hard. Hill was vastly better thamthe other two half backs,,Begbie having more than he could cope with Chadwickand Millward. Frank Watt, oflKilbirnie, and Baird, of the Heart of Midlothian, did the best work among the forwards, but they suffered for lack of better support.

div.head: LABOUR COMMISSION.
div.p: THE LABOUR COMMISSION.

It is understood that the list of nominations to the • Labour Commission, which now awaits the Queen's ap- ,proval, contains twenty-four names, including the fol- lowing :—Lord Hartington (chairman), the President of the Board of Mrade, Sir J. G. Gorst, Mr. David Dale, J.P. (Darlington), Mr. Mundella, Mr. H. H. Fowler, Mr. Abraham, Lord Derby, Mr. Austin (Secretary of the Cork Associated Trades), and either Mr. Henry Tait (Secretary of the Scottish Railway Servants' Association), or Mr. Harford (Secretary of the English Railway Servants' Association). In a communication to Mr. M`Carthy, the First Lord of the Treasury has (says the "Daily News ") expressed a readiness on the part of the Government to nominate to the Labour Commission anyone the Irish members may agree upon other than Mr. Devitt. Mr. M'Carthy, how- ever, does not intend to take further action in the matter, and has so informed Mr. Smith. On behalf of tlae Irish members he proposed the person best qualified in the public interest, and the Government declining to adopt the suggestion, the full responsibility of the position will be left with them.

div.head: SHOCKING TRAGEDY AT TYLDESLEY.
div.p: SHOCKING TRAGEDY AT TYLDESLEY.
MURDER AND SIIICIDE.--SEQVEL TO A FEND-
'NO DIVORCE SIJIT,

For the first time in the history of the township of Tyldesley it has been the scene of g murder. The particulars are extremely shocking,and the greatest consternation has been caused amongst the inhabit- ants. ft appears- that at five minutes to seven o'clock on Wednesday morning, as Mr. Thomas 'Syms, the general manager of the weaving depart- ment at Messrs. Frederick Burton and Son's Mill, was proceeding to the' works along Factory-st., be ' was met by one of the' bookkeepers namedi Philip 1 Hill, who presenting a, five-chambered reiolver at him, fired a shot 'which struck him in the. right breast. Syms uttered a cry„ and ran about a 4 dozen yards, when he fell, dying almost immediately- The murderer,seeing his victim run off ,fired a second shot, but the bullet struck the wall. The murderer then made his way into the mill, and meeting a woman named Mrs. Vaughan, an employee, cried out, 'Where's James; where's James (meaning another bookkeeper). I cannot live; I cannot stand it any longer." He ran through the ware- house, and let himself into his own office, and, immediately shot himself in the right side of his head, death. being instantaneous. When Syme- was taken home and a doctor sent for he at first said death was due to a fit or apoplexy. It was discovered immediately afterwards however, that blood was flowing from the breast, and the doctor, mak- ing a further examination, found that the deceased had received a bullet wound, from which there was no doubt death had resulted. Both men were-well known in the neighbourhood, each having been employed at the mills for over thirty years. Hill, it is said,hae entertained the idea for some time past that his fellow-workmen have been conspiring against him, and endeavouring to oust him from his situation; but so far as carebe ascertained, there was no foundation for any such belieff. To use Hill's own words-,.he felt himself boycotted, and it is strongly suspected that when he called out "Where's- James ?" he had an intention' of also shooting James iThsworth, the other bookkeeper. The general opinion is that Hill's mind has become unhinged from a variety of causes, the chief being that he waea co-respondent in a divorce suit which was shortly to be, held, in which the petitioner claimed £O,OOO -damages: On the previous day (Thesday) Hill and his two sisters had been in consultation with a local firm of solicitors hr connection with the matter. The shocking affair has created a profound sensation in the district, and is the chief topic of conversation: The mur- dered man was sixty-three years of age. and Hill had turned fifty-two years of age. Mrs. Vaughan, of Chapel-street, Tyldesley, vehn is em- ployed as a roller coverer at the mill, states that at a ; quarter to seven on Wednesday morning, she was in the ' warehouse cellar when she heard reports of a pistol_ She saw Philip Hill, who seemed strangely excited,. tremb- ling violently, with ai pistol in his hand. Hill asked her " Where is James ?' meaning Unsworth "-I:cannot stand it any longer. I cannot live." She turned away, whereupon he said he would not harm her. She went again into the cellar;, and heard reports of shots, and afterwards the sound- of a body falling. She • did- not know why Hill wanted Unsworth, as she was not aware that there was any difference between the two- men. Much difficulty was experienced in getting the stbry from the woman, as she is confined to her house, the shock to- her nerves having prostrated her. Hill, the murderer, had been- at the mill for over thirty years, and had worked,himself up from-the position of a scavenger:. The ' relations-of-the two men appeared to be of a friendly nature. Much sympathy isexpressed with the family of Syms, who was widely respected. He leaves a widow,, two daughters and a son.

div.head: rHE. INQUEST.
div.p: rHE. INQUEST.

An inquest was opened,on Thursday morning atiTyl desley, on the body of Thomas Syms, aged 63,1. manager, and Philieas Hill, a bookkeeper. The coroner was Mr. S. D.. Butcher, who, in opening the proceedings,. briefly alluded to the nature of the tragedy. Evidence was given' by Mary Ann Ainsworth about seeing,Hiil. shoot at Syms, and by John Kelly, relative to Hill, .fol- lowing his victim. Eliza Vaughan stated that after shoot- ing Synas the murderer asked for the bookkeeper, James- U nsworth.• John- Dickinson, night watchman, said 'that Hill was -of very weak, intellect, and was always- complaining about being boycotted by Sims • and, Unsworthi. The jury returned a verdict of wilful tzur-- der against. Hill. In the inquiry about Hill's death,Sarah Ann Woods, his sister, said her brother was weak 'botht in mind and body. The evidence of the former witness was confirmed, after which a verdict of self-murder :was. returned:.

div.head: TITE NEW RAILWAY,
div.p: TITE NEW RAILWAY,
PE'rI'rION FROM WARRINGTON.

The Warrington Town COuncil at their meetingz on, Tuesday unanimously adopted the following petitimato be presented to Parliament :--" Lancashire, Derbyshire, and Eitat•Coast Railway Bill: That a Bill is now pandit*. in your Tight honourable House, intituled 'An Act fOr making and maintaining railways in the counties-of Chester; Lancaster, Derby; Nottingham and Lincoin,". to be Tailed "The Lancashire, Derbyshire, and F,ast• Coast Railway and for other purposes.' That the town of Warrington is-one of the• chief manufacturing towns of Lancashire, and indeed bids fare eventually to become • one of the leading industrial towns of the kingdom. That whilst the town possesses entensive railway facilities, it nevertheless has no railway connection whatever with o. large- and rich agricultural portion of the county of Chester immediately adjoining the town on the south- east and eminently situated for residental purposes, and' in addition the existing railway communication between Warrington and Knutsford, Macclesfield, Buxton, Chesterfield, Lincoln, and the Midland Counties is incon— venient and circuitous, anctleaves much to be desired. That the railway proposed to be authorized by the said, Bill will, in the opinion of your petitioners, supply the deficiency in the railway facilities of Warrington, pointed outin the preceding paragraph of this petition, Connect Warrington by a new and direct route with the great coalfield of North Derbyshire and Nottinghamshire, afford, additional means of transit, develop trade, increase the presperitv of the town, and be a great public benefit and advantage. Your- petitioners, therefore, .mot humbly pray your right honourable House that the-said Billitnay pass into law..

div.head: LICEITSING QUESTION.
div.p: THE LICEITSING QUESTION.

Mt. Scott Bankes, chairman of the Flinshire Quarter Sessions, referred to the licensing question in his charge to the Grand Jury on. Wednesday. He should not- like see the magistrates withdraw licenses " capriciously," but he pointed out that there were in the county far too many public-houses fcrthe needs of the people. Inlaid petty sessional division there were 110 licensed houses tor 10,000 people, and in another division 40 such houses for 4,000 people. NO. new licenses, he held, would be. granted in the county for a long time to come. Lord Dradbourne, another chairman of Quarter Sessions, ad- dressing the Graneljnry at Canterbury, expressed the opinion that applicants for" renewals" were notoin the same position " inlaw "as applicants for new. licenses. Otherwise, he said,." it would be the greatest, discour- agement to trade and the greatest injustice to vested interests." His lordship would do well to read again 'carefully the judgment of Lords Herschell and 3ramwe4l in "Sharp v. Waltellekl." Mr. Penhryn, ef the Surrey Sessions,has advised." the trade "to do something them- selves in the way of lessening the number, of pubbc- houses ; but it is doubtful if the "happy, despatch" will be populapwith the publicans. The decision of the House of Lordsin "Sharp v. Wakefield " waareferred to op Wednesday at Bolton Quarter Sessions, by Mr. S. Pope, Q.C., the Recorder, as one that would' have far- reaching effects.. Be wished to point out, however,that as the result of theruling was to establish the fact that magistrates could exercise their discretion in dealing with renewals just as in the case of fresh applications for licenses, so they must taut care not to be carried away by any preconceived ideas, but do theirs duty. j)odicially and dispose.a all cases on their merits..

div.head: IRELAND.
div.p: IRELAND.
MR. PARNELL IN DUBLIN.

On Sunday afternoon a great meeting was held in Phcenix Park, Dublin under the auspices of the Political Prisoners' Amnesty Association, the•object of' which is to obtain the release of Irish political prisoners confined in English gaols. Mr. Parnell and the speakers addressed audiences from a brake, which was drawn up in that portion of the park known as the ".Nine acres."—Mr. Parnell said the Liberals had always been distinguished for making political prisoners and, the Tories for letting there out of prison—(laughter)—and white the Liberals had pelted the Irish people with hailstones, the Tories hid. sometimes 'given them some of the gentle rain from heaven. (Cheers.) The resolution was then put to the meeting and carried, after which the proceedings ter- minated. The Press Association says :—Mr. Gladstone, telegraph- ing from Brighton in reply to the inquiry whether there was any truth in the statement made by Mr. Parnell in the Phcenix Park on Sunday,,that Mr. Gladstone received some of the dynamite party of America at Hawarden, and ascertained their opinion as to whether they would accept the Nome Rule Bill of 1888 as a final settlement of the Irish question. says the statement described is abso- lutely false from beginning to end.

div.head: IRISH TENANTS' DEFENCE.
div.p: IRISH TENANTS' DEFENCE.

At a meeting of the, Irish Tenants' Defence Association on Tuesday in Dublin Mr. Sexton, M.P., presiding, the secretary was instructed to write to Mr. M'Carthy and Mr. Parnell, pointing out that the Estates Committee account in the name of Mr. John Dillon was overdrawn £3,000, and there were further urgent liabilities to the extent of zamo and calling upon them to release a sunffromthe Paris fund Rufficient to meet these demands and provide for future liabilities. Mr. Harrington and Dr. Kenny, who did not attend the meeting, wrote com- plaining of inadequate notice.
WARRINGTON MUSICAL- SOCIETY.
LAST CONCERT OF TEE, SEASON.

The Warrington Musical Society,gave its fourth and closing concert for the season in, the Public Hall, on Tuesday evening, when, for the.4.-Irst time before a Warrington audience, Mendelssohn's "Hymn of Praise " was performed. The second part of the programme consisted of a number of miscellaneous vocal and instrumental items. The hallpresented an animated appearance, being filled in ,every part by an enthusiastic audience. From the gallery espe- cially the effect was even. brilliant;. the strong muster in the dress seats, and the overfrowing numbers in the ranks of the chorus and ' or- chestra lending a pleasing variety of colour to the scene. The society is to he congratulated on the eloice of capablo• artistes for the principal vocal parts, and also in the selection of a, solo instru- mentalist who added not a little to the interest of the concert.

The "Hymn of Praise" differs materially from oratorios and cantatas generally, inasmuch as great irominenc,e is given to the orchestral portions of the work. The com- position is best described as a"Symphony-cantata." Three movements,utilising the whole resources of the orchestra, prelude the entry the voices, and each of these pos- sesses features strongly contrasted in subject and tone colour. Probably the second will find most favour, though the concluding "Adagio," preparing the audience, as it does, for the graver sentiment of vocal portions immediately following it, must be awarded the palm for beauty of phrase and diversity of treatment. It is ple,asing to record that the ordeal of the symphony was passed through in a manner which does infinite credit to the Musical Society's fine orchestra, and its painstak- ing and energetic conductor. The Society has made un- mistakable progress,both as to its band and thorus,.with- in the season just closing, and though Tuesday's perform- ance must rank as cne of its finest achievements,further developments may beconfidently looked forward to, as the result of the Society's improved organisation and management. The chemises throughout the "Hymn of Praise," and the part-songs in the second portion, of the concert, were all characterised by a promptness in the "attack," and a flexihilty in volume ef tone and general expression, which is the sure outward token of con- scientious work done in rehearsal. The great chorus is, of course, that announcing the departing night and heralding the approaching day, and in this and in the sueceeding unaccomr.anied "choral," the best qualities of the society's chorus were made manifest. The part- song "Beware," was undoubtedly the gem of the second half of the programme, so far as the chorus was con- cerned. It is seldom that a finer effect of "oneness" is reached by so large a body of singers. The quaint archness of expression thrown into it resulted in a hearty encore, the second performance being even better than the first. Miss Anna. Williams was in fine voice. Her singing is at all timeaimbued with more orless dramatic fervour, and her rendering of the principal part in the cantata left nothing, to be desired. The well,known duet " I waited on the Lord," in which Mrs. Dobson was associated with Mis,s Williams, was sung with fine expression and a nice balance of both the principal parts and the subdued choral accom- paniment. Mrs. Dobson must certainly be credited with a moiety of the honours of this impaAant number. Miss Williams later in the evening sang" There's a bower of roses " (Villiers Stanford), and "When the heart is young" (D. Buck). The last was perhapsthe most pleas- ing of the two, bu:ethe interpretation of both was ade- quate and wholly artistic. The tenor soles-In the cantata were safe in the hands of Mr. Edwin Houghton, who has already won favour frinn a Warrington audience. 4. He counteth all your sorrows," received all the tender and thoughtful treatment necessary to its due perform- ance, and the duet; "My song shall always," in which Miss Williams and Mr. Houghton joined, proved one of the features of the. evening. Mr. Houghton sang in the second part of the programme "The flight of ages," and rising to the climax of this song easily and with no undue straining, he won a vociferous recall. To this he responded with Vincent Wallace's ever-popular "Let me like a soldier fall," and still further delighted the audience. As a solo violincellist, Fierr•Carl Fuchs, must, as a matter of course, be expected to carry off a large share of the honours. His charming style is already familar to habitues of the concert-room iraWarringtori. Suffice it therefore to say that, alibe.in the graver por- tions of Marcello's " Sonate " and in the. graceful intricacies of Popper's " Tarentella,':- Herr Fuchs gave unalloyed pleasure to the audience and added still another to his signal successes. Mr. Frank H. Crossley, the Musical Society's conductor, muslt;le heartily congratu- lated upon the undoubted ability and energy he has shewn in carrying forward the woric,cf the seciety through the season just closing, a season which will be notable in the society's annals both as to the- character of the works essayed in peefonnance, and as to the manner in which those works have been put before the public. It should be mentioned that Mr. J. B. Caldwell presided ably and efficently at the organ,and that Mt. F. W. Reynolds played the pianoforte accompaniments, to the songs and cello solos, with unexceptionable taste and skill. The society's indefatigable secretary, Mr. W. B. Atkin, also merits a meed of praise for his admirable organisation of the sea- son's concerts.

div.head: ST. PETER'S TEA PARTY.
div.p: ST. PETER'S TEA PARTY.

This annual gathering, which this year has been held later than usual, took place in the schoolroom, John-st., on Monday. Nearly a hundred of the parishioners sat down to tea, the tables being pre- sided over and the arrangements carried out by the following ladies :—Mesdames Green, Payne, Hill, Richardson, Davies, Ratcliffe; the Misses Edgar,BilA- shaw, Jnes,. 4te. After tea the usual meeting and entertainment took place. The Vicar (the Rev. T. Rigby" presided. The Vicar referred to some of the events of the past year. With reference to their new church, he thought that as they had waited so long for it it ought to have abright future, a future of usefulness and prosperity. The prosperity of a church did not de- pend upcnthe clergy entirely, though it did to a certain extent, but upon the laity. The first thing that was re- quired was-zeal. When the laity were proud of their church and anxiou,sto.help it in every way, anxious for its usefulness and welfare, then the church was pros- perous. The churchneeded keeping up. Some people thought that a church paid for itself. The people at St. Peter's, he considercd,were very fortunate. If they be- longed to any other religious body but the Church of England thsy.would have te keep their own clergy. The parishioners-of St. Paces were not asked to contribute anything to. the stipend of Mr. Buckton or himself; all they were asked to do.was to support the ordinary ex.-- penses of the church and the Sunday school. They had two Sunday echools in connection with St. Peter's, with about 400 scholars on the books. As the schools needed money to carry, themeni.he proposed to have special an- nual sermons •to pay the working expenses. They could also do with a great deal more money for the siciri and, poor in a parish like theirs. When they had done other things necessary ia the parish,. he thought. the endowment of the living should next be considered. Though he had heen their Vicar for 2t years, he had as yet received nothing like £2OO. 140 thought they should feel thankful to their neighbours in Warrington and round about for what they had done for St. Peter's. (Applause:). If they looked at the list or subscriptions to the church they would see what a great number of people had helped them. people upon whom' they had not the-slightest claim The greater portion ofp the proceeds of the bazaar-came out of the pockets 0.- people who did not belong to St. Peter's, and he really thought the congregation and parishioners ought to be ' very thankful to. the people who had come forward so. nobly. After paying all expenses-, they had left the hand- some balance of £832. Of ciourse„ta att!bin that result much hard work,had been entailed, and tn cOnCIUSiAn might say that he did not know a single church which had been started under such favourable circumstances as St. Peter's. (Applause.) An interesting. programme was then gone through. Songs were given by Mrs. Sutton, Mr. and Mrs. Ward, and instrumental music was furnished by the liev. 11- Buckton and Mr_ and Miss Mather. Mr. Riley was the accompanist.

CONCERT AT THE WARRINGTON LIBERAL CLUB. COUNCILLOR PIERPOINT SPEAKS OUT.

On Monday evening another concert was given in the Warrington Liberal Club in aid of the forthcom- ing Liberal Association bazaar. There was a good attendance. Mr. W. Pierpoint presided, and, after the proceedings had been opened with a piano solo, "Zampa" (Herrod), by Mr. Walter A. Wood,addressed those present. He said the object of their meeting there that night was to provide funds for the pur- pose of helping the Committee to organise and carry out and bring to a satisfactory conclusion the Liberal bazaar, and he thought the Liberal party had really very good grounds of excuse for bringing before them the subject of a bazaar. Let them con- sider for a few moments the position of the Liberal party in Warrington, and remember that the political propaganda of Liberalism there had been carried on for a great number of there Years by a small band of gentlemen who had provided nearly the whole of the funds necessary for carrying on that work. He would remind the audience also that the party had suffered to his mind almost irre- Parably in the loss of Mr. Gordon McMinnies, Mr. George Crosfield, Mr. Samuel Rigby, and other of their friends who in consequence of political difficulties had seen fit to sever their connection with them. He hoped it would not be very long before they,seeing the error of their ways,would come back to the Liberal camp, which Lie felt they had never any right to leave. (Applause.) Although the Liberals of Warrington had amongst them a great number of earnest members, and young men of ability who were willing and anxious to give all the time they possibly could to further Liberal interests, of course, this could not be done without pounds, shillings, and Pence. While he could tell that audience as treasurer to the Liberal party in the district that they carried on the organisation of the party at a very moderate sum—he believed he was correct in saying it cost the Conserva- tive party at least treble as much—yet he claimed that the Liberal party in Warrington, despite the deficiency of funds which appeared to exist, never were so strong LS at the present moment. (Applause.) He would just ask those present to go back with him to the Ist of November last, when they had been des- cribed by some portion of the locll press as a dis- organised, disreputable lot of rabble. (Laughter.) On the Ist of November he thought they showed that Political paper that, at all events, they were very much alive, and he believed that on the declaration of the poll that day their adversaries were very much astonished to find that the Liberal party had preserved their vitality to such a remarkable extent, and had been able to give the local Conservatives the biggest licking that they ever bad in the whole of their political career. Well, he claimed that though they had done this they ought to do more. They wanted more funds placed at their disposal in order that they might have more public meetings,and distribute more literature, and generally educate the People as to what was best for them and the country. That was the excuse for the bazaar, and that was the reason they asked for money. Remarks had been made that the Liberals had no candidate, and that their object Was to provide themselves with money so that they 1 baight induce some carpet-bagger to come and contest the borough. He denied that at once. (Hear, hear.) VVhen the time came a candidate would be found. They bad one now, under certain conditions, but they wanted a permanent candidate, one who would fight and win, or, !f he lost, would be a man of sufficient courage and fight- log power to say " Well, gentlemen, we have done all We can in this election. I will stay with you and fight 4gain." (Applause.) The concert then proceeded. No fewer than six Pianoforte solos were given, in beautiful style, by Mr. W. A• Wood, Mr. A. Perris contributed a most versatile series of elocutionary performances consisting of five eitals and three readings from Shakespeare, Tennyson, and other authors, winning by his execution of ern the enthusiastic applause of the audience. Miss k,oubrough in the first part of the programme was well received in her effective rendering of " Before the Shrine." In the second part she sang " The dear little shamrock," and in response to the rapturous encore she obtained for this gave Bonnie Dundee" In the course of the evening Mr. Plinston, secretary of the amusements "Drninittee, made some remarks as to the forthcoming con- t, and on the proposition of the Rev. F. K. FREESTON, ZeOrlded by Councillor SEAW GREEN, and supported by r. TROIKAS IfORRIS, a vote of thanks was accorded with ‘rithusiasm to the Chairman and to Mr. Perris and the Other artistes.
TRE LIBERAL BAZAAR AT ST. HELENS.

The third and last days proceedings of the bazaar in the St. Helens Town Hall, under the auspices of the Liberal Association and the Women's Liberal Association, were opened on Friday by Alderman T. Cook, J.p., president of the Liberal Association, and by Mrs. Cook.—Councillor J. B. Leach, who presided, remarked that they were honoured that afternoon by the presence of those who were near and dear to them, theii president (Alderman Cook) and Mrs. Cook. Mr. Cook was their president; he was their leader, and they felt in their time of adversity that he had been a tower of strength to them. They wished to testify in every way they could their great esteem for him in coming forward at the time he did and taking their leadership and so consistently, so resolutely, and so firmly leading them through the past. Their prospects were that he would lead them to a successful issue. (Applause.) Alderman Cook said he thought they had not come to talk politics that afternoon, but had come to raise money for political purposes. In regard to the results of the forthcoming election, whenever it might come, he had very little misgiving. He thought there was no question about it, that if the industrial popula- tion of this country looked into the matter fairly and honestly they would very soon ascertain for themselves as to the side upon which their best interests were to be found. He was sure the policy which had been pur- sued by the Liberal party for many years past Past, and what they proposed to do in the future, ."uld commend itself to the attention of every right- nlinded man. He had great pleasure in declaring the bazaar open. (Loud applause.)—Councillor Walsh pro- -I:so...sed a cordial vote of thanks to Alderman Cook and 41.28. Cook for their attendance, and Councillor Jones ionded the resolution, which was passed with acclama- 1011.—In responding Alderman Cook moved a similar oMpliment to the chairman, which was seconded by Mr. -L.• Brown and adopted.—The Chairman in thanking his .Lliends for the vote, announced that Mr. Muspratt, of ....nidnes, had forwarded a contribution of £5; Mr. -Neville, M.P., of Liverpool, had sent them his greetings .r.s!lel wishes for the success of his friend Mr. Kennedy. ;„"-e also forwarded a contribution, and so had Mr. Van ;_vart, a Liverpool merchant. Similar communications 'tad also been received from other gentlemen, including kr. James Tomkinson, ex-High Sheriff of Cheshire, and the Marquis of Ripon. (Applause.)—The sales were then koeeeded with.

THE PROCEEDS. About half-past ten at night Councillor J. B. Leach flounced that the sales were over, and that the reckon- tine had come.—Councillor John Forster said that torn the commencement there had been nothing but entllusiasm on the part of all those who had made up their minds to have such a bazaar. It was no secret hat a good many people said the Liberal bazaar would end.in a fiasco, but when he told them what had been tealised they would find such prophecies were incorrect. On the first day they realised £270 13s. 101-cl., on the second day £lB3 2s. 10d., and on that, the third and el°sing day, £24o—(loud cheers)—making a total of over , • which was a most handsome and liberal contribu- ,"nn on the part of the working people of St. Helens to the Liberal cause. On behalf of the Liberal Association "thegged to tender hearty thanks to the ladies who had 'worked so arduously, to the chairman of the Bazaar Committee, and to all who had assisted.—After other gentlemen had given addresses bearing on the satisfactory results, the proceedings came to a close.

FLETT'S CELEBRATED MARMALADE.

THE WARRINGTON EXAMINER SAYS : " Tax MARMALADE TRADE.—The severe" "weather we have recently experienced in'. "this quarter has extended as far south as' "Seville. It is in the neighbourhood of" "Seville, that the oranges best suited for " " marmalade making are grown. A recent" frost (the like of which has not been ex-" " perienced for ten years); illayed havoc" "with the fruit, and, althOGgh though the" "full extent of the damage is not yet" " known, it is believed that fully one half" "the orange crop has been destroyed." "Luckily one shipment has been made to" ** Liverpool before the disaster occurred, by" , "SS " Zurburan," which has just arrived. " The Liverpool firm of W. H. Flett." "Limited, have been fortunate enough to" "have a large consignment on Board this" "vessel, but they do not anticipate getting ", "nearly sufficient to meet the demand for ' "their well known marmalade, the sale of" " which is fast increasing."
