' 818 LE HISTORY. Sir,—Your correspondent " H. C. Barnard," in what I am willing to accept as an honest though perfectly futile ' attempt "to explain" SOM6 of the "Bible difficulties" which appeared in your last issue, merely restates and confirms one of my main arguments, or rather a state- _ ment upon which an argument is founded. The central and essential idea, so far as I have been able to disen- tangle it from the somewhat involved "extracts," is that Moses was not the first and only possessor of this , fabled creation story. In this we both agree. But what ij a lame conclusion" H.C. Barnard" draws from the fact • I take the liberty to restate the idea in connection with thoconclusion .and ask your correspondent if he likes the .„ look of it: someone else knew of this fable before Moses; _ "therefore it was revealed to him by God himself." If the "friends of revealed religion," can rest their hypothesis upon this, they are content with. a very slen- der foundation. Upon one statement in this " extract" I should like further enlightenment. How does" H. C. ; Birnaid"- Lime that these fables "evidently contain the "c).. . fragments of one original truth " ? Can the universal acceptance of an error convert that into a truth? • The geocentric theory of our planetary system was no less erroneous when widely accepted than it is now when as . widely.discredited: But the real question is this—ls your correspondent prepared to sacrifice what he knows (or can know if he will.take the trouble) to be true, in .order to accept a mere tradition, contradicted by that knowledge.?—Yours Scc., Nr.• Peaketh, 5,4, 91.
JOHN PEERS.

, HONOI3R TO WHOM. :HONOUR IS DUE." -Sir;—The local papers of Saturday -last record in- -stances of bravery on the part of Warringtonians that are deserving of more than passing mention.. In the first instance,ConstaNeTurner,'of the borough force, jumped into the Mersey and rescued a child from drowning, and in the second Mr. Walter Sarnpson, of River-view, Wil- derspool-road, at great risk, got from the water an exr hausted old lady, who has, Untertunately, since died. - In the work of rescue he was assisted by Police-Sergeant Rowbotham, and in this letter I wish to give all credit to the members of the force who have so distinguished themselves. But I think that in this seCond case, it should, in justice to Mr. Sampson, be made known, that it was he who risked his life in the brave endeavour to save that e,f another, and that the part taken by the 'policeman, though useful, was after all, but a secondary on. Mr. Sampson, through some reason or 'other, Wag not asked to attend the coroner's inquest that was held last -week, or the circumstances under which he made the rescue might have been elicited in a way that it was beyond the power of the ether witnesses to state

Personally, I do not know Mr. Sampson, but I am informed that on the night the poor old lady wan- dered into the Mersey, he was suffering from indisposi- tion, and had, in fact, retired to rest when her Ceti for help was heard. Heedless of the great risk to himself,he hastily threw on a few clothes, and literally rushed from his warm bed straight into the bitterly cold water of the river, at what danger to himself can readily be imagined. An action of this kind shows so much pure unselfishness, and so much true courage, that I really cannot help ask- ing you to allow me to express my sincere admiration.— Yours, &c.,

THE GOSPELS AND THEIR AUTHORSHIP.

Sir,—Mr. Gandy has at last come face to face with the question at issue; and he proceeds to deal with Irenteus, Papia-s,and Polycarp. After his many excursions through regions of irrelevant matter, such as inapplicable and imPerfect quotations, from Mosheim, legends of councils and jumping books, questions as to Renan's and Huxley's unbelief, and lastly, but most foreign of all—Kingsley's " Hypatia "7-it is quite refreshing at length to meet my friend in something like a corner. _ _

Let me first dispose of another of his inaccurate, and too often :indiscriminative statements. He refers to my quotation from Dr. Westcott, dnd tells us that I intro- duced it to prove that the gospels were written by Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John! Now I did nothing of the kind, It was introduced todisprovehis own assertion with respect to the formation of the Canon by Councils ; and Dr. Westcott's point had not the slightest reference to the authorship of the gospels, or to any other of the sacred books. The subject with him at the moment was what books had been traditionally received as holy Scrip- ture irrespective of any question of authorship whatever. If I had another opponent to deal with except my honest-minded friend, I should have to accuse him of juggling in this matter; but this I an44,ure he is not capable of. I can only'account for it tWs he was scared by that, to him, spectre-word " tradaton," and that 'without any further examination, or reflection, herushed at it full-tilt, as the knight in " Don Quixote "always does at the sight of a windmill. He may dismiss there- fore as the wildest fancy that Dr. Weetcott gives any support to the notions that the gospels are not the pro- duction of their reputed authors. But to come to the testimony of Peplos, I must frankly confess that a more garbled statement, coupled with a more absurd specimen of logic, I have seldom met with, than in the brief paragraph Mr. Gandy gives us touching Papias. Remember that this ancient witness was born about the year A.D., 70; that he knew men who were the personal disciples of seven of the apostles ; of John, Matthew, Andrew, Peter, Philip, Thomas, and James. He knew two daughters of the Apostle Phillip who belonged •to the church in Hieropolis, of which he (Peplos) was bishop; and he had also known' twa men who were immediate disciples of our Lord. With all these sources of information concerning our Lord's life and teaching, he declares that the Gospel of Mark is an authentic narrative. He does so in the following words: —" The Elder John," he says told him, "that Mark hav- ing become the interpreter of Peter wrote down accurately everything that he remembered with- out, however, recording in order what was either said or done by Christ.' For neither did he hear the Lord nor did he follow him, but afterwards, as I said, attended Peter, who adapted his instructions to the needs of his hearers, but had no design of giving a connected account of the Lord's Oracles. So then Mark made no mistake when he wrote down some things as he remembered them ; for he made it his one care not to omit anything that he heard, or to set down any false statement therein" (Eusebius B. chap. 39.) Now this passage is taken from a work by Papias called an " Exposition " or "Interpretation of the Lord's Oracles which work was extant long after the time of Eusebius. In the preface to the same, Papias says—" I shall not regret to. subjoin to my interpretations whatsoever I have at anytime accurately ascertained and treasured up in my memory, as I have received it from the Elders,and have recorded it in order to give additional confirmation to the truth, by my testimony.' For I have never, like many, been delighted to hear those that tell many things; but those that teach the truth ; neither those that record foreign precepte, but those that are given from the Lord to our faith and that come from the truth itself. But if I met with any one who had been a follower of the Elders anywhere, I made it a point to enquire what' were the declarations of the Elders. What was said by Andrew, Peter. or Philip—Thomas, James,John,Matthew or any other of the disciples of our Lord. What was said by Aristion and the Presbyter John, disciples of the Lord; for I do not think that I derived so much benefit from books as from the living voice of those that are still, surviving." (Euseb. 111. chap. 39,) Now what are the facts involved in this testimony? Papias sits down to write an " Exposition " or a corn-, mentary upon what he calls "The Oracles of the Lord." He mentions the narratives written by Matthew and Mark respectively; he then seeks for illustrations additional and confirmatory not from other "books," or traditions, which then abounded on every hand, out from men who were the immediate disciples of the Apostles, and from two disciples of the Lord whom he had known personally, He discards other current "books "—not the works of Matthew and Mark which Were a part of the "Oracles of the Lord" he is about to interpret, but he seeks con- firmation of these from the utterances of "'rho living ot those that are still surviving." Notice then the perverse twist, as absurd en the face of it as it is perverse, to say "that he frankly tells us he attached more value to oral trer3itieu than to written documents" such as Matthew and Mark. How could he mean any Such thing when he affirms "that Meek made no mie- take but wrote down accurately whatever he had heard Of Peter's discourses?" What sane man, as Dr. Lightfoot observes, "could prefer a conversation repeated by another to the immediate and direct account of the same events by the person himself ?" And what stupidity it implies on the part of Papias "to prefer the second-hand report of what Matthew had said about the Lord's dis- courses to the account of these discourses which Matthew himself had set down in writing." On the other hand " Papias judged rightly enough that an',' statement of Andrew, of Peter, and of John, or other Apostles and disciples of the Lord would be far more valuable to elucidate his text than anything hemight find in current books." Your readers may see this miserable evasion of the .force of Papias's testimony most completely exposed and 'refuted by Dr. Lightfoot in his" Reply to the Author of Supernatural Religion." Every rag of the argument has been torn to tatters and scattered to the winds by this able critic. This fact is generally acknowledged. Mr. Gandy may seek Consolation from any further source he likes ; I will venture to tell him he will find none. He is sim- ply in a corner, from which there is absolutely no escape. The evidence of Papias is—that down to the middle ,of the 2nd century the Gospels of Matthew and Mark were received by him as the production of these writers, and that this fact was vouched to him on the word of friends of the Apostles, and two disciples of Christ with whom he was intimate. The evidence is decisive ; and I need only refer to Professor Carpenter's remark as quoted by Mr. Gandy touching the" order" of Mark's narrative. "The feature of Mark's version of Peter's recollectiOns was its want of proper arrangement," says Dr. Car- penter, " which must, one would think, impair the accuracw of the record "(the italics are mine.‘ Now I demur to the word" proper" in the above quotation. There is no warrant for it. Mark's object was not to give an exact arrangement of the facts of our Lord's life, but under the guidance of the premised spirit he makes a selection from the discourses which he had'heard from Peter's own lips, and which would be specially suited to the Roman people for whom they were evidently intended (see Dr. Gregory's " Why four Gospels ?") Much less will any one admit that the accuracy of ,a record must needs be impaired—as Dr. Carpenter suggests—because its facts are not related in exact chronological order, I must not trepass further, at present upon your space. In my next letter, Mr. Gandy's equally absurd and illogi- cal handlings of Irenteue and Polycarp shall have a full and due reply.—Yours truly,
JOEIN DIGNUM.
Penketh, 7th April, 1891.

ANE ASSEMBLY HALL FOR WARRINGTON Sir,—Amongst those who take an interest in dramatic and musical performances and social gatherings generally, the question is often discussed, IS A NEW ASSEMBLY HALL NECESSARY?, If any conclusion is arrived at, it is always in the affirmative. And why P. The,o,nly public Hall, available ,for a large concourse of people, is the Hall in Rylands- . street, the property of a Limited Company. An ever-in- creasing population, and a demand for dramatic amuse- ments has subverted or changed the chardcter o, this hall into that of a theatre. By moving in this direction the directors acted according to the best commercial instincts, to Make their investments yield the best pok. sible dividends ; it would have been bad busineato Noe, acted otherWlse. 1 "q-`
WIIAT IS THE CONSEQUENCE:?.

The Public Hall being converted into a theatre, Writ]: fully engaged as such during that part of the year' when popular gatheringsare most common:the public have been and are greatly inconvenienced for the? want of proper accommodation, whether for:moetingsj.c9ncerts, or popular entertainments generally.-- - - --- Theatrical companies engage the Hall some weeks; or months in advance, and, the contra-As" being Sigped, they must be fulfilled. Now, some important local gathering is to be held, it may be political, musical; etc, ; special speakers or artistes are communicated with and engage- meats sought ; their evenings at liberty (upon whiCh the sucOess of the whole thing depends are made known; applications for the hail are mad 6 Ter those parqcular evenings, when, to the annoyance of the managersi they dre InfOrmed tq the secretitry of the Public =1141,1 that the Said dateisk creek ire inipessible, or indeed aAr eveu- ing for several weeks afterwards. The Working-men's Hospital Committee fix upon a

certain date to suit particular artistes, for their annual concert in aid of eur hospital, when they are informed that for such an evening the hall is engaged by some "Music Hall" artistes or some suck company, and another evening must be arranged. Take the case of that memorable week in November last; the Musical society held its concert on the Tuesday, Mr. Pearson's concert was on the Wednesday, and the Parish Church held its annual gathering on,the Thursday evening. The Exchequer of the Musical Society cart bear testimony that this was " bad business." The other two undertakings must have suffered in consequence ; if they did well, it is proof positive that they would have done better, had the interval been greater. If the managers of these entertainments could have acted otherwise, would they have committed themselves to suqh foolish arrangements ?

: THE MUSICAL SOCIETY. This Society has, I believe, a prescriptive right to hold four concerts during the season in the Public Hall. The organ, I may incidentally remark, is the property of the Society, and'hut of the Public Hall, Co., and much good the Society derives from the instrument. It should be in:a hall available for rehearsals, instead of which the *ir is compelled to endure the accompaniments of "a box of whistles " ; enough to produce an epidemic of /a yrißpe. But this is by the way. As a matter of feet, the SOcietrought to be in the position to fix the dates of its ccincerts, so as to suit the character of the compositions to be performed (as one work may require more rehear- sals than another) and the engagements of artistes; but itican do nothing of the land. Four evenings are fixed by the Public Hall Co., which dates are not always tfio most convenient, but they must be taken or let alone. Now, it is unnecessary for me to multiply instances, but I eave others who interest themselves in such matters, to bear testimony as to the truth of my assertions (a) That the engagement of the Public Hall is a difficulty. (b) That this is consequently a source of great
annoyance. .• • (c) That it is a public logs, and in more trays. than owe! It will not be very long before the question will force

itheif to the front— • iARE WE TO HAVE A NEW ASSEMBLY MALL? A Town Hall for the management of municipal busi- ness we have, and one of which we feel proud. I mean al hall capable of seating about 1,600 people, constructed With proper conveniences and affording comfort to audiences, and with the best acoustic effects. The Public Hall, Limited, for popular gatherings is toosmall ; the population has nitgrown it; and as for its con- -veniencies and comforts, why; the least said the better. Does anyone question the truth of this remark? Then lit him take, for any performance, a " Dress seat" ticket and sit in the front row, or a front gallery, and it on the entrance side ; if he has not an attack of the inuffies, he will be fortunate. 1 A Gymnasium is to be built ere long. I have asked Several gentlemen interested whether, or not a large Concert Hall 'could be built over it. The idea, however practical, is not possible;becauSe the Charity Commis- iluogrigeer ss ts iwouldtself n toot ms aen7ttig en scuocrhpaorsapthi oe mn ec.o nAtne ma Ipt ei artneast itvhee rection of New Baths and Washhouses. Is it not possible that over these such an Assembly Room could be built? Any evil effects arising from damp may be dismissed, as not worth consideration. The , suggestion has one great recommendation; and an important `one, viz., that the extra expenditure for a building site would be saved. THE POSITIONS Of', OTHER TOWNS. From a reliable source Of information, I have made' a: list of the towns in England (not including Ireland, Scot- land and Wales), each of which has a Town Hall and the owners of which are" The Corporation." There are 50. I have not included the city of London, nor any part of it under the control ot the County Council. There are 21 ,which possess Halls capable of seating 500 to 900,persons., 24 towns etc., etc., 1,000 te2,000 persons ' 6 IV 1, If t 2 000 and upwards. . There are several towns with a population of 30,000 and less which have Halls capable of seating 1,000 persons. St. Helens, population',s7,ooo ; Rochdale,6B,ooo ; Chorley, 20,000; Congleton,l2,ooo •, Luton, 30,000; Dover,2B,ooo; Barrow-in-Furness, 47,000; these have Corporation Assembly Rooms capable Of seating over 1,000 people'. THE NECESSARY CAPITAL. The Corporation, I am informed, is about to apply for " power " to borrow money for the erection of new Baths and Wash-houses. Now, assuming the idea of erecting, over these, a spacious assembly'. hall is worth consideration, why net Obtain power to borrow an addi- tional £6,000, which, I think, would be sufficient, the land being already provided? The capital of the Public Hall Co., Limited, is £5,500, £4,300 being ndminal capital, and £1,200 a loan, and what is represented bY this amount is common knowledge. Such a building as I suggest, would afford a " seating "for 1,600 persons, and provide an orchestra capable of holding 250 per- formers. I mention this casually, because the active members of the Musical Society now number 160; and next season this will be materially augmented. There are several schools that give annual entertainments. I have seen the children packed most uncomfortably on the stage. Mr. Milton Ray informed me that two-thirds ef his'" property "for " Aladdin " was left at the rail- way station for want of accommodation. I could extend this evidence. The necessary £6,000 could be °Seined at 31 per cent., which would mean £2lO per annum interest on capital ; the cost of "hall keeper " and " gas " would be charged against those hiring the hall. No secretary would bere- quired ; in all such cases applications for the hall are made either to the Borough Treasurer or the Town Clerk. It is self-evident, that with proper management the in- come derived from " letting ' the hall would-cover the interest on the capital, and probably there might be some profit. But the latter is not the main argument. Here, I would state an important fact, that the origi- nal investors in the Public Hall Co., Limited, did not engage in the undertaking seeking any pecuniary ad- vantages, but simply to provide the public with a suit- able assembly- room ; and this room the population has outgrown. Ido not regard this as a question of experiment,nor even as a source of profit; but simply as a question of providing efficient accommodation for popu- lar assemblies, social and intellectual in their character, without being an extra burden upon taxation. The Cor- poration has spent money to less advantage and benefit to the taxpayers, more than once, but never intentionally. The question must be decided upon its merits : (a) Is the present hall suitable to the growth of popu- lation? (b) 13 it available when required? (c) Is it a source of inconvenience and annoyance to the managers of popular gatherings? (d) Could a new assembly hall be built without any additional levy upon the rates? I have only endeavoured to touch the main points of a scheme as it suggests itself to me ; to do more than this was not my intention.=.Apologisin for the length of my letter, I remain yours 'truly, GEORGE WOODS. Lower Walton, March- 31st; 1891. a
t ALLEGED MURDEROUS ASSAULT BY A
WOMAN AT FRODSHAM

At Frodsham Police-Moue, before Mr. A. Thomas, on Monday afternoon, Eliza Mercer WAS charged, on . remand, with having inflicted grievous bodilv.barm on Jane Latham, on the Ist inst. The following evidence in addition to that already reported was given : • Jane Latham, a married woman, wife of John Latham, a labourer, living at Frodsham-quay, said that at noon on the Ist inst., in consequence of what she heard the prisoner say to her husband, she went ' up to her, and asked her to come to her mother-in- law's house: At that time prisoner had a poker in her hand, with which she threatened', to split wit- ness's "flaming". head open if witness did not go away from her door. Witness went in her house, which adjoins the prisoner's, and at night went into the prisoner's house between six and soven and said, Eliza, will you go up to your mother-in-law's, and face this bother out P" Witness turned her back, and pri- soner struck her on the back of the bead with a poker (produced.) She did not fall, and prisoner then pulled her by the right sleeve of her dress, threw her down on the floor, and knelt on her chest. Prisoner struck her with the poker whilst she was on the floor, this time on the front of her head. Witness caught hold of the prisoner by the hair of her head, and pulled herself up, her head at that time bleeding. Prisoner then pushed wit- ness into a rocking chair, and struck her three or four more blows on the head, and also bit her on the left cheek, remarking at the same time "I'll finish you." Witness got away from the prisoner, and in the middle of the floor, prisoner struck her on the back of the head. , Prisoner locked the door, and complainant stood near it, when Mrs. Harvey came up and asked what was the ' matter. Mrs. Twist also came on the scene, and wit- • ness told them what had occurred. After standing on . the quay a minute or two, she fainted, and had since , been attended by Dr. Weaver. Prisoner: I did'nt hit you on the head with a poker. _Did_you not fall against the stairs P—No, I was nevor near the stairs.—Prisoner: There are marks against the I stairs where she fell. Weatherby, stationed at Frodsham, deposed that • 4prehended the prisoner at 5 o'clock in the afternoon .011,041,2nd. inst.. He also took possession of the poker, • and the ,clpthrs the pr?secutrix was wearing, and took - the prisOner to the police station; where the latter, in . answer, to .the .charge, replied that she did not hit tke complainant on the head with the poker; she fell against , the stairs. . Prioner-still maintained that She did not hit com- plainant with the poker. ,or bite her.,-,The prisoner was committed to take her trial on the charge at the • Cheshire Quarter Sessions.

MR. STANLEY?

Henry M. Stanley, the great explorer, was born, at in 1841, and passed his childhood in the Workhouse at St. Asaph He subsequently sailed as, a cabin boy to the New Orleans. where he was adopted by Mr. Stanley, whose name he took, but whose death, not making provision for him, again com- pelled him to start the world on his own account. After a series of adventures,he became
a journalist during the Amen-

attached as reporter to the staff ew York Herald." In 1868 he was sent to accompany the British expedition into Abyssinia, as war correspondent for that paper. Subsequent to this be made a tour to the Black Sea, and thence through Persia into India. In 1869, Livingstone in Africa, had not been heard of for a long time,and Mr. Gordon Bennett, proprietor of the "New York Herald," ordered Stanlv to "go and find him." Early in 1871 Stanley left Zanzibar and plunged into the unknown continent. Before the end of that year he had found Livingstone. In 1873-4 he accompanied the British expedition into Ashanti, up to Kumassi, as a war correspondent again. In 1876 the "New York Herald" and the London "Daily Telegraph" conk-Antly sent him to Central Africa to take up the thread of Livingstone's die- ceveries. He left Zanzibar in that year, and in 1877 emerged on the west coast, having circumna- vigated Victoria Nyanza and forced his way, in spite of terrible obstacles, down the whole course of the hitherto unknown Congo. In 1879, the King of the Belgians gave Stanley the command of an expedition formed by the International African Association, for the purpose of exploring the Congo. Stanley succeeded in planting stations and securing steam navigation upon the upper river' and may be said to have made what is now the Congo Free State. The latest and perhaps the most memorable of Stanley's exploits was the Emin relief expedition, the chequered incidents of which have recently been very forcibly impressed upon the public mind,

AMALGAMATED FRIENDLY SOCIETIES' ' MEDICAL ASSOCIATION. The annual report and statement of accounts of the above-named most useful society, havelust,been issued, and are of a highly satisfactdry character. In the report two years ago, mention was made of an important step which was then about to be taken, namely, the acquisition of the Palmyra Square pro- perty. The present report announees that all that has•now been completed, and that the work of, the Society is going on as satisfactorily as can be de- sired. Every care has been taken for the convenience of patients; and the house so loft that it would be fit for the Medical Officer to reside there. In this property the Committee feel they, have such accommodation, both as a residence for tho doctor, Waiting and consulting- rooms, and surgery, &c., that they cannot well be bettered, if equalled. The report states 'that the total Membership of the Association is now 3,750, divided as follows :—Lodge Members, 1,975 ; dispensary, 1,775. The report of the Medical Officer shows that during the past, year no less than 17,391 prescriptions have been dispensed, 4,909 visits made to patients, and 42 deaths have occurreel. Compared with last year, tke number of prescriptions dispensed have been 419 more ; visits to patients- at their homes 54 less; deaths 1 more. The•financial statement shows an income including cash in the treasurer's hands at the commencement of the year, £27 2s.- 9d.—of £697 es. sd. and an expenditure of £655 16s. 4d., leaving a balance of £4l 10s. id. in hand. A net cash gain of £l4 7s. 4d. in the year is shown, this being most satisfactory considering that £B3- Hs. 2d. haabeen spent in adapting and improving the Association's property. Mr. Wm. Bibby is the secretary of the Association, Mr. Alban Stirrup,treasurer; Mr. Joseph AlbinsOn is president, and Mr. Geo.l4oughley is vice-president.

MR. JOHN MORLEY.
Mr. John Morley made a Parliamentary reputa- on with an astounding rapidity, and is the first

instance on record of a man stepping from an editor's desk to a seat in the Cabinet. Mr. Morley was born) in Black- .4l burn in 1838. He went to Cheltenham and afterwards to • Lincoln College, Oxford, at neither of which, like others who had risen, did he give a • signs of his future greatness ,and went up to London to try his ack letters. Partial friends told him he had "style," and style at three-and-twenty, is rare. He turned the " style " on with effect in the "Literary Gazette "and was" everything in turns and noth- ing long," equally at home in cutting up an old author and slashing a new play. This skill in the literary c3rving line was noticed by Mr. Cook, the famous editor of the "Saturday Review,' and it was a proud day for Mr. Morley when he read his first " middle*" in that famous weekly. Then Mr. Morley published a stray volume or two of the "Saturday Review" essays, was called to the bar, and succeeded Mr. Lewes as editor of the" Fort- nightly Review." He made the "Fortnightly" a famous and powerful organ for the promulgation of certain creeds. He read law with his friend Mr. Flrederic Harrison, but never practised, and for a time retired to the country, when he wrote his virell-known works on Voltaire, Diderot, Rousseau, be, sides his volume on "Compromise." He was in 1869 an unsuccessful candidate for Blackburn, and in 1880, was also unsuccesful for Westminster. He became editor of the "Pall Mall Gazette," and ShilSt editing that paper, wrote his "Life of Cob- deu':-"- lie was ambitious for Parliamentary honour, and in 1883, his chance came, for lie was elected in that 'year for Newcastle-on-Tyne. When Mr. Glad; stone propounded his Home Rule scheme, he found in Mr. Morley one of his ablest and most enthusias- tic supporters. Mr. Morley was for a time Chief Secretary of Ireland.

div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.

ANOTHER FATAL ACCIDENT, AT RUNCORN. „ Yesterday, Harry Ankers, a young man employed im the Ship Canal Works at Runcorn, was killed. He was employed in assistini, the pile-driving opera- tinn when the pin which held the wheel of the ulley broke and fell, striking Ankers on the head and knocking him into the river. The wheel re- bounded from the platform,and again struck Ankers :while he was in the water. .He was picked up in pan unconscious condition, bleeding from the head nnil mouth, and was at once conveyed to Latchford Hospital, where he died shortly after his arriYal. MANCHESTER CORPORATION'S BILL. An application, has been lodged in the Private Bill Office of the House of Commons for leave to deposit a petition for a Bill providing ' for additional capital for the completion of the Manchester Ship Canal. The ap- plication— called a "petition. "—sets forth the history ,of the undertaking. It added that the Council -and the !ratepayers have sanctioned the promotion of the Bill. :The petition is signed on behalf of the Corporation by the Mayor and the Town Clerk of Manchester, and by, I.Sir Joseph Lee, Mr. J. K. Bythell, and the Secretary of the Ship Canal Company. DECISION OF THE STANDING ORDERS COMMITTEE. Yesterday afternoon the Committee, without hearing any arguments, declined to dispense with the usual standing orders, and the Bill will now be taken before Parliament in the ordinary course. SALFORD PROVIDES £1,000,000. The ratepayers of Salford at a meeting held on Mon- day night decided by a large majority in favour of the Corporation endeavouring to give financial assistance to Manchester Ship Canal Company. In the resolution which was adopted it was stimulated that the amount to be provided by Salford should not exceed a million at the utmost. It is expected that if the million is given the Salford ratepayers will be allowed one representative on the directorate of the company. A GERMAN SHIP CANAL. Noticing the opening- of the North Sea and Baltic Canal, the "Daily Chronicle" observes: A work of immense importance to Germany was formally inaugu- rated en Monday with an absence of fuss and ceremony that is quite refreshing in an age ever-much given to making ceremonial mountains out of utilitarian mole- hills. The work in question was the piercing of the last dim that kept the waters of the North Sea from meeting those Of the Baltic. The scheme, after having been long projected in Germany, was actually begun nearly four years ago, when the first Emperor William was on the throne. Its purpose is two-fold—to facilitate commerce between the two Northern Seas, and—which perhaps should have been placed first—to aid the work of Ger- man coast defence. The canal runs from Kiel Bay to the inkuth of the Elbe, crossing Schleswig-Holstein by way of Rendsburg. Its actual length is sixty-one miles, and it has a surface width of 196 feet, which shelves down to 85 feet at the bed, with a depth of 28- feet. It is thus adapted for the passage of the largest ships of war, which it is calculated will be able to steam from Kiel Bay to the Elbe, including passing through the two decks, one at each end, in something like eight hours. , 'OE OUTRAGE ON THE SHIP CANAL WORKS. At Cheshire Quarter Sessions on Thursday the Grand Silty ignored the bill against the youth John Samuel Fleicher, charged with inflicting bodily harm by pour- ing a quantity ot lucigen oil down the chimney of a fire in a cabin on the Ship Canal works at Fiodsbam, whereby tWo lads *ere'burnei seriously. They also ex- pressed a unanimous opinion that the Canal Company were much to blame for the carelesi manner in which lucigen oil was stored and controlled-at the c?.aal. _ TENKETII. TAKING THE CENSUS. 7. On Monday, the enumerators for Sankey and Penketh, viz., Messrs. B. Hobson, F. Hughes, and J; A. Travers, were busily engaged collecting the schedules for the census. Commencing early in the morning, they were employed all day, audit was about 6 p.m. before the collection was completed.; Mr. Hobson (the registrar) and all the other enum- erators agree that the duty they hadlo perform was a very pleasant one, as during the whole day they were courteously received by every one, no disagreeable remarks of any kind being made.. Several amusing incidents occurred during the day.. At one house where the enumerater called the paper had been mislaid, and they could be heard asking the various members of the family what had become of that " skeddil." One woman, in filling up the paper, had described herself as a "widower' with five children, and then' proceeded to put the names and ages of the children all across the page, instead of filling in the various colums as required by the law. In several papers crosses had been put in all the three columns headed. " Employer," "Employed," and" Neither employer nor employed, &c. Notwithstanding a number-of slight mistakes such as the above, the majority of the 'papers are most correctly done. Daniel Rogers, Statham., 463-; James Gibbon' Camsley, 439: The three first are there-- fore elected. Mr. Rogers is an old member' .and Messrs. Holt and Whitelegg, are new members of the Board. Hugh Cameron was the•returning officer. There was &- good poll. SATURDAY NIGIIT PENNY- CONCERTS.—OU Saturday- night the closing concert of the season was eren. The' programme was provided by Mrs. Fox, and' notwith-- standing the inclement weather, the room was well tilled at the time of commencement. Mr. R. A. Naylor, of Thelwall,occupied the chair,and gave the customary short- temperance address. The following took part in render- ing an excellent programme :—Miss M. Fox, Miss lardine, - Misses Warburton. Dr. and Mrs. Williamson, Miss E.. Todhunter, Miss Macpherson, Mr. J. T. Hall, Mr. F. Morris, Mr. Mort, and Miss Pothecary. VOLUNTEERS.—The financial position of the H (Lyrnm) - Company of the Volunteers is at present in a most satis- factory condition. The aceounts -of the financial year have been made up to March 31; and show a balance in favour of the company of £59 16i. 4a. Consideringthat some five years ago the company was in debt to the extent of £447 4s. 21d., the management which has placed it ID. its present position is to be highly congratulated. In 1887, by a determined effort, £225 4s. 1.00. was paid off. In 1888 the sum of £73 9s. I.ld. was paid: 1889, £72 9s. -7a4, 1890, £56 12s. 4d. ; and the residue of £l9 7s. 6d. wag paid off this year, leaving, as we have said, a balance in- Parr's Bank to the credit of the company of £59 16s. 4d. CONGREGATIONAL BAND OF HOPE.—The last public meeting and entertainment of the session was held on , Monday evening in the schoolroom.. There was a cark- tal attendance, the pastor (the Rev. Charles Clay) occu- , pying the chair. A programme of special merit was - submitted. Mr. George Manning gave an address recom- mending the adoption of temperance principles. A. number of recitations and songs were also given by the members and friends. A dozen of the Band of Hope boyS, gave a piece in character, entitled "The Little workers. 7 The special feature of the entertainment was the render- ' ing of the "Flower Queen's Court,". consisting of the queen and her 18 flower nymphs. The Chairman distri- buted a aumber of handsome prima to the reciters during the evening. The society has had r a very successful) season, the membership having been considerably In- creased.

div.head: NEW RAILWAY AT WIRRINGITONi•
div.p: THE NEW RAILWAY AT WIRRINGITONi•

Thepromoters of the Lancashire, Derbyshire, and Bast Coast Railway have decided to make some :alteraticns in their original plans as they related to ' the Warington end of the railway. ,It was at fir'st, 'proposed that the main line should be carried twice 'across Knutsford-road on bridges:so as to reach the ' :proposed new docks, but now it has been decided tO ‘ruu the main line straight across Wilderspool MOW. !Claws to the station behind St. James's Church. Coro4' munications will, howeVer, stilYbe maintained .with the docks by means of a branch or sidina,which will , diverge from the main line near Wilderspool, and ,by means of which coal and other ,commodities ' will be carried straight to .the clocks. There are one or two advantages to commend this variation on the original plans. In the first place, only one bridge will be needed to cross Wilderspool Cause- way instead of two as formerly intended, and in the second place this new arrangement will pre, serve a good deal of the Causeway frontage for building purposes, which, had the original scheme been carried out, would have been entirely spoiled . for that purpose. The Bill that is being promoted by the Company is expected to come before the Parliamentary Com- mittee next Wednesday. The Mayor (Alderman Francorab), Alderman Burgess, Mr. George WoodSt and Mr. W. Walker (of the firm of Messrs. Walker and Company, brewers), will give evidence beforo- the Committee in favour of the Bill.

div.head: DRUNK IN CHARGE OF A HORSE.
div.p: DRUNK IN CHARGE OF A HORSE.

A DISASTROUS STREET COLLISION. At the Warrington Police Court, yesterday, WM.,: Shutfleton and Frank Cachinello were charged wit°. being drunk in charge of a horse, in front of the Police- Station, at a quarterto nine the previoits. night,. also with running on the wrong side of the road.. Inspector Cox said at the time mentioned Ile was in the Police Station, and heard a tremendous crash in the street in front. He, Sergeant Chand,lol.9 and PX.Phillip ran out,and saw the two defendalts drunk in charge of a horse and gig, coming from the direction of Church-st., and oa the wrong side a the road. They ran into a landau: coming in the oprxiit° direction. and .the nhaft.. . the— gig ran the- ihmdau horse's breast, to the length nearly two feet. Witness, here produced the broken shaft. The horse was- not killed, because the shaft did not penetrate the arteries ; and the ,far- rier thought he would be-able to bring the horse round:. Shuffleton was driving. Both the gig and the landau belonged to Mr. McGill, cab proprkatO, the defendants having hired the gig from • hire' —Polite-Sergeant Chandler , deposed to taking the • shaft out of the animal's breast. The horse was now do- ing, fairly well.—The driver of the tandau said the defor dents were going at the rate a 13 miles an hour, ,and he •at the rate of six miles an hour. The shaft of the gig; struck the horse, penetrating it, and it fell. Air• Peter Robinson broueht songetow out and stopped the bleeding. Mr. Shawcross, •7seterinary surgeon„ apd Air. Dixon came, and amongst themitkey got the horse house; —Shuffieten said he was turning out of Fenn:2-st., the horse suddenly junaped and got out of his .contrc.),`, when the collision occurxed.—Sergeant Chandler Slitifileten had been locked ap because ho.Alsod varld: impudent language to bins, swore at him, all; threatened him. He took:outi his horse and vranteav:: run it against the °Ulm, poor animal.--SheAgoa fined 40s. and costs, in .default two months:: dimprov--- want, and Cachinello was fined ss. and costa.

A TOWN LOOTED BY SLAVES. --- A Zanzibar correspondent telegraphs that H.M.S. Red- breast brings news from Zambesi and Johanna Island, that the French resident in the Comores tried to land at Johanna recently, but armed slaves lined the beach and the resident returned. A French man-of-war after two hours' notice fired five or six shots into the town. British- merchants took refuge in ships in harbour. The Preach left without landing. The slaves then looted the !Own, causing loss to British-Indian subjects, and the Island is now held by armed slaves. MURDER OF A WIFE AT PORTS- MOUTH. On Saturday afternoon a naval pensioner, named tlaward Henry Fawcett Watts, 38 years of age, who had Zen separated from his wife, went to a house where she 'as staying with her parents, at Stamshaw, an outlying hurb of Portsmouth, and, it is believed, endeavoured to ....Induce her to resume cohabitation. Failing in this he '°lc out a six-chambered revolver and fired at her. The stihots took effect in the hes,d,throat,and right breast, and sound to instantaneous. When arrested Watts was he to be bleeding from a wound in the left wrist,whicla 01 accidentally inflicted upon himself, but the injury is a trifling character. Mrs. Watts was about 311 years Of age, and the mother of several children. Watts was 'n_der the influence of drink when he commit ted the erune.
